stem: A security team needs VPC Flow Logs delivered to a third-party SIEM in near real time via a streaming pipeline, while a separate compliance team needs the same flow log data retained cheaply for seven years and queried occasionally with Amazon Athena. Which two flow log destinations should be configured to meet both needs? (Select TWO)

choices.text: CloudWatch Logs only, used for both streaming and retention
Data Firehose streaming to the SIEM
AWS Config, for long-term retention and Athena querying
Amazon S3 with Athena for retention
AWS CloudTrail, for both real-time streaming and long-term retention

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Data Firehose streams flow logs to the SIEM in near real time, and S3 with Athena provides low-cost long-term retention and querying.

Why the other options are wrong:
• CloudWatch Logs for both: costly retention and not a streaming pipeline to the SIEM.
• Config: configuration, not flow logs.
• CloudTrail: API calls.

Key takeaway: stream to SIEM + archive in S3.

stem: A company must ensure that a set of VPCs handling PCI-regulated workloads can never establish direct network connectivity to a set of general-purpose VPCs, even though both sets are attached to the same Transit Gateway and occasionally need to reach a shared services VPC. How should Transit Gateway route tables be designed?

choices.text: Disable route propagation on the Transit Gateway and segment only with VPC-level network ACLs
Attach the PCI VPCs to a separate Transit Gateway and copy security group rules between them manually
Separate TGW route tables; only shared-services routes propagate to both
Use one Transit Gateway route table for all attachments and block PCI traffic with security groups alone

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Separate TGW route tables let PCI attachments learn only shared-services routes, so PCI VPCs have no route to non-PCI VPCs.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Disable propagation without separation: doesn't isolate.
• Separate TGW copying SGs: SGs don't control TGW routing.
• One table with blocking: fragile.

Key takeaway: segmentation on TGW = route table association/propagation.

stem: A SaaS provider runs its service behind a Network Load Balancer in its own VPC and wants customer VPCs in other AWS accounts to privately consume the service without VPC peering, without traffic ever traversing the public internet, and while retaining full control over which consumer accounts can connect. Which architecture should they implement?

choices.text: A gateway VPC endpoint for the NLB, shared to consumer accounts through AWS RAM
An NLB-backed endpoint service with consumer interface endpoints
A public ALB restricted by security groups to each customer's NAT gateway IP
VPC peering with every consumer VPC, advertising the NLB's private IP over BGP

explanation:
Why this is correct:
An NLB-backed endpoint service lets consumer VPCs create interface endpoints, exposing only the service privately.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Gateway endpoint for an NLB: gateway endpoints are only for S3 and DynamoDB.
• Public ALB: internet exposure.
• Peering with every consumer: exposes networks.

Key takeaway: private SaaS exposure → PrivateLink.

stem: A cloud security team wants to periodically scan an entire AWS Organization's VPCs to proactively find any unintended network paths that violate a defined security posture, for example any path allowing internet access to a database tier, rather than testing one specific source-destination pair at a time. Which tool is better suited to this broader, policy-based discovery compared to testing individual paths?

choices.text: AWS Config conformance packs alone, without network path analysis
Reachability Analyzer run manually for every pair of ENIs in the organization
Network Access Analyzer with defined access scopes
Amazon CloudWatch Network Monitor probes

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Network Access Analyzer evaluates network paths against defined access scopes (for example, internet to sensitive subnets) across VPCs to find unintended access.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Conformance packs: no path analysis.
• Reachability Analyzer per pair: not scalable.
• Network Monitor: performance probes.

Key takeaway: find unintended network paths → Network Access Analyzer.

stem: A startup needs encrypted connectivity from its office to a VPC this week, with about 200 Mbps of unpredictable traffic, while it evaluates Direct Connect over the next quarter. Which option fits, and what is its main limitation?

choices.text: Site-to-Site VPN; each tunnel tops out around 1.25 Gbps
VPC peering to the office network over the internet
A dedicated 10 Gbps Direct Connect port, which is always cheaper than VPN
A hosted Direct Connect connection, which encrypts traffic by default

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Site-to-Site VPN is IPsec-encrypted, can be set up in minutes with no long-term commitment, and easily carries 200 Mbps. Its main limit is per-tunnel throughput (about 1.25 Gbps) over the variable internet path.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Dedicated 10 Gbps DX: takes weeks to provision, and port hours are costly for 200 Mbps.
• Hosted DX: not encrypted by default, and provisioning takes time through a partner.
• VPC peering: connects VPCs only, not on-premises networks.

Key takeaway: fast, encrypted, low commitment → VPN; consistent high bandwidth → Direct Connect.

stem: A company runs many EC2 instances in private subnets that make frequent calls to Amazon S3 and DynamoDB, currently routed through a NAT Gateway. The monthly bill shows a significant NAT Gateway data processing charge. What is the most effective way to reduce this specific cost while keeping the traffic off the public internet?

choices.text: Replace the NAT gateway with a NAT instance
Add multiple Elastic IP addresses to the NAT gateway to spread the load
Gateway endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB to bypass the NAT
Interface endpoints (PrivateLink) for S3 and DynamoDB, cheaper than NAT

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Gateway endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB route that traffic privately, bypassing NAT processing charges.

Why the other options are wrong:
• NAT instance: still in the path.
• More EIPs: no cost reduction.
• Interface endpoints cheaper than gateway: gateway endpoints are free.

Key takeaway: S3/DynamoDB → gateway endpoints.

stem: A security engineer configures an AWS Network Firewall policy with a stateless default action of aws:forward_to_sfe, plus a stateless rule group containing one rule that matches TCP traffic on destination port 443 with the action aws:pass. After deployment, outbound HTTPS connections from the protected subnet initiate successfully, but responses from the internet never arrive and the connections eventually time out. What is the most likely cause and correct fix?

choices.text: Stateless rule groups cannot match TCP 443; only stateful groups match ports.
aws:pass skips state tracking, so return traffic misses; forward to a stateful PASS rule.
The firewall subnet's route table lacks a route back to the internet gateway, black-holing replies.
Network Firewall needs a NAT gateway in the firewall subnet for TLS handshakes to complete.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A stateless pass action forwards packets without state tracking, so return traffic isn't recognized as part of the flow. Forward traffic to the stateful engine (aws:forward_to_sfe) so return traffic is handled.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Stateless can't match 443: it can.
• Missing route: not indicated.
• NAT for TLS: not required.

Key takeaway: use stateful inspection for bidirectional flows.

stem: A company has Shield Advanced on an internet-facing ALB and wants automatic application-layer DDoS mitigation, with rules created and removed during attacks without manual work. What is required?

choices.text: Put the ALB behind CloudFront, since automatic L7 mitigation works only there
Associate a WAF web ACL with the ALB and enable automatic mitigation
Use a fixed target group without Auto Scaling
Disable AWS WAF, since Shield Advanced replaces its rule engine

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Shield Advanced's automatic application layer mitigation places rules in a WAF web ACL associated with the protected resource. Without a web ACL on the ALB, it has nowhere to put mitigation rules.

Why the other options are wrong:
• CloudFront only: ALBs are supported when a web ACL is associated.
• Disabling WAF: removes the mechanism mitigation depends on.
• Fixed target group: unrelated to mitigation.

Key takeaway: Shield Advanced L7 auto-mitigation = rules inside your WAF web ACL.

stem: A team requests a public ACM certificate for use with an Application Load Balancer and wants the certificate to renew automatically without manual intervention indefinitely, as long as the underlying domain configuration remains unchanged. Which validation method should they choose, and why?

choices.text: Either method renews identically.
DNS validation, renewed automatically while the CNAME remains.
HTTP validation, since ALB certificates renew only when validated by an HTTP token.
Email validation, the only method that renews without any customer action.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
DNS validation renews automatically as long as the validation CNAME stays in DNS.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Identical renewal: email needs action.
• HTTP validation for ALB: not the ACM method here.
• Email renews without action: it needs approval.

Key takeaway: auto-renewing ACM → DNS validation.

stem: A security team receives hundreds of GuardDuty findings daily in 30 accounts. It wants only findings with severity 7 or higher to page on-call immediately, and lower findings to go to a ticket queue. Which design fits?

choices.text: EventBridge rules with numeric severity filters routing to different targets
A CloudWatch metric filter on the GuardDuty console log
Configure GuardDuty in each account to generate only findings with severity 7 or higher
Security Hub's built-in paging for high findings

explanation:
Why this is correct:
GuardDuty publishes findings to EventBridge. Numeric matching on detail.severity (for example, ≥7) routes high findings to a paging target and lower ones to a ticketing target. With a delegated administrator, findings arrive centrally.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Only high findings: GuardDuty can't be limited this way; suppression rules archive, not route.
• Console log metric filter: there's no such log to filter.
• Security Hub paging: no built-in paging; it also emits to EventBridge.

Key takeaway: route findings by severity with EventBridge content filtering.

stem: A team implemented a CIS AWS Foundations Benchmark-aligned control that should alert whenever the IAM root user is used. They created a CloudWatch Logs metric filter matching userIdentity.type = Root against a log group and attached an alarm, but the alarm never enters ALARM state even during a verified root login test. The CloudTrail trail is confirmed to be logging management events correctly to an S3 bucket. What is the MOST likely cause?

choices.text: The metric filter's default value is 0
GuardDuty must be enabled before metric filters can process CloudTrail events
The metric filter pattern uses invalid JSON path syntax
The trail doesn't deliver to the filter's log group

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A metric filter only sees events in its log group. If the trail doesn't deliver to that log group, the filter never matches.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Default value 0: doesn't prevent matches.
• GuardDuty prerequisite: unrelated.
• Invalid JSON path: possible, but the delivery gap is the likely cause here.

Key takeaway: metric filters need the trail to deliver to that log group.

stem: A company operates workloads across 6 AWS Regions and wants a single dashboard showing Security Hub findings from all Regions without manually switching Region in the console. Which approach requires the LEAST ongoing operational effort?

choices.text: Review each Region's Security Hub console manually every day
A Lambda function per Region that forwards GetFindings results via SNS to a central account
Enable Security Hub in each Region with cross-Region aggregation into one Region
Export each Region's findings to a shared S3 bucket and build a QuickSight dashboard

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Enable Security Hub in each Region and use cross-Region aggregation into one Region for a single dashboard.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Manual review: tedious.
• Custom forwarders: unnecessary.
• S3 export with QuickSight: custom build.

Key takeaway: multi-Region findings → cross-Region aggregation.

stem: A security lead wants a dashboard view in Security Hub showing which 10 resources have the most failed high-severity findings across all accounts, updated automatically. Which feature fits?

choices.text: A security standard enabled for the organization
An automation rule that suppresses low-severity findings
A custom insight grouping filtered findings by resource ID
A custom action that sends findings to EventBridge

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Insights are saved queries that group findings by an attribute. A custom insight filtered to failed high-severity findings and grouped by resource ID shows the most affected resources, updating as findings change.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Custom action: sends selected findings to EventBridge; not a view.
• Automation rule: modifies findings, such as suppressing them; not reporting.
• Standard: generates findings; doesn't aggregate them by resource.

Key takeaway: 'group findings by X' = insight.

stem: A security team wants only GuardDuty findings with a severity of 7.0 or higher to trigger a Slack notification via AWS Chatbot, while lower-severity findings should only be stored in Security Hub for periodic review. Which design meets this requirement most efficiently?

choices.text: An EventBridge rule filtering GuardDuty findings on severity >= 7, to SNS/Chatbot
Configure GuardDuty to generate only findings with severity 7.0 or higher
A metric filter on the GuardDuty console audit log that detects severity 7.0 findings
Security Hub's default notification feature, which already filters by severity threshold

explanation:
Why this is correct:
An EventBridge rule with a numeric filter on detail.severity (≥ 7) routes only high-severity findings to the Slack target.

Why the other options are wrong:
• GuardDuty can't be limited: no such setting.
• Metric filter on console logs: not a thing.
• Security Hub default notifications: not built-in filtering to Slack.

Key takeaway: route by severity with EventBridge filters.

stem: A security team in a central security-tooling account wants to receive GuardDuty and Security Hub findings from 40 member accounts in near real time for automated triage, without granting the central account broad cross-account IAM read access into each member account. Which architecture best satisfies this while minimizing per-account maintenance?

choices.text: Each account writes findings to a local bucket, polled hourly with Athena from the tooling account
A central event bus with an org PutEvents policy and forwarding rules via StackSets
Each account assumes a role in the tooling account and pushes findings via GetFindings on a schedule
Security Hub aggregation only

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A central event bus with a resource policy allowing the organization to PutEvents, plus forwarding rules in each account, centralizes findings.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Local buckets polled hourly: slow.
• Assume roles to push: complex.
• Security Hub aggregation only: covers Security Hub, not every source here.

Key takeaway: cross-account events → central bus + org policy.

stem: After a GuardDuty finding indicates a potential backdoor on an EC2 instance, the security team wants GuardDuty to automatically scan the instance's attached EBS volumes for malware when specific finding types occur, without manually invoking a scan each time. Which GuardDuty feature should they enable?

choices.text: GuardDuty Malware Protection for EC2
GuardDuty S3 Protection
Amazon Inspector network reachability analysis
GuardDuty RDS Protection

explanation:
Why this is correct:
GuardDuty Malware Protection for EC2 scans the instance's EBS volumes when suspicious activity is detected.

Why the other options are wrong:
• S3 Protection: S3 access.
• Inspector reachability: network exposure.
• RDS Protection: database logins.

Key takeaway: scan for malware on EC2 → Malware Protection for EC2.

stem: A security architect is deciding whether to rely on Security Hub's aggregated finding view versus having analysts check the GuardDuty, Macie, and Inspector consoles individually each day. What is the PRIMARY tradeoff introduced by relying solely on individual service consoles instead of Security Hub?

choices.text: GuardDuty, Macie, and Inspector generate no findings unless Security Hub is enabled first
No single normalized view, so cross-service correlations are easier to miss
Individual service consoles do not support IAM permissions
Individual consoles show only 24 hours of findings, while Security Hub keeps them indefinitely

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Without a normalized, aggregated view, analysts must correlate findings across separate consoles, which is slower and misses cross-service patterns.

Why the other options are wrong:
• No findings without Security Hub: services generate findings independently.
• Consoles lack IAM: false.
• 24-hour history: false.

Key takeaway: aggregation speeds triage.

stem: A team publishes a custom CloudWatch metric named GuardDutyHighSeverityCount from a Lambda function triggered by EventBridge whenever a High severity GuardDuty finding occurs. The associated alarm uses a 5-minute evaluation period and a threshold of 1. During periods with zero findings, the alarm shows INSUFFICIENT_DATA instead of OK, confusing stakeholders reviewing dashboards. What change addresses this without weakening detection?

choices.text: Change the metric's unit from Count to None
Delete the alarm and rely on the Security Hub console for severity review
Raise the alarm threshold to 2 to avoid triggering on isolated findings
Set the alarm to treat missing data as notBreaching (OK) instead of insufficient

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A metric published only when findings occur has no data otherwise. Treating missing data as notBreaching keeps the alarm OK between findings.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Change the unit: unrelated.
• Delete the alarm: loses alerting.
• Raise threshold: may miss single high findings.

Key takeaway: sparse metrics → set missing data behavior.

stem: A SOC currently receives separate pages for an unauthorized API call alarm and a root account usage alarm, which frequently fire together during the same incident and cause alert fatigue. Which CloudWatch feature lets the team page on-call staff only once when both underlying alarms are in ALARM state simultaneously, while still preserving each individual alarm for historical review?

choices.text: A CloudWatch composite alarm combining both alarms with AND logic
Merging both metric filters into one saved Logs Insights query
CloudWatch anomaly detection bands applied to both metrics
Reducing the evaluation period of both alarms to 1 minute

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A composite alarm with AND logic pages once when both alarms are in ALARM together, reducing duplicate pages.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Merged query: not an alarm.
• Anomaly bands: don't combine alarms.
• Shorter periods: more noise.

Key takeaway: reduce correlated pages → composite alarms.

stem: A trail logs default events. During an incident, the team can see who changed a bucket policy but not who downloaded objects from the bucket. Why, and how is it fixed?

choices.text: Downloads are management events that expire after 24 hours
Object reads are logged only when S3 Versioning is enabled on the bucket
CloudTrail never logs S3 activity; use VPC Flow Logs
Object reads are data events; enable S3 data events (selector)

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Bucket policy changes are management (control plane) events, logged by default. Object-level reads (GetObject) are data events, logged only when enabled, preferably with advanced event selectors scoped to the relevant buckets to control cost.

Why the other options are wrong:
• 24-hour expiry: management events are kept 90 days in event history and indefinitely in a trail.
• Never logs S3: data events do exactly this.
• Versioning: unrelated to logging.

Key takeaway: control plane = management events; object or item operations = data events.

stem: A company wants CloudTrail visibility into S3 object-level API calls such as GetObject and PutObject for forensic readiness, but is concerned about cost because data events are billed per event and the environment has extremely high S3 request volume across 200 buckets, only 5 of which hold sensitive regulated data. What is the MOST cost-effective way to achieve the required visibility?

choices.text: Disable data events and rely on management events for forensic investigations
Enable data events for all S3 buckets in the trail
Advanced event selectors scoped to the 5 regulated buckets
Enable data events only in the Region with the highest request volume

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Advanced event selectors can limit S3 data events to the five regulated buckets, controlling cost while keeping forensic detail.

Why the other options are wrong:
• No data events: loses object-level visibility.
• All buckets: high cost.
• One Region: incomplete.

Key takeaway: scope data events with advanced selectors.

stem: A VPC Flow Log record shows source 203.0.113.5, destination 10.0.1.20, srcport 443, dstport 51000, protocol 6 (TCP), action REJECT. The instance owning the destination ENI has a security group allowing inbound TCP on ephemeral ports from anywhere. What is the most likely reason this traffic was rejected, and what should the analyst check next?

choices.text: The security group is stateless and blocked the return traffic; make it stateful.
Flow logs never record REJECT for traffic a security group allows, so this is a logging error.
Likely the NACL; flow logs don't say which layer rejected.
The traffic was blocked automatically by AWS Shield Advanced.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Return traffic to an ephemeral port was rejected. Security groups are stateful and allow it, so the likely cause is a NACL. Flow logs don't say which layer rejected.

Why the other options are wrong:
• SG stateless: false.
• Never REJECT when SG allows: NACL can reject.
• Shield blocked it: not how flow logs show it.

Key takeaway: REJECT on return traffic → suspect NACLs.

stem: During an investigation, an analyst cannot find any VPC Flow Log records showing DNS query traffic between an EC2 instance and the VPC's default Amazon-provided DNS resolver at the .2 address, even though the flow log is confirmed ACTIVE and capturing the ALL traffic type. What is the correct explanation?

choices.text: Change the flow log's traffic type filter from ALL to DNS to capture this traffic
Flow logs exclude Amazon DNS traffic; use Resolver query logging
The capture interval missed the DNS packets because they use UDP
DNS traffic appears only in flow logs delivered to S3, not CloudWatch Logs

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Flow logs don't capture traffic to the Amazon-provided DNS resolver. Use Route 53 Resolver query logging for DNS visibility.

Why the other options are wrong:
• DNS traffic filter: not an option.
• UDP missed: not the reason.
• S3-only: false.

Key takeaway: DNS visibility → Resolver query logs.

stem: A security team needs to determine which IAM principal performed a specific S3 PutObject call on a sensitive bucket, including the caller's source IP and whether MFA was used during the session. Which logging mechanism should they rely on primarily, and why?

choices.text: VPC Flow Logs, which log the source IP of every S3 API call
CloudTrail S3 data events (full userIdentity, session, MFA)
S3 server access logs, which include the full principal ARN and MFA status for every request
AWS Config history, which tracks all changes to S3 object ACLs

explanation:
Why this is correct:
CloudTrail S3 data events record the full userIdentity, session context, and MFA status for PutObject.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Flow logs: IPs only.
• Server access logs: less identity detail.
• Config: configuration, not object writes.

Key takeaway: who wrote an object → CloudTrail data events.

stem: A company wants Macie to automatically and periodically re-scan only S3 buckets tagged Classification=Confidential for newly added objects containing PII, rather than performing a single one-time scan of the entire account. Which Macie configuration achieves this?

choices.text: A GuardDuty S3 Protection finding filter on the Classification tag
A one-time classification job with bucket criteria on the Classification tag
A recurring Macie job scoped by the tag, scanning new or changed objects
Automated sensitive data discovery, which always scans every bucket regardless of tags

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A recurring (scheduled) Macie classification job scoped by the Classification=Confidential tag rescans those buckets, including new or changed objects.

Why the other options are wrong:
• GuardDuty filter: not classification.
• One-time job: not periodic.
• Automated discovery: samples broadly, not a tag-scoped rescan.

Key takeaway: targeted periodic scans → scheduled Macie jobs.

stem: Which two statements correctly describe Amazon Macie's sensitive data discovery capabilities? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Macie can scan only objects smaller than 1 KB
Automated discovery samples S3 objects account-wide without a scoped job
Macie remediates public buckets automatically by applying Block Public Access
Macie encrypts S3 objects at rest as part of its scanning process
Jobs can be scheduled and scoped by bucket tag or name

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Automated discovery samples objects across the account continuously, and classification jobs can be scheduled and scoped by bucket tags or names.

Why the other options are wrong:
• 1 KB limit: false.
• Auto-remediates public buckets: Macie reports, doesn't fix.
• Encrypts objects: false.

Key takeaway: Macie = discovery and classification, not remediation.

stem: A security group's inbound rules changed unexpectedly, opening port 22 to 0.0.0.0/0. AWS Config is enabled and recording this resource type. Which Config capability lets an analyst see exactly when the rule changed, what the previous configuration was, and, via CloudTrail integration, which principal made the API call?

choices.text: Config's proactive compliance evaluation mode
Config conformance packs
Config aggregators
The resource's Config timeline, linked to CloudTrail events

explanation:
Why this is correct:
The resource's Config timeline shows configuration changes over time and links to the CloudTrail events that made them.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Proactive mode: pre-deployment checks.
• Conformance packs: rule bundles.
• Aggregators: multi-account views.

Key takeaway: what changed and who → Config timeline + CloudTrail.

stem: A company wants a single account to view AWS Config compliance status and resource configuration data across 50 member accounts and 3 Regions, without needing to assume a role into each account manually. Which Config feature should be used?

choices.text: CloudTrail Lake federated queries across all accounts
Config rules deployed in the central account for each member account's resources
Security Hub aggregation, which aggregates Config data natively without an aggregator
A Config aggregator in the central account using the Organizations source

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A Config aggregator using the Organizations source collects compliance and configuration data from all member accounts.

Why the other options are wrong:
• CloudTrail Lake federated queries: API activity.
• Rules in the central account: evaluate only that account.
• Security Hub native aggregation of Config data: not a replacement.

Key takeaway: multi-account Config view → aggregator.

stem: Which two statements about CloudTrail Insights are correct? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Insight events go to the trail's destinations and can trigger EventBridge rules
Insights also analyzes VPC Flow Log traffic patterns in addition to API calls
Insights needs manual numeric thresholds per API operation before it detects anomalies
Insights baselines management activity and flags significant deviations
Insights requires S3 data events to be enabled for at least one resource type

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Insights baselines normal management activity and flags significant deviations, and Insights events are delivered to trail destinations and EventBridge.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Analyzes Flow Logs: no.
• Manual thresholds: no.
• Requires S3 data events: no.

Key takeaway: CloudTrail Insights = baseline + anomalies on management events.

stem: A newly created CloudTrail trail shows logging enabled in the console, but no log files have appeared in the target S3 bucket after several hours, and CloudTrail's error notifications indicate Access Denied. The bucket was created manually rather than through the CloudTrail console wizard. What is the most likely root cause?

choices.text: The trail's log file prefix contains an invalid character
The bucket policy doesn't allow CloudTrail PutObject and GetBucketAcl
The trail's KMS key has been disabled
Trails created via the CLI cannot deliver to manually created buckets

explanation:
Why this is correct:
The bucket policy must allow CloudTrail to check the ACL (GetBucketAcl) and write objects (PutObject). Without it, no logs arrive.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Invalid prefix: possible, but the common issue is the policy.
• Disabled KMS key: only if encryption with that key is configured.
• CLI trails can't use manual buckets: false.

Key takeaway: trail delivery needs a correct bucket policy.

stem: A CloudTrail trail is configured to send an SNS notification each time a new log file is delivered to S3, but subscribers report they have stopped receiving notifications, even though log files continue to appear in the S3 bucket on schedule. What should the analyst check first?

choices.text: Whether the bucket's server-side encryption settings changed
Whether the trail is configured as a multi-Region trail
Whether the topic policy still allows CloudTrail to publish
Whether CloudTrail Insights is enabled on the trail

explanation:
Why this is correct:
CloudTrail needs permission in the SNS topic policy to publish. If it was changed, notifications stop.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Bucket encryption: unrelated to SNS.
• Multi-Region: unrelated.
• Insights: unrelated.

Key takeaway: check the topic policy for missing notifications.

stem: A company runs an authorized internal vulnerability scanner from a fixed set of EC2 instances, which repeatedly triggers GuardDuty Recon:EC2/PortProbeUnprotectedPort findings against other instances in the same VPC. The security team wants these specific, well-understood findings to be automatically archived going forward without disabling the finding type account-wide. What should they configure?

choices.text: Disable the Recon:EC2/PortProbeUnprotectedPort finding type entirely
A suppression rule matching that finding type and the scanner
Add the scanner's IP addresses to a GuardDuty threat list
A GuardDuty trusted IP list containing the scanner's IP addresses

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A suppression rule matching the finding type and the scanner's instances archives these expected findings automatically, while keeping other findings.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Disable the finding type: loses real detections.
• Threat list: generates more findings.
• Trusted IP list: applies to specific finding types and whole IPs.

Key takeaway: known benign activity → narrow suppression rules.

stem: Which statement correctly compares GuardDuty trusted IP lists and threat lists?

choices.text: Trusted IP lists can be configured only in Security Hub, not in GuardDuty
Threat lists are generated by AWS automatically and cannot be customized
Trusted IPs suppress some findings; threat-list IPs generate findings
Both lists serve the identical purpose and are interchangeable

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Trusted IP lists stop findings for traffic from listed IPs (for certain finding types), while threat lists generate findings for activity involving listed IPs.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Only in Security Hub: they're GuardDuty features.
• Threat lists not customizable: they are.
• Interchangeable: opposite effects.

Key takeaway: trusted = suppress; threat = alert.

stem: Three weeks after configuring a GuardDuty suppression rule intended only to silence low-severity Recon findings from a specific CI/CD subnet, the security team discovers that a genuine UnauthorizedAccess:IAMUser/InstanceCredentialExfiltration finding from a different, compromised instance in that same subnet was also automatically archived and never alerted on. What most likely explains this, and what is the recommended fix?

choices.text: Suppression rules can't cause this; a trusted IP list must have suppressed the finding
Suppressed findings are deleted permanently, so there's no way to detect this happened
The rule was too broad; narrow it to the finding type and specific source
Suppression applies only to findings older than 7 days

explanation:
Why this is correct:
An overly broad suppression rule hid more than intended. Narrow it to the finding type and specific resources, and review archived findings.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Can't cause this: suppression can.
• Deleted permanently: archived, not deleted.
• Only older findings: false.

Key takeaway: keep suppression rules narrow.

stem: A member account administrator in an organization with an organization-wide CloudTrail trail attempts to stop logging or delete the trail from their own account using the CLI, and receives an authorization error despite having AdministratorAccess permissions in that member account. What explains this behavior?

choices.text: Organization trails need an SCP allowing cloudtrail:DeleteTrail in every member account
Only the management or delegated admin account can manage organization trails
The member account has exceeded its daily trail modification quota
AdministratorAccess lacks cloudtrail:StopLogging, which must be added manually

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Organization trails are managed only from the management account or a delegated administrator. Member accounts can't stop or change them.

Why the other options are wrong:
• SCP allow required: no.
• Daily quota: no.
• AdministratorAccess lacks StopLogging: it has it; the org trail is protected.

Key takeaway: org trails are centrally controlled.

stem: An analyst created an Athena table for CloudTrail logs stored in S3 using the CloudTrail console's Create Athena table feature, which partitions data by Region and date. Queries for events from three months ago return results correctly, but queries for last week's events return zero rows, even though the CloudTrail S3 prefix clearly contains log files for last week. What is the most likely cause?

choices.text: No partitions were added for the new dates; add them or use partition projection
Athena cannot query CloudTrail logs newer than 30 days
CloudTrail compresses log files with an unsupported codec after 90 days
The bucket's versioning setting prevents new objects from being queried

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A partitioned Athena table needs partitions added for new dates, or partition projection to compute them automatically.

Why the other options are wrong:
• 30-day limit: false.
• Unsupported codec: false.
• Versioning: unrelated.

Key takeaway: new data not showing → partitions.

stem: A team enabled VPC Flow Logs using a custom format that includes additional fields such as pkt-srcaddr, pkt-dstaddr, and tcp-flags beyond the default field set, delivering to S3. When they run Athena queries against a table created using the default 14-field VPC Flow Logs DDL from AWS documentation, queries fail or return misaligned or null columns for the extra fields. What is the correct fix?

choices.text: Redefine the table DDL to match the custom field order
Convert the S3 objects to Parquet
Run a Glue crawler, which fixes column mapping regardless of the DDL used
Athena cannot query custom-format flow logs; only the default format is supported

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Athena reads columns by position, so the table DDL must match the custom format's field order.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Parquet conversion: not required.
• Crawler fixes regardless: not reliable for custom order.
• Can't query custom formats: they can.

Key takeaway: custom log formats need matching DDL.

stem: During an incident investigation, a security team suspects that CloudTrail log files stored in S3 may have been tampered with after delivery. The trail was configured with log file validation enabled from creation. What should the team do to verify whether any log files were modified or deleted after delivery?

choices.text: Compare S3 object ETags manually with values shown in the CloudTrail console
Run aws cloudtrail validate-logs for the time range
Re-download CloudTrail Insights events
Enable GuardDuty, which retroactively validates historical log file integrity

explanation:
Why this is correct:
aws cloudtrail validate-logs checks the digest chain to prove whether log files were modified or deleted.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Manual ETag comparison: not reliable.
• Insights events: unrelated.
• GuardDuty retroactive validation: no.

Key takeaway: prove log integrity → validate-logs.

stem: A security team is building an incident response playbook for suspected ransomware activity on EC2 instances that encrypt EBS-backed data volumes. Which sequence of actions best reflects AWS-recommended containment-before-eradication practice while preserving forensic evidence?

choices.text: Terminate the instance immediately
Detach and delete the EBS volumes to prevent further encryption, then rebuild
Quarantine security group, EBS snapshot, then investigate
Apply an SCP that denies all API calls in the account to stop lateral movement

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Isolate with a quarantine security group, snapshot the EBS volumes for evidence, then investigate before remediating.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Terminate immediately: destroys evidence.
• Delete volumes: destroys evidence.
• Account-wide SCP deny: disrupts everything.

Key takeaway: contain, preserve, then investigate.

stem: After a GuardDuty finding on an EC2 instance, an analyst needs to see, without writing queries, which IPs it talked to, which roles it used, and how its API activity compared with its normal baseline over the past weeks. Which service fits?

choices.text: Amazon Macie
Amazon Inspector
AWS Config
Amazon Detective

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Detective automatically builds behavior graphs from flow logs, CloudTrail, and GuardDuty findings, and presents entity profiles and baselines for investigation without manual queries.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Inspector: vulnerability management.
• Macie: sensitive data discovery.
• Config: resource configuration history, not behavioral activity.

Key takeaway: investigate who, what, and how unusual → Detective.

stem: During an investigation of a GuardDuty finding indicating an EC2 instance is communicating with a known command-and-control IP address, an analyst pivots into Amazon Detective from the finding. Which capability does Detective provide that GuardDuty alone does not?

choices.text: Historical connections, API volume, and role usage over time
A CVE-based vulnerability report for the instance's packages
Automatic quarantine of the instance's security group
Real-time blocking of the malicious IP address at the VPC level

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Detective shows historical network connections, API call volumes, and role usage over time for the instance.

Why the other options are wrong:
• CVE reports: Inspector.
• Automatic quarantine: not Detective.
• Real-time blocking: not Detective.

Key takeaway: investigation context → Detective.

stem: When GuardDuty reports a compromised instance, a company wants isolation, disk and memory capture, and evidence stored in a forensics account, repeatably and with no manual steps. Which approach fits?

choices.text: An Inspector rule that terminates the instance
A Config rule that rebuilds the instance from its AMI
The Automated Forensics Orchestrator for EC2 solution
Auto Scaling health checks replacing the instance

explanation:
Why this is correct:
The Automated Forensics Orchestrator uses EventBridge and Step Functions to isolate the instance, acquire disk and memory, and move evidence to a forensics account, triggered by security findings.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Termination: destroys volatile evidence.
• Rebuilding from an AMI: loses evidence and doesn't isolate.
• ASG replacement: terminates the compromised instance, losing evidence.

Key takeaway: preserve evidence before remediation; automate the steps.

stem: A company deployed the Automated Forensics Orchestrator for Amazon EC2, triggered by GuardDuty findings via EventBridge. During a recent incident, the Step Functions state machine successfully isolated the instance and captured an EBS snapshot, but the forensic artifacts were not copied into the dedicated forensics account as expected. Which misconfiguration is the most likely cause?

choices.text: Cross-account role or KMS key policy for sharing the snapshot was misconfigured
The finding's severity was below the EventBridge rule's configured threshold
VPC Flow Logs were disabled on the subnet containing the instance
The EC2 instance did not have the SSM Agent installed

explanation:
Why this is correct:
If snapshots weren't shared to the forensics account, a cross-account role or the KMS key policy for encrypted snapshots was likely missing.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Severity threshold: would stop the whole workflow.
• Flow logs: unrelated to snapshot sharing.
• SSM Agent: relevant for memory capture, not snapshot sharing.

Key takeaway: cross-account evidence needs role and key permissions.

stem: A security team is preparing a tabletop exercise to test their incident response plan for a simulated IAM access key compromise. Which element is most important to include to ensure the exercise validates the organization's actual operational readiness, not just the technical runbook?

choices.text: A post-incident report template pre-filled with the expected findings
A complete list of every IAM permission on the compromised principal
A CloudFormation template that recreates the compromised environment
Cross-functional participants walking decisions and escalations

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A tabletop exercise walks cross-functional participants through decisions and escalations to find gaps in the plan.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Prefilled reports: not an exercise.
• Full permission lists: not the goal.
• Rebuild templates: not a tabletop.

Key takeaway: tabletop = people and decisions.

stem: A security team's incident response playbook for suspected S3 data exfiltration instructs responders to immediately revoke all temporary credentials associated with the accessing IAM role by applying a service control policy that denies all actions for the entire account. During a post-incident review, they discover this action also disrupted unrelated production workloads across the account. Which change would best balance rapid containment with blast-radius control for future incidents of this type?​

choices.text: Keep account-wide deny SCPs but schedule them for off-peak hours
Disable CloudTrail logging temporarily to reduce noise during containment
Delete the S3 bucket involved to stop further data loss immediately
Targeted deny on the principal, revoking sessions via aws:TokenIssueTime

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A targeted deny on the compromised principal, including revoking sessions issued before a time (aws:TokenIssueTime), contains the incident without disrupting everyone.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Account-wide SCPs off-peak: still disruptive.
• Disable CloudTrail: destroys evidence.
• Delete the bucket: destroys evidence and data.

Key takeaway: contain narrowly.

stem: An organization is deciding between two approaches for its DDoS incident response playbook: enabling AWS Shield Advanced with a defined Shield Response Team engagement process, versus relying solely on manual scaling and WAF rule updates during an active Layer 7 DDoS event. What is the key operational advantage of the Shield Advanced approach for the playbook?

choices.text: Event management, cost protection, and Shield Response Team access
Shield Advanced replaces the need for a documented incident response playbook
Shield Advanced terminates and rebuilds affected EC2 instances automatically
Shield Advanced removes the need for WAF rules entirely

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Shield Advanced adds event management, DDoS cost protection, and Shield Response Team support, which strengthens a DDoS response playbook.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Replaces the plan: no.
• Rebuilds instances: no.
• No WAF needed: WAF is still used for L7.

Key takeaway: Shield Advanced complements, not replaces, IR plans.

stem: A security analyst enables Amazon Detective in the organization's delegated administrator account but finds that when investigating a GuardDuty finding from a member account, the Detective behavior graph shows little historical data prior to the finding date, limiting root-cause analysis. What is the most likely explanation?

choices.text: Detective requires Amazon Macie in the member account to build historical graphs
Detective retains data only for accounts that had at least one prior GuardDuty finding
The account joined Detective recently, so little history exists
The finding involved S3, and Detective does not support S3-related data sources

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Detective builds behavior graphs from data ingested after an account joins, so recently added accounts have little history.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Needs Macie: no.
• Prior findings required: no.
• No S3 support: not the reason.

Key takeaway: Detective history starts when data ingestion starts.

stem: A company wants an automated, repeatable process so that whenever GuardDuty generates a high-severity Backdoor or CryptoCurrency finding on an EC2 instance, the instance is automatically isolated via security group changes, and both EBS volume snapshots and a memory capture are collected into a separate, restricted forensics AWS account without requiring manual intervention. Which AWS-provided solution most directly addresses this requirement out of the box?

choices.text: The Automated Forensics Orchestrator for EC2, via EventBridge and Step Functions
SSM Automation documents triggered manually by the team
AWS Config custom rules with Lambda auto-remediation
Amazon Inspector with automated remediation enabled

explanation:
Why this is correct:
The Automated Forensics Orchestrator for EC2, triggered through EventBridge and Step Functions, repeatably isolates and captures evidence.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Manual SSM: not automated.
• Config remediation: not forensics.
• Inspector remediation: not forensics.

Key takeaway: repeatable forensics → the orchestrator solution.

stem: During a ransomware drill, responders lost 40 minutes finding which role to assume, which forensics account to use, and who could approve isolation. What would MOST reduce this delay?

choices.text: Rely on responders searching AWS documentation during incidents
Enable more GuardDuty protection plans
Grant all responders AdministratorAccess in every account
Versioned runbooks with exact accounts, roles, and approvers

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Runbooks list pre-approved steps, the exact account IDs, role ARNs, and decision owners, so responders act immediately and consistently. Tabletop exercises should keep them current.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Admin everywhere: expands attack surface and still lacks procedure.
• Searching docs: exactly what caused the delay.
• More detection: doesn't speed up response.

Key takeaway: speed comes from preparation: specific, tested runbooks.

stem: While designing an incident response playbook for insider threat scenarios involving a privileged IAM user, a security team debates whether to grant the incident responder's break-glass role standing, always-active administrative access, versus a just-in-time access model requiring approval and time-bound elevation. What is the primary security tradeoff of the standing access approach?

choices.text: Standing access is more auditable
Standing access is required, since Identity Center can't grant temporary elevation
Standing access removes the need for MFA on the break-glass role
Faster response, but a permanently larger attack surface

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Standing privileged access speeds response but permanently increases attack surface. Just-in-time access reduces exposure.

Why the other options are wrong:
• More auditable: not inherently.
• Identity Center can't grant temporary: it can.
• Removes MFA need: no.

Key takeaway: prefer just-in-time privileged access.

stem: A Detective investigation reveals that an EC2 instance's IAM role made an unusual spike in iam:CreateAccessKey and iam:AttachUserPolicy API calls shortly after a GuardDuty UnauthorizedAccess EC2 metadata finding. Based on this behavior graph evidence, what is the most likely conclusion an analyst should draw to guide the next containment step?

choices.text: The instance is experiencing benign configuration drift and needs no action
The role is read-only, so the IAM calls must have come from another account
Stolen role credentials used for persistence; revoke and review the role
It's a false positive, since Detective doesn't correlate IAM events with GuardDuty

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A spike in CreateAccessKey from an instance role suggests stolen credentials used for persistence. Revoke sessions, remove created keys, and review activity.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Benign drift: unlikely.
• Read-only role: then it wouldn't succeed.
• False positive: Detective correlates IAM events.

Key takeaway: unusual key creation = persistence attempt.

stem: After running a tabletop exercise simulating a ransomware incident, the team identifies that responders were unsure which AWS account owned the forensics S3 bucket and did not know the exact IAM role ARN needed to assume cross-account access during containment. What is the best corrective action to add to the incident response plan?

choices.text: Put current account IDs, ARNs, and role names in the runbook
Remove the forensics account requirement from the playbook to simplify it
Give all responders permanent AdministratorAccess in every account
Have responders search AWS documentation during the live incident

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Runbooks should list current account IDs, role ARNs, and names so responders can act immediately.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Remove forensics account: weakens response.
• Permanent admin: risky.
• Search docs live: slow.

Key takeaway: specific runbooks speed response.

stem: A security team discovers that an IAM user's long-term access key has been publicly exposed in a GitHub repository and used to launch unauthorized EC2 instances in an unfamiliar region. What is the correct first remediation step?

choices.text: Deactivate the key, then revoke sessions it created
Enable AWS Config to begin tracking the user's future activity
Delete the IAM user entirely to stop all access immediately
Rotate the account root user password

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Deactivate the exposed key immediately, then revoke sessions created with it (for example, with an inline deny based on aws:TokenIssueTime), then investigate.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Config tracking: doesn't stop access.
• Delete the user: loses evidence and may not end existing sessions.
• Rotate root: unrelated.

Key takeaway: exposed key → deactivate and revoke sessions.

stem: An incident responder deactivates a compromised IAM user's access keys, but GuardDuty continues to generate findings showing API activity from the same principal for another twenty minutes. What is the most likely explanation, and what additional action should the responder take?

choices.text: STS sessions predate deactivation; deny by aws:TokenIssueTime
They're false positives, since deactivating a key ends all sessions immediately
GuardDuty findings lag by hours
Key deactivation takes up to 24 hours to take effect in IAM evaluation

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Deactivating the key doesn't invalidate STS sessions already issued. Deny actions for tokens issued before a time (aws:TokenIssueTime).

Why the other options are wrong:
• False positives: sessions still work.
• GuardDuty lag: not the main reason.
• 24-hour delay: false.

Key takeaway: revoke existing temporary credentials explicitly.

stem: A security team must contain a compromised IAM role assumed by an EC2 instance profile. They are comparing two containment options: revoking active sessions for the role by attaching a session-revocation deny policy, versus simply removing the instance profile from the EC2 instance. Which statement correctly compares these approaches?

choices.text: Both approaches are functionally identical and interchangeable in every case
Removing the profile doesn't revoke credentials already cached on the instance
A deny policy is the only way AWS supports revoking any active role session
Removing the profile immediately invalidates credentials already obtained on the instance

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Removing the instance profile doesn't revoke credentials already cached on the instance. A deny policy based on token issue time revokes them.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Identical: they differ.
• Only way: role session revocation is one of several steps.
• Removal invalidates cached creds: it doesn't.

Key takeaway: revoke role sessions, don't just detach profiles.

stem: A GuardDuty finding indicates an EC2 instance is actively participating in a botnet and communicating with a command-and-control server. The team needs to isolate the instance from the network for forensic preservation while keeping it running for later memory analysis. Which approach achieves this most effectively?

choices.text: Terminate the instance and restore the workload from a known-good AMI
Stop the instance to halt its network communication
Point the instance's route table to a black-hole route
Isolation security group, leaving the instance running

explanation:
Why this is correct:
An isolation security group cuts communication while keeping the instance running for memory and disk forensics.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Terminate: loses evidence.
• Stop: loses memory.
• Black-hole route: affects the whole subnet.

Key takeaway: isolate but preserve.

stem: A responder isolates a compromised EC2 instance by attaching a restrictive security group, but a follow-up review shows the instance continued to exfiltrate data for several minutes afterward. Investigation reveals the attacker had also attached a secondary elastic network interface to the instance in a different subnet before isolation occurred. What additional isolation step should have been taken to fully contain this instance?

choices.text: Disable the instance profile
Nothing further, since security groups take precedence over all network paths
Check every ENI; the SG change applied only to one interface
Restart the instance to force it to re-read its network configuration

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Security groups apply per ENI. If the instance has multiple ENIs, each needs the isolation group.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Disable the profile: not network isolation.
• Nothing further: other ENIs remain open.
• Restart: unnecessary and loses memory.

Key takeaway: isolate every network interface.

stem: An instance in a subnet with 20 other instances is suspected compromised. The team must cut off only this instance while keeping it running for forensics. Which control fits?

choices.text: Stop the instance and detach its volumes
Remove the subnet's route to the NAT gateway
Add deny rules for the instance's IP to the subnet's network ACL
Replace its security groups with an isolation security group

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Security groups apply per network interface, so changing only this instance's groups isolates it without affecting the other 20. Note that existing tracked connections may persist, so combine with other controls if needed.

Why the other options are wrong:
• NACL: affects every instance in the subnet.
• Route removal: also affects the whole subnet, and only outbound.
• Stopping: destroys memory evidence.

Key takeaway: instance-level isolation → security group swap.

stem: A Macie finding and subsequent investigation confirm that an S3 bucket containing sensitive customer data was made publicly readable due to a misconfigured bucket policy, and objects were accessed from unrecognized external IP addresses. What is the most effective immediate action to stop further unauthorized access while preserving evidence for investigation?

choices.text: Delete the S3 bucket to eliminate the exposure entirely
Block Public Access, fix the policy, and preserve evidence (legal hold)
Enable default SSE-KMS encryption, which revokes public access automatically
Rotate the bucket's access keys to prevent further unauthorized reads

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Enable Block Public Access, fix the bucket policy, and preserve evidence (for example, object versions and logs, with legal hold if needed).

Why the other options are wrong:
• Delete the bucket: destroys evidence and data.
• Encryption: doesn't revoke public access.
• Rotate access keys: buckets don't have keys.

Key takeaway: close exposure and preserve evidence.

stem: After discovering an exposed S3 bucket, the security team is deciding between two lockdown approaches: applying an explicit deny statement in the bucket policy for all principals except a trusted list, versus enabling S3 Block Public Access settings at the account level. What is an important tradeoff to consider when choosing account-level Block Public Access as the primary containment control?

choices.text: Account-level BPA contains fast but may break legitimate public uses
Block Public Access cannot be applied at the account level, only per bucket
Deny bucket policies are evaluated after BPA, making the policy approach redundant
BPA affects only newly created buckets

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Account-level Block Public Access contains exposure quickly across all buckets but may break legitimate public uses. A targeted deny policy is narrower but slower.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Account level unsupported: it is.
• Deny evaluated after BPA: not the point.
• Only new buckets: applies to all.

Key takeaway: broad BPA vs. targeted policy is a blast-radius tradeoff.

stem: A responder applies an account-level S3 Block Public Access configuration to remediate an exposed bucket, but external access continues briefly and CloudTrail shows successful GetObject calls from an external principal after the change. What is the most likely explanation?

choices.text: CloudTrail was caching stale entries from before the change was made
Unexpired pre-signed URLs from permitted principals still work
Block Public Access settings take up to 24 hours to propagate globally
The principal uses a same-account role, so Block Public Access doesn't apply

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Block Public Access affects anonymous and public access. Unexpired pre-signed URLs from permitted principals still work until they expire or the signer's credentials are revoked.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Stale CloudTrail: no.
• 24-hour propagation: no.
• Same-account role unaffected: not the case described.

Key takeaway: revoke signer credentials to kill pre-signed URLs.

stem: A security team wants Security Hub findings for S3 buckets that are publicly accessible to automatically trigger a remediation workflow that removes public bucket ACLs, notifies the security team, and creates a ticket, without requiring manual analyst intervention for well-understood, low-risk finding types. Which architecture best achieves this?

choices.text: EventBridge to Step Functions orchestrating remediation, SNS, and tickets
Configure Security Hub to email the security team directly for every finding
Use AWS Config auto-remediation only
Review each finding in the Security Hub console and remediate individually

explanation:
Why this is correct:
EventBridge routes Security Hub findings to a Step Functions workflow that remediates, notifies via SNS, and opens a ticket.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Email only: manual.
• Config auto-remediation only: not the full workflow.
• Manual console review: slow.

Key takeaway: orchestrated remediation → EventBridge + Step Functions.

stem: A security team is designing an automated remediation Step Functions workflow triggered by GuardDuty findings that will automatically revoke IAM credentials and isolate EC2 instances without any human approval. What is the primary risk this design introduces that a human-in-the-loop approval step would mitigate?

choices.text: False positives could trigger disruptive actions with no human check
Step Functions cannot invoke more than one Lambda function per execution
GuardDuty findings cannot be consumed by EventBridge
Automated workflows cannot be logged to CloudTrail, reducing auditability

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Fully automated remediation risks disruptive actions on false positives. Add human approval for destructive steps.

Why the other options are wrong:
• One Lambda per execution: false.
• GuardDuty not in EventBridge: false.
• Not logged: Step Functions and CloudTrail log it.

Key takeaway: gate destructive automation.

stem: An automated remediation Lambda function, triggered by a Security Hub custom action, is designed to attach a deny-all IAM policy to a compromised IAM role. In production, the function fails intermittently with an AccessDenied error when calling iam:PutRolePolicy. Investigation shows the Lambda's execution role has iam:PutRolePolicy permission, but a permissions boundary is attached to the execution role that does not include this action. What is the correct fix?

choices.text: Remove the permissions boundary from the execution role entirely
Boundaries apply only to IAM users
Grant the function AdministratorAccess to bypass the permissions boundary
Add iam:PutRolePolicy to the role's permissions boundary

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Effective permissions are limited by the permissions boundary. Adding iam:PutRolePolicy to the boundary lets the function attach the deny policy.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Remove the boundary: weakens guardrails.
• Boundaries only for users: they apply to roles.
• AdministratorAccess: still limited by the boundary.

Key takeaway: boundaries cap permissions; update the boundary.

stem: An organization suspects the AWS account root user credentials may have been compromised, evidenced by a GuardDuty PenTest IAMUser root finding combined with unexpected root sign-in events in CloudTrail. Which combination of actions represents the most appropriate immediate response?

choices.text: Delete the root user, since best practice is to never use it
Reset password, remove root keys, confirm MFA, review CloudTrail
Apply an SCP denying all root actions as the only containment step
Rely on IAM Identity Center to lock the root user after suspicious activity

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Reset the root password, remove any root access keys, confirm MFA, and review CloudTrail for root activity.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Delete root: not possible.
• SCP only: doesn't cover the management account and isn't enough.
• Identity Center locks root: no.

Key takeaway: root compromise → reset, remove keys, MFA, investigate.

stem: A team needs to isolate a compromised EC2 instance from the network but still requires the ability to run forensic commands and collect data from the instance via AWS Systems Manager after isolation. Which approach satisfies both requirements?

choices.text: Deny all except HTTPS egress to SSM endpoints
Remove all security group rules; Session Manager still works normally
Detach the instance profile so Systems Manager can bypass network isolation
Disable the network interface

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A security group allowing only HTTPS egress to SSM endpoints (for example, via VPC endpoints) keeps Session Manager and Run Command working while isolating the instance.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Remove all rules: SSM stops working.
• Detach profile: SSM needs the role.
• Disable the ENI: loses access.

Key takeaway: isolate while keeping management access.

stem: A company serves an API behind Amazon CloudFront and AWS WAF (CLOUDFRONT scope). After enabling the AWS Managed Rules SQL Database rule group, legitimate JSON requests containing a business field named 'SELECT_PLAN' are being blocked. The security team must eliminate the false positives while keeping SQL injection protection active for all other traffic. What should they do?

choices.text: Remove the SQL database managed rule group from the web ACL entirely
Replace WAF with Shield Advanced
Switch the web ACL scope from CLOUDFRONT to REGIONAL to change evaluation
Override only the offending rule's action to Count

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Overriding only the offending rule's action to Count stops false positives while keeping the rest of the managed rule group active.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Remove the whole group: loses protection.
• Shield Advanced: not a WAF rule fix.
• Change scope: not how it works.

Key takeaway: false positives → override one rule.

stem: A retailer expects DDoS attacks during a sale. It wants 24/7 expert help during attacks, proactive engagement when health checks fail, and credits for attack-driven scaling. Which subscription provides these?

choices.text: GuardDuty with Runtime Monitoring
Shield Advanced, with proactive engagement configured
AWS WAF Bot Control managed rules
Shield Standard, which is included for all customers

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Shield Advanced adds access to the Shield Response Team, proactive engagement (SRT contacts you when associated health checks show impact during an event), and DDoS cost protection.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Shield Standard: automatic L3/L4 protection only.
• Bot Control: WAF rules for bots, not DDoS support.
• GuardDuty: threat detection.

Key takeaway: people + proactive contact + cost protection → Shield Advanced.

stem: A team is migrating a CloudFront distribution's S3 origin from an Origin Access Identity (OAI) to Origin Access Control (OAC). The bucket stores objects encrypted with a customer-managed AWS KMS key (SSE-KMS). After switching to OAC and updating the S3 bucket policy, CloudFront returns 403 errors when serving objects. What additional change is required?

choices.text: Key policy granting kms:Decrypt to CloudFront, scoped by aws:SourceArn
Re-enable the legacy OAI alongside OAC, since OAC doesn't support SSE-KMS
Disable default encryption on the bucket so CloudFront can skip KMS
Grant the distribution's viewer certificate ACM permissions to decrypt objects

explanation:
Why this is correct:
With OAC and SSE-KMS, the KMS key policy must allow CloudFront's service principal to decrypt, scoped with aws:SourceArn to the distribution.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Re-enable OAI: OAC supports SSE-KMS.
• Disable encryption: weakens security.
• Viewer certificate permissions: unrelated.

Key takeaway: OAC + SSE-KMS → key policy for CloudFront.

stem: A security architect is designing centralized outbound traffic inspection using AWS Network Firewall in an inspection VPC. The requirement is to block outbound connections to known malicious domains at the TLS handshake stage without terminating or decrypting TLS traffic. Which Network Firewall capability satisfies this requirement?

choices.text: A stateless rule group matching destination IP ranges only
VPC Flow Logs configured to drop flagged flows in real time
A CloudFront WAF web ACL associated with the inspection VPC
A stateful rule group with domain-list rules that inspect the TLS SNI field

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A stateful rule group with domain-list rules inspects the TLS SNI (and HTTP host) to allow or block outbound domains.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Stateless IP rules: domains change IPs.
• Flow logs dropping flows: not possible.
• CloudFront WAF: inbound web traffic.

Key takeaway: egress domain filtering → Network Firewall domain lists.

stem: One web ACL must protect a CloudFront distribution and another an ALB in us-west-2. A team tried to create both in us-west-2 and couldn't associate one of them. Which setup is correct?

choices.text: Scope is chosen automatically by AWS WAF based on each resource's tags
Both with CLOUDFRONT scope, since the scopes are shared
CloudFront ACL: CLOUDFRONT scope (us-east-1); ALB ACL: REGIONAL in us-west-2
Both with REGIONAL scope in us-west-2

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Web ACLs for CloudFront use the CLOUDFRONT (global) scope, managed in us-east-1. Web ACLs for ALB, API Gateway, and similar resources use REGIONAL scope in the resource's Region.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Both REGIONAL: can't be associated with CloudFront.
• Both CLOUDFRONT: can't be associated with an ALB.
• Automatic scope: you choose it explicitly.

Key takeaway: CloudFront = global scope in us-east-1; everything else = the resource's Region.

stem: During a Layer 7 DDoS attack against a CloudFront distribution, an organization's AWS bill spikes sharply due to origin auto-scaling triggered by the attack traffic. The distribution is protected by Shield Advanced and associated with a AWS WAF web ACL. Which requirement determines whether the organization is eligible for Shield Advanced's DDoS cost protection for the resulting scaling charges?

choices.text: Charges must stem from a DDoS on a Shield Advanced-protected resource
The account needs Enterprise Support and a signed Business Associate Agreement
Cost protection applies only if Route 53 health checks were disabled during the event
The DRT must have pre-approved the architecture in writing before the attack

explanation:
Why this is correct:
DDoS cost protection applies to charges caused by a DDoS on a Shield Advanced-protected resource. Request credits through Support.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Enterprise Support and BAA: not required.
• Health checks disabled: unrelated.
• DRT pre-approval: not required.

Key takeaway: cost protection only for protected resources.

stem: A high-traffic public website needs to inject the Strict-Transport-Security, X-Content-Type-Options, and Content-Security-Policy headers on every viewer response served through CloudFront. The logic is simple string manipulation with no need to call external APIs or access the request body. Which edge compute option is most appropriate for minimizing latency and cost?

choices.text: A Lambda@Edge function triggered on origin request
A CloudFront Function triggered on viewer response
An Amazon API Gateway Lambda authorizer
An AWS WAF custom response rule with a Block action

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A CloudFront Function on viewer response adds security headers at the edge cheaply and with minimal latency for every response. (Response headers policies are another built-in option.)

Why the other options are wrong:
• Lambda@Edge origin request: wrong event and more cost.
• API Gateway authorizer: unrelated.
• WAF block response: not for adding headers.

Key takeaway: lightweight header changes → CloudFront Functions or response headers policies.

stem: A login endpoint is being targeted by a credential stuffing campaign originating from a large, rotating pool of residential IP addresses, making a standard per-source-IP rate-based rule ineffective. The application includes a custom header 'X-Account-Attempted' identifying the target username on each login POST. How should the security team configure AWS WAF to throttle this attack more effectively?

choices.text: Custom aggregate key: source IP plus the attempted-account header
Extend the rate-based rule's window to 24 hours, keeping IP-only aggregation
Replace it with a geo match rule blocking traffic outside the home country
Switch the rule to CAPTCHA action only, without changing aggregation
Disable the rule and rely on Shield Advanced's Layer 3/4 mitigations

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Rotating IPs evade IP-only rate limits. A custom aggregate key combining source IP with the attempted-account header (or just the account header) rate-limits attempts per target account.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Longer window with IP only: rotating IPs still evade.
• Geo block: attackers are global or local.
• CAPTCHA without aggregation change: still keyed on IP.
• Disable the rule: L3/L4 mitigation doesn't stop credential stuffing.

Key takeaway: match the aggregation key to the attack pattern.

stem: An organization runs a centralized egress inspection architecture: spoke VPCs attach to a Transit Gateway, and an inspection VPC hosts AWS Network Firewall endpoints across two Availability Zones for stateful traffic inspection. After deployment, engineers observe that a portion of long-lived TCP sessions are intermittently dropped by the firewall, and CloudWatch metrics show state-tracking errors. Traffic for a single flow is sometimes seen entering one AZ's firewall endpoint and returning through the other AZ's endpoint. What is the most likely fix?

choices.text: Enable appliance mode on the inspection VPC's Transit Gateway attachment
Move all firewall endpoints into a single AZ to eliminate cross-AZ routing
Replace stateful rule groups with stateless ones to avoid connection tracking
Increase the firewall's stateful rule group capacity units

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Appliance mode on the inspection VPC attachment keeps both directions of each flow in the same AZ, so stateful firewalls see complete sessions.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Single AZ: loses resilience.
• Stateless rules: lose stateful inspection.
• More capacity units: doesn't fix asymmetry.

Key takeaway: TGW + stateful inspection → appliance mode.

stem: A team migrated a CloudFront distribution's S3 origin from Origin Access Identity (OAI) to Origin Access Control (OAC) using the AWS console recommended update, but end users now receive 403 Access Denied errors for all requests. Which configuration is the most likely cause?

choices.text: OAC is incompatible with S3 buckets that have versioning enabled
Distributions using OAC cannot serve content over HTTPS
OAC needs a public bucket, and Block Public Access is enabled
The bucket policy still names the old OAI, not the CloudFront service principal

explanation:
Why this is correct:
With OAC, the bucket policy must allow the cloudfront.amazonaws.com service principal (with an AWS:SourceArn condition for the distribution), not the old OAI.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Versioning incompatible: no.
• No HTTPS with OAC: false.
• Public bucket needed: no.

Key takeaway: migrating to OAC → update the bucket policy.

stem: A pentest shows an SSRF flaw could read instance role credentials. Containers on the host legitimately need IMDS. Which change blocks SSRF-style access while keeping container access working?

choices.text: Block 169.254.169.254 with a security group rule
Rotate the instance role credentials every 15 minutes with a scheduled Lambda
Disable IMDS entirely on all instances
Require IMDSv2; set hop limit 2 only where containers need it

explanation:
Why this is correct:
IMDSv2 requires a PUT to get a session token, which typical SSRF can't perform. A hop limit of 2 lets containers behind a bridge reach IMDS; hosts without containers can keep hop limit 1.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Disable IMDS: breaks containers that need credentials.
• SG rule: security groups can't filter link-local metadata traffic.
• Faster rotation: stolen credentials still work until expiry.

Key takeaway: SSRF protection for IMDS → IMDSv2; tune hop limits for containers.

stem: An organization enforces IMDSv2 with the default PutResponseHopLimit of 1 on all new EC2 launch templates. After rollout, containerized applications running under Docker's default bridge network on these EC2 instances start failing to retrieve credentials from the instance metadata endpoint, while non-containerized processes on the same instances work fine. What is the most likely cause and fix?

choices.text: The security group must explicitly allow traffic to 169.254.169.254
Hop limit 1 blocks the container's extra hop; raise it to 2
Containers cannot use IMDSv2 and must use hardcoded static credentials
The bridge hop exceeds the token TTL, so IMDSv2 must be disabled

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Containers behind a bridge add a network hop, so IMDSv2 responses with hop limit 1 don't reach them. Raise the hop limit to 2 where containers need IMDS.

Why the other options are wrong:
• SG rule to 169.254.169.254: SGs don't govern IMDS.
• Containers can't use IMDSv2: they can.
• Token TTL: unrelated to hops.

Key takeaway: containers + IMDSv2 → hop limit 2.

stem: Amazon ECS tasks run on EC2 instances (EC2 launch type) using bridge network mode. A penetration test reveals that a compromised container can query the EC2 instance's IMDS directly and obtain the broader EC2 instance profile's IAM credentials rather than being limited to its intended, narrowly-scoped ECS task IAM role. Which combination best resolves this while keeping the workload on EC2?

choices.text: Give the instance profile and every task role the same broad role
A security group rule denying outbound access to 169.254.169.254/32
awsvpc mode with ECS_AWSVPC_BLOCK_IMDS (or iptables) blocking IMDS
IMDSv2 with hop limit 1, since bridge-mode containers can never reach IMDS then

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Using awsvpc mode with ECS_AWSVPC_BLOCK_IMDS (or iptables rules) blocks tasks from reaching the instance role via IMDS, so each task uses only its task role.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Same broad role everywhere: no least privilege.
• SG outbound deny to IMDS: SGs can't block it.
• IMDSv2 hop limit 1 in bridge mode: blocks IMDS but the option's claim is overstated.

Key takeaway: stop tasks from borrowing the instance role.
