stem: A security team wants continuous vulnerability scanning of container images stored in Amazon ECR, covering not just operating system package CVEs but also vulnerabilities in application-level dependencies (such as a vulnerable Java library), with rescanning triggered automatically as new CVEs are published, without needing to re-push images. Which ECR feature should they enable?

choices.text: GuardDuty Malware Protection for ECR repositories
ECR enhanced scanning (Amazon Inspector)
AWS Config conformance packs on the ECR repository
ECR basic scanning at push time

explanation:
Why this is correct:
ECR enhanced scanning (Inspector) continuously scans OS and programming language packages and rescans when new CVEs appear.

Why the other options are wrong:
• GuardDuty Malware for ECR: not CVE scanning.
• Config conformance packs: configuration.
• Basic scanning: OS packages at push only.

Key takeaway: continuous image CVE scanning → enhanced scanning.

stem: A compliance requirement mandates that critical security patches be applied to a fleet of EC2 instances within 3 days of release, while all other approved patches roll out during a monthly maintenance window, and the security team needs an auditable compliance report per instance. Using AWS Systems Manager, what is the best approach?

choices.text: Use AWS Config remediation actions to install OS patches automatically
Use the default AWS patch baseline, which cannot be customized by severity
Custom baseline with severity-based auto-approval, patch groups, and windows
SSH into each instance monthly to run updates and record results in a spreadsheet

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A custom patch baseline with severity-based auto-approval, patch groups, and maintenance windows installs critical patches within the required time, with compliance reporting.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Config installing patches: not its role.
• Default baseline can't be customized: you create custom ones.
• Monthly SSH: slow and manual.

Key takeaway: patch SLAs → custom baselines + windows.

stem: A new critical CVE is disclosed. Security must list every EC2 instance, ECR image, and Lambda function affected across 50 accounts within hours, prioritized by network exposure. Which service fits?

choices.text: AWS Config advanced queries on instance tags and installed software inventory
Amazon GuardDuty Malware Protection
Amazon Inspector with an org delegated administrator
Amazon Macie automated discovery

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Inspector continuously scans EC2, ECR, and Lambda, automatically re-evaluates when new CVEs are published, and its findings can be filtered by CVE ID across the organization, with risk scores that factor in network reachability.

Why the other options are wrong:
• GuardDuty Malware: malware, not CVEs.
• Config queries: have no CVE data.
• Macie: sensitive data.

Key takeaway: 'which of our resources have CVE-X' → Inspector.

stem: An incident investigation reveals that an EC2 instance running a public-facing web application was compromised via an SSRF vulnerability, and the attacker used the leaked IMDSv1 session to assume the instance's IAM role and exfiltrate data from an S3 bucket. To prevent recurrence account-wide going forward, which combination of actions should the security team take?

choices.text: Rotate the account root user credentials
Enable S3 Block Public Access on every bucket, which prevents this attack class
Delete the role and store long-term access keys in the application code
Restrict the instance security group to deny all inbound traffic
Require IMDSv2 in launch templates and on running instances

explanation:
Why this is correct:
If the web app was abused (for example, via SSRF) to read role credentials from IMDS, requiring IMDSv2 on launch templates and running instances blocks that path.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Rotate root: unrelated.
• Block Public Access: unrelated.
• Long-term keys: worse.
• Deny all inbound: breaks the site.

Key takeaway: SSRF credential theft → IMDSv2.

stem: A platform team running Amazon EKS wants each pod in a shared node group to only have the exact AWS permissions its specific workload requires, rather than inheriting the broader permissions of the EC2 worker node's instance role, which is shared by all pods scheduled on that node. What is the primary trade-off of adopting IAM Roles for Service Accounts (IRSA) to achieve this compared to relying on the node instance role?

choices.text: IRSA works only with Fargate pods and is unavailable on EC2 worker nodes
IRSA requires every pod to run privileged, increasing the attack surface
Pod-level least privilege, at the cost of more roles to manage
IRSA removes the need for any IAM roles in the cluster, with no trade-off

explanation:
Why this is correct:
IRSA gives each pod's service account its own role, achieving pod-level least privilege at the cost of more roles to manage.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Fargate only: works on EC2 nodes too.
• Requires privileged pods: no.
• No roles needed: it uses roles.

Key takeaway: pod-level IAM → IRSA.

stem: A compliance report requires missing patches to be known daily, but installation must happen only in Sunday maintenance windows. How should Patch Manager be configured?

choices.text: Install on every boot using EC2 user data
A daily Install operation, since Install also reports compliance
A daily Scan operation, with Install scheduled in a Sunday window
Scan only, since Install requires Session Manager

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Scan checks instances against the patch baseline and reports compliance without changing anything. Install applies approved missing patches (and may reboot), so it belongs in the maintenance window.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Daily Install: patches and reboots outside the approved window.
• Install via Session Manager: Install runs through Run Command documents.
• User data: runs only at launch.

Key takeaway: Scan to report, Install to change.

stem: A team enabled Amazon Inspector for their account expecting it to report code-level vulnerabilities in their AWS Lambda functions, but no Lambda findings appear after several days. Which is the most likely explanation?

choices.text: The function's execution role needs AdministratorAccess for Inspector to scan it
Functions are scanned only if they are invoked at least once per second
Inspector cannot scan Lambda functions and supports only EC2 and ECR
Lambda code scanning must be enabled, for supported runtimes

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Inspector's Lambda code scanning is a separate feature that must be enabled and supports specific runtimes.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Needs AdministratorAccess: no.
• Must be invoked: not required.
• Can't scan Lambda: it can.

Key takeaway: enable each Inspector scan type.

stem: A container security team is comparing Amazon ECR's basic image scanning against enhanced scanning for their production repositories. Which statement correctly distinguishes the two?

choices.text: Basic scans OS packages at push; enhanced rescans OS and language packages continuously
Basic covers language packages, while enhanced covers only OS packages
They are identical except that enhanced scanning has a different price
Enhanced is a one-time scan at push, while basic scanning is continuous

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Basic scanning checks OS packages at push time. Enhanced scanning (Inspector) covers OS and language packages and rescans continuously.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Reversed coverage: incorrect.
• Identical: they differ.
• Enhanced one-time: it's continuous.

Key takeaway: enhanced = broader and continuous.

stem: A fleet of EC2 instances runs a workload that authenticates to AWS services using credentials injected at boot via user data and never needs to query the Instance Metadata Service afterward. To minimize the SSRF attack surface as much as possible for these specific instances, what is the strongest available hardening option?

choices.text: Disable the metadata service entirely (HttpEndpoint=disabled)
Require IMDSv2, since that is the maximum protection and IMDS can't be disabled
Set the hop limit to 0 so that no metadata request can succeed
A security group rule denying outbound traffic to 169.254.169.254/32

explanation:
Why this is correct:
If the workload doesn't use IMDS at all, disabling the metadata endpoint (HttpEndpoint=disabled) removes the attack surface entirely.

Why the other options are wrong:
• IMDSv2 is maximum: disabling is stronger when IMDS isn't needed.
• Hop limit 0: invalid.
• SG rule to IMDS: SGs can't block it.

Key takeaway: not needed → disable IMDS.

stem: An app server initiates HTTPS calls to an external API. Its SG allows all outbound traffic, and the subnet NACL allows outbound 443 and inbound 443 only. Calls time out. Why?

choices.text: The API must allow port 443 in its own NACL
The stateless NACL must allow inbound ephemeral ports for replies
The security group needs an inbound rule allowing replies from the API's IP range
NACLs don't apply to outbound-initiated traffic

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Replies from the API come back to the server's ephemeral source port. Security groups track the connection, but NACLs are stateless, so inbound ephemeral ports (1024-65535) must be allowed.

Why the other options are wrong:
• SG inbound rule: stateful SGs allow return traffic automatically.
• NACLs apply to all traffic crossing the subnet.
• The API side: not within the customer's control, and not the cause here.

Key takeaway: with NACLs, think in both directions and remember ephemeral ports.

stem: EC2 instances in a private subnet can successfully send outbound HTTPS requests through a NAT gateway, but responses never arrive back at the instances; packet captures confirm the NAT gateway forwards the return traffic toward the subnet. The subnet's security group allows all outbound traffic and the subnet's network ACL has an inbound rule allowing 0.0.0.0/0 on port 443, plus an outbound rule allowing 0.0.0.0/0 on port 443. What is the most likely misconfiguration?

choices.text: The NAT gateway's route table is missing a route to the internet gateway
The NACL lacks an inbound rule for ephemeral return ports
Network ACLs cannot be used in subnets with a NAT gateway route
The security group is missing an inbound rule allowing port 443

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Responses come back to ephemeral ports. A stateless NACL must allow inbound ephemeral ports from the internet.

Why the other options are wrong:
• NAT route missing: requests succeed, so outbound works.
• NACLs can't be used: they can.
• Inbound 443 on SG: return traffic is stateful.

Key takeaway: NACLs need rules for return traffic.

stem: A company uses an S3 Gateway VPC endpoint for private access to S3 from a data processing VPC. They must ensure that instances in that VPC can only read/write objects in one specific company-owned bucket via the endpoint, even if an instance's IAM role is later broadened. Which combination provides defense-in-depth for this requirement?

choices.text: An explicit NACL Deny for all S3 IP ranges except the bucket's Region
Rely on the IAM role, since endpoint policies can't restrict specific resources
Disable the gateway endpoint and send S3 traffic through a NAT gateway
Endpoint policy scoped to the bucket, plus an aws:sourceVpce bucket policy

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A gateway endpoint policy scoped to the approved bucket limits what the VPC can reach, and a bucket policy with aws:sourceVpce limits the bucket to that endpoint.

Why the other options are wrong:
• NACL S3 IP denies: impractical.
• IAM alone: endpoint policies can restrict buckets.
• NAT instead: loses the private path.

Key takeaway: two-way lock-down: endpoint policy + bucket policy.

stem: An application team created an interface VPC endpoint for Amazon DynamoDB (via PrivateLink-based interface endpoint, not the gateway endpoint) but confirms via traceroute that traffic is still exiting through the NAT gateway to the public DynamoDB service endpoint instead of using the interface endpoint's private IP. What is the most likely cause?

choices.text: The NAT gateway must be deleted before interface endpoint traffic is used
Private DNS or the VPC DNS attributes aren't enabled
Interface endpoints for DynamoDB don't support private DNS in any configuration
Interface endpoints work only for resources launched after they are created

explanation:
Why this is correct:
For requests to resolve to the interface endpoint, private DNS must be enabled on the endpoint and the VPC's enableDnsSupport and enableDnsHostnames must be on.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Delete NAT first: not required.
• No private DNS for DynamoDB interface endpoints: private DNS options exist.
• Only new resources: not true.

Key takeaway: interface endpoints rely on private DNS.

stem: A malicious IP address has been observed scanning a public subnet, and the security team needs to immediately block all traffic from that single source IP across every resource in the subnet, regardless of each resource's individual security group configuration. Which approach is appropriate, and why is a security group not sufficient on its own?

choices.text: Add a Deny rule for the IP to every security group in the subnet
Block the IP with a WAF rule
A NACL Deny rule for the IP; security groups can't deny
Security groups support explicit Deny rules like NACLs, so either works

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Security groups can't deny traffic. A NACL deny rule (with a low rule number) blocks the IP for the subnet immediately.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Deny in SGs: not possible.
• WAF: only for web traffic through supported resources.
• SGs support deny: false.

Key takeaway: block an IP at the subnet → NACL deny.

stem: An organization built a Transit Gateway hub-and-spoke design intending strict segmentation between a PCI-scoped VPC and all other VPCs. During an audit, it is discovered that instances in a non-PCI VPC can reach instances in the PCI VPC over the Transit Gateway. Investigation shows all VPC attachments are associated with the Transit Gateway's default route table, and all attachments propagate their routes into that same default route table. What is the root cause and the correct remediation?

choices.text: An overly permissive security group on the PCI instances, unrelated to TGW routing
Transit Gateway cannot segment traffic, so VPC peering is needed for PCI isolation
Appliance mode on the Transit Gateway segments PCI and non-PCI traffic automatically
One shared, fully propagated route table; give PCI its own route table
Disable route propagation account-wide

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A single shared route table with full propagation lets every VPC reach every other. Give PCI attachments their own route table with only approved routes.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Permissive SG: not the segmentation failure.
• TGW can't segment: it can.
• Appliance mode: symmetry, not segmentation.
• Disable propagation account-wide: disruptive.

Key takeaway: segmentation needs separate route tables.

stem: A financial services company must ensure that application servers in a VPC never send traffic for a specific AWS API (e.g., AWS Secrets Manager) over any path that could traverse the public internet, even accidentally through a misconfigured route table, and compliance requires this be structurally enforced rather than relying on monitoring alone. They are weighing an interface VPC endpoint (PrivateLink) against keeping the default public endpoint reachable only via a security-group-restricted path over their Direct Connect connection. What is the key trade-off in choosing the interface VPC endpoint approach?

choices.text: No security gain over a restricted public endpoint
Interface endpoints eliminate all AWS charges for API calls to the service
Interface endpoints require decommissioning the Direct Connect connection
No public-internet path, at the cost of per-AZ endpoint fees and ENIs

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Interface endpoints keep traffic to the AWS API off the public internet, at the cost of per-AZ hourly and data processing fees.

Why the other options are wrong:
• No security gain: removes internet exposure.
• No API charges: false.
• Must drop Direct Connect: false.

Key takeaway: private API access costs per endpoint.

stem: A company manages 40 AWS accounts through AWS Organizations. The security team wants employees to sign in once with their corporate identity provider and then access any of the accounts they are authorized for, including federated access to third-party SAML applications, without provisioning individual IAM users in each account. Which solution best satisfies these requirements with the least ongoing administrative overhead?

choices.text: A SAML provider in every member account with manually maintained IAM roles
IAM Identity Center with an external IdP and permission sets
IAM users in the management account plus cross-account switch-role links
AWS Managed Microsoft AD with RDP to a bastion in each account as the only access

explanation:
Why this is correct:
IAM Identity Center with an external IdP and permission sets provides single sign-on to all 40 accounts with centrally managed access.

Why the other options are wrong:
• SAML per account: unmanageable.
• IAM users + switch role: long-term credentials.
• AD with RDP bastions: not AWS access.

Key takeaway: multi-account SSO → Identity Center.

stem: An administrator assigns a new permission set named DataAnalystAccess to a group in AWS IAM Identity Center for a specific member account. Group members report that when they sign in to the AWS access portal, the account is not listed and they cannot access it. The permission set and group assignment both appear correctly configured in the Identity Center console. What is the most likely cause and fix?

choices.text: The corporate IdP hasn't synced group membership in the last 5 minutes
The account isn't a delegated administrator for IAM Identity Center
The permission set wasn't provisioned to the account
Identity Center supports assignments to individual users only, not groups

explanation:
Why this is correct:
The permission set must be provisioned to the account (which creates the role) before users see access.

Why the other options are wrong:
• IdP sync delay: possible but not the stated cause.
• Delegated admin: not required.
• Users only: groups are supported.

Key takeaway: assign and provision permission sets.

stem: A security architect is deciding between using AWS IAM Identity Center permission sets versus configuring a SAML 2.0 identity provider directly in each AWS account's IAM console with hand-maintained IAM roles. Which factor is the strongest justification for choosing IAM Identity Center in a 25-account AWS Organization?

choices.text: Configuring SAML providers per account is not supported by IAM
Identity Center syncs permission-set roles to all assigned accounts
Identity Center removes the need for any IAM roles in member accounts
Identity Center is the only method that issues temporary security credentials

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Identity Center creates and updates roles from permission sets in all assigned accounts, centralizing management. Per-account SAML providers require maintaining roles in each account.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Per-account SAML unsupported: supported.
• No roles needed: it creates roles.
• Only method for temporary credentials: SAML also gives temporary credentials.

Key takeaway: central permission management → Identity Center.

stem: An admin updated a permission set, but users in some accounts still see old permissions, and in one account a local admin edited the AWSReservedSSO role directly. What is true?

choices.text: Local edits to the SSO role are the recommended way to customize access
Permission sets apply only to the management account
Permission sets are evaluated live by Identity Center, not IAM
Sets become IAM roles per account; reprovision to update or overwrite

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Identity Center creates and manages an IAM role in each assigned account from the permission set. Updates reach accounts when the permission set is provisioned, and local edits to these managed roles are unsupported and can be overwritten.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Live evaluation: IAM evaluates the role in each account.
• Local edits: not a supported customization path.
• Management account only: permission sets apply to any assigned account.

Key takeaway: permission set → managed IAM role per account; reprovision after changes.

stem: A company enables attribute-based access control in AWS IAM Identity Center and maps a CostCenter attribute from its external identity provider to be passed as a session tag. Permission sets use policies referencing aws:PrincipalTag/CostCenter to scope access to resources tagged with the matching cost center. After enabling this, some users can still access resources from other cost centers. What should the security team check first?

choices.text: Whether the policies actually compare aws:PrincipalTag/CostCenter to the resource tag
Whether the users have enabled MFA on their sign-in
Whether AWS Config rules exist for the CostCenter tag
Whether the account is the Organizations management account

explanation:
Why this is correct:
ABAC only works if policies compare aws:PrincipalTag/CostCenter with resource tags. Check the policy conditions.

Why the other options are wrong:
• MFA: unrelated.
• Config rules: unrelated.
• Management account: unrelated.

Key takeaway: ABAC requires tag-comparing policies.

stem: A mobile application needs to let customers sign up and sign in with email/password (with optional MFA), and after authentication the app must call Amazon S3 directly from the device using short-lived, least-privilege AWS credentials scoped to that user's own folder in a bucket. Which combination of Amazon Cognito components should the team use?

choices.text: A Cognito identity pool alone with unauthenticated identities for all users
A Cognito user pool alone, using the ID token directly as AWS credentials for S3
IAM Identity Center with a SAML application pointing at the mobile app
A user pool for sign-in plus an identity pool for scoped IAM credentials

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A user pool handles sign-up and sign-in (with MFA), and an identity pool exchanges tokens for scoped temporary AWS credentials.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Identity pool unauthenticated only: no sign-in.
• User pool ID token as AWS credentials: it isn't.
• Identity Center: workforce, not customers.

Key takeaway: app users + AWS access → user pool + identity pool.

stem: Users successfully sign in to an Amazon Cognito user pool and receive valid tokens, but calls to obtain AWS credentials from the associated Cognito identity pool fail with an error indicating the role cannot be assumed. The identity pool's authenticated role mapping is set to use rules based on a custom token claim. What should the team verify first?

choices.text: That the user pool app client has a client secret configured
The role trust for cognito-identity and the identity pool's role mapping
That CloudFront is configured in front of the Cognito hosted UI
That the identity pool is in the same account as the S3 bucket

explanation:
Why this is correct:
GetCredentialsForIdentity fails if the IAM role's trust policy doesn't trust cognito-identity.amazonaws.com with the right conditions, or if role mapping is misconfigured.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Client secret: user pool concern.
• CloudFront: unrelated.
• Same account as bucket: not required.

Key takeaway: identity pool issues → role trust and mappings.

stem: A SPA uses Cognito user pool hosted UI. The backend API must authorize requests, and the app must keep users signed in for 30 days without re-entering passwords. Which tokens should be used how?

choices.text: Refresh token sent on every API call as a bearer token
ID token as AWS credentials to call S3 and the API
Session token from STS returned directly by the user pool
Access token to call the API; refresh token for new tokens

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Cognito returns ID, access, and refresh tokens. APIs should authorize with the access token (scopes), the ID token describes the user to the app, and the refresh token gets new tokens without re-authentication for its configured lifetime.

Why the other options are wrong:
• ID token as AWS credentials: it's a JWT, not AWS credentials; those come from identity pools.
• Refresh token on API calls: exposes a long-lived token and isn't meant for authorization.
• STS session tokens: not issued by user pools.

Key takeaway: API authorization → access token; identity → ID token; longevity → refresh token.

stem: A SaaS company wants each tenant's users to only access that tenant's data in DynamoDB using IAM policy conditions based on a TenantID attribute, and the TenantID must come from a trusted source rather than a value the client can freely edit in a custom attribute. Which approach best achieves this while integrating with Cognito identity pools for ABAC?

choices.text: Disable identity pools and hardcode one IAM role per tenant without tags
Store TenantID in client local storage and pass it as a header to DynamoDB
Let users set custom:tenant_id at sign-up and reference it in IAM policies
Inject TenantID via Pre Token Generation and map it to a principal tag

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A Pre Token Generation trigger can add a trusted TenantID claim, mapped to a principal tag for IAM conditions, so users can't set it themselves.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Hardcoded roles per tenant: scaling issues.
• Client-supplied header: untrusted.
• User-set custom attribute: users could change it.

Key takeaway: tenant isolation needs trusted claims.

stem: A company runs Active Directory Federation Services (AD FS) on-premises and wants employees to federate into AWS accounts using their existing corporate credentials, without IAM Identity Center. Which combination of steps correctly implements SAML 2.0 federation for console access?

choices.text: Create an OIDC identity provider in IAM pointing at the AD FS metadata URL
SAML provider from AD FS metadata, a trusting role, and Role claims in assertions
Create an IAM user per employee and enable SAML as a password policy
Configure AD FS to call the IAM CreateUser API with a service account

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Create a SAML identity provider in IAM from the AD FS metadata, a role that trusts it, and configure AD FS to send Role and RoleSessionName claims.

Why the other options are wrong:
• OIDC provider for AD FS: SAML is the fit here.
• IAM user per employee: not federation.
• AD FS calling CreateUser: not federation.

Key takeaway: SAML federation = provider + trusting role + claims.

stem: Employees federating into AWS through an on-premises SAML IdP intermittently receive an error stating the SAML assertion has expired, even though sign-in appears to happen promptly. What is the most likely root cause?

choices.text: Clock skew on the IdP server versus assertion validity windows
MFA was not enforced on the SAML identity provider
The IAM role's maximum session duration is set too high
The SAML provider metadata was uploaded in the wrong AWS Region

explanation:
Why this is correct:
SAML assertions have validity windows. Clock skew on the IdP server makes assertions appear expired or not yet valid.

Why the other options are wrong:
• MFA not enforced: different error.
• Session duration too high: different error.
• Wrong Region: IAM is global.

Key takeaway: intermittent SAML validity errors → check clocks.

stem: A DevOps team wants a GitHub Actions workflow to deploy to AWS without storing long-lived IAM access keys as GitHub secrets. Which approach follows AWS security best practices?

choices.text: GitHub OIDC provider and a role trust scoped by sub/aud
A long-lived IAM access key stored as encrypted GitHub Actions secrets
The account root user's access keys embedded in the workflow YAML
An IAM user for the runner whose password is rotated every 90 days

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Registering GitHub's OIDC provider and scoping the role trust with sub and aud conditions lets workflows get temporary credentials without stored keys.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Stored access keys: long-term.
• Root keys: never.
• IAM user password: not for API access.

Key takeaway: CI without keys → OIDC federation.

stem: A security team is evaluating whether to use SAML 2.0 federation or OIDC federation for a new workload identity use case: allowing a Kubernetes service account running in an external, non-AWS Kubernetes cluster to assume an IAM role. Which statement correctly compares the two for this scenario?

choices.text: Both SAML and OIDC federation require IAM Identity Center to be enabled first
OIDC cannot be used for workload identities; only SAML supports them
SAML is required because OIDC is supported only for Cognito user pools
OIDC: register the cluster issuer and use AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity

explanation:
Why this is correct:
For workloads with an OIDC issuer (such as a Kubernetes cluster), register the issuer and use AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Both need Identity Center: no.
• OIDC not for workloads: it's common for them.
• OIDC only for Cognito: false.

Key takeaway: workload identity → OIDC.

stem: A CI/CD pipeline configured with AWS IAM OIDC federation to assume a role receives AccessDenied on the sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity call. The IAM OIDC provider was created correctly with the right thumbprint and issuer URL. What is the most likely misconfiguration in the IAM role's trust policy?

choices.text: The pipeline is using an access key instead of a session token
The trust conditions don't match the token's aud and sub claims
The role's permissions policy lacks an Allow for the target service
The OIDC provider was created in a different AWS partition

explanation:
Why this is correct:
AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity fails if the trust policy's conditions don't match the token's aud and sub claims.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Access key instead of token: not this flow.
• Missing permissions policy: affects later calls, not assuming the role.
• Different partition: unlikely.

Key takeaway: OIDC trust conditions must match token claims.

stem: A security team wants to deny all IAM actions except a small set needed to configure MFA, for any IAM user who has not yet enabled MFA, while allowing full access once MFA is enabled and present in the session. Which IAM policy approach correctly implements this without locking users out?

choices.text: Require MFA via root account settings, which IAM users inherit automatically
Deny all actions unless aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent is true, with no exceptions
An SCP with a Deny on iam:* for the entire organization
Deny without MFA, except self-service MFA setup actions

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Deny all actions when MFA is absent, except the self-service actions needed to set up MFA (such as iam:CreateVirtualMFADevice and EnableMFADevice).

Why the other options are wrong:
• Root settings inherited: no.
• Deny everything without exceptions: users can't set up MFA.
• SCP denying iam:*: too broad.

Key takeaway: MFA enforcement needs a bootstrap exception.

stem: A security team is choosing between enforcing MFA through an IAM identity-based policy condition on aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent versus enforcing it through a service control policy (SCP) with the same condition key at the AWS Organizations level. Which tradeoff is accurate?

choices.text: SCPs can grant permissions beyond IAM policies, making them stronger for MFA
aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent cannot be evaluated in SCPs, only in identity policies
Identity policies apply organization-wide automatically, making SCPs redundant
SCPs apply uniformly across the OU but never grant permissions themselves

explanation:
Why this is correct:
SCPs apply uniformly across the OU but never grant permissions. Identity policies can be edited by account admins and apply per principal.

Why the other options are wrong:
• SCPs grant permissions: they don't.
• Condition not in SCPs: SCPs support conditions.
• Identity policies org-wide: they're per principal.

Key takeaway: SCP = uniform ceiling; identity policy = per-principal.

stem: Administrators were phished via a fake AWS sign-in page that relayed TOTP codes in real time. Which MFA type would have prevented this?

choices.text: Hardware TOTP tokens kept in a safe and used only by administrators
SMS codes to registered phones
FIDO2/WebAuthn security keys bound to the real origin
Virtual TOTP apps with shorter 15-second codes

explanation:
Why this is correct:
FIDO2/WebAuthn keys cryptographically bind the sign-in to the legitimate domain, so a relay site can't use the response. Any code a user can type (TOTP or SMS) can be relayed.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Shorter TOTP: still relayable in real time.
• SMS: relayable, and also vulnerable to SIM swap.
• Hardware TOTP: still produces relayable codes.

Key takeaway: phishing-resistant = origin-bound (FIDO2).

stem: A company wants to allow IAM users to perform routine read-only operations without MFA, but require that any request to delete an S3 bucket, modify an IAM policy, or disable CloudTrail logging include a valid MFA context in the session. Which policy design meets this requirement?

choices.text: A boundary granting iam:* only with MFA, removed for read-only users
AWS Config rules that reverse sensitive actions performed without MFA
Require MFA for every API call
Deny only sensitive actions when MFA is absent (BoolIfExists)

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A Deny on only sensitive actions with BoolIfExists aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent false requires MFA where it matters without blocking read-only work.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Boundary removed for read-only: fragile.
• Config reversal: after the fact.
• MFA for every call: disruptive.

Key takeaway: require MFA selectively for sensitive actions.

stem: A role's identity policy allows s3:*, the bucket policy allows the role, and a permissions boundary allows s3:*, but an SCP denies s3:DeleteObject. What happens when the role deletes an object?

choices.text: Denied only if the bucket is in another account
Allowed: three policies allow it and only one denies
Allowed: resource policies override SCPs in the same account
Denied: an explicit Deny in any applicable policy wins

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Policy evaluation checks for explicit denies across all applicable policy types first. Any explicit Deny, including from an SCP, ends the evaluation with deny, regardless of allows elsewhere.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Majority rules: IAM doesn't count votes.
• Resource policy overriding SCP: SCPs limit principals in member accounts regardless.
• Cross-account only: the SCP applies in the same account too.

Key takeaway: explicit Deny anywhere = denied.

stem: A developer's IAM identity-based policy explicitly allows dynamodb:PutItem on a specific table, and no SCP or resource-based policy denies the action, yet the developer receives AccessDenied. Investigation shows the developer's IAM user has a permission boundary attached. What is the most likely explanation?

choices.text: The boundary omits dynamodb:PutItem; effective permissions are the intersection
Permissions boundaries apply only to roles, never users, so this can't be the cause
The boundary must duplicate the identity policy exactly, or IAM always denies
DynamoDB does not support permissions boundaries as an evaluation concept

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A permissions boundary limits effective permissions. If it doesn't include dynamodb:PutItem, the identity policy's allow has no effect.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Boundaries only for roles: they apply to users and roles.
• Must duplicate exactly: it must include the action.
• DynamoDB unsupported: boundaries are IAM-wide.

Key takeaway: effective = identity ∩ boundary.

stem: A platform team wants to let application developers create and manage their own IAM roles for their services, but must guarantee that no developer-created role can ever exceed a fixed set of permissions or grant broader access than developers themselves have. Which control should the platform team apply?

choices.text: Grant developers AdministratorAccess and trust them to self-police
Use resource-based policies instead, since roles don't support boundaries
Rely only on Config rules to detect overly permissive roles after creation
Require a specific permissions boundary on every role developers create

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Requiring a specific permissions boundary on every role developers create keeps delegated roles within safe limits.

Why the other options are wrong:
• AdministratorAccess: unsafe.
• Roles don't support boundaries: they do.
• Config detection only: after the fact.

Key takeaway: delegated role creation → boundaries.

stem: An engineer in Account A attempts to assume an IAM role in Account B. The role's trust policy in Account B correctly lists Account A's account ID as a trusted principal, but the sts:AssumeRole call still fails with AccessDenied. What additional configuration is most likely missing?

choices.text: The role in Account B also needs a bucket policy referencing Account A
Cross-account AssumeRole calls are denied unless AWS Organizations is used
The trust policy must list the user ARN, never just the account ID
The caller's policy in Account A doesn't allow sts:AssumeRole on the role

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Besides the target's trust policy, the caller in Account A needs an identity policy allowing sts:AssumeRole on that role.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Bucket policy: unrelated.
• Organizations required: no.
• Must list user ARN: account ID trust works.

Key takeaway: AssumeRole needs trust and caller permission.

stem: Which statement correctly compares service control policies (SCPs), permission boundaries, and resource-based policies within the overall IAM policy evaluation logic?

choices.text: Boundaries apply at the Organizations level, while SCPs apply to single principals
Only resource-based policies can contain explicit Deny statements
SCPs and boundaries only cap permissions; resource policies can grant access
SCPs, boundaries, and resource policies are interchangeable in every service

explanation:
Why this is correct:
SCPs and permissions boundaries only limit permissions. Resource-based policies can grant access, including to other accounts.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Boundaries at org level: they're per principal.
• Only resource policies deny: all can deny.
• Interchangeable: they differ.

Key takeaway: limits vs. grants.

stem: Account A owns an S3 bucket and needs to grant a role in Account B read access to a specific prefix in that bucket. Which combination of actions correctly grants this cross-account access using least privilege?

choices.text: Create an IAM user in Account A and share its access keys with Account B
Make the bucket public and rely on obscure object keys for security
A bucket policy for the role plus a matching identity policy in Account B
A bucket policy in Account A only; Account B needs no IAM policy

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A bucket policy in Account A granting B's role access to the prefix, plus an identity policy in B allowing it, enables cross-account access.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Shared IAM user keys: insecure.
• Public bucket: insecure.
• Bucket policy only: B's role also needs permission (cross-account).

Key takeaway: cross-account = both sides.

stem: An application role has an IAM identity-based policy allowing kms:Decrypt on a specific KMS key ARN, but calls to decrypt data using that key fail with AccessDeniedException. The key was created with a custom key policy that replaced the default key policy. What is the most likely cause?

choices.text: The key policy neither grants the role nor delegates to IAM policies
IAM identity policies are ignored entirely for KMS actions
The role needs an SCP explicitly allowing kms:Decrypt
KMS keys do not support resource-based policies at all

explanation:
Why this is correct:
KMS requires the key policy to allow the principal or delegate to IAM policies (via the account root statement). Otherwise the IAM allow is ignored.

Why the other options are wrong:
• IAM ignored entirely: not if the key policy delegates.
• SCP allow needed: SCPs don't grant.
• No resource policies: key policies are resource policies.

Key takeaway: KMS access starts with the key policy.

stem: A security team wants to ensure that an S3 bucket can only be accessed by principals belonging to their own AWS Organization, even if a bucket policy is later misconfigured to grant broader access by mistake. Which control provides this defense-in-depth guarantee at the resource level?

choices.text: Enable S3 Versioning on the bucket
Enable S3 Block Public Access only, with no policy conditions
A bucket policy Deny when aws:PrincipalOrgID doesn't match
Rely on IAM user policies in each external account to prevent access

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A bucket policy denying access when aws:PrincipalOrgID doesn't match the organization's ID blocks principals outside the org.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Versioning: unrelated.
• Block Public Access only: doesn't stop authenticated outside accounts.
• External account policies: not under your control.

Key takeaway: org-only access → aws:PrincipalOrgID.

stem: A service needs to grant a Lambda function temporary, fine-grained permission to use a specific KMS key for encryption operations on behalf of a specific end user, with permissions created and revoked programmatically at high frequency without modifying the key policy each time. Which mechanism is best suited to this use case compared to editing the KMS key policy directly?

choices.text: Edit the key policy on every request, adding and removing statements per session
Use an SCP that is updated per request to allow or deny the KMS action
Grants aren't supported by KMS; only key policies and IAM policies exist
Use KMS grants created and retired through the API

explanation:
Why this is correct:
KMS grants give temporary, fine-grained permissions to a principal and can be created and retired via API without editing the key policy.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Edit key policy per request: fragile.
• SCP per request: inappropriate.
• Grants unsupported: they exist.

Key takeaway: temporary key access → KMS grants.

stem: A KMS key in Account A must be used by a Lambda role in Account B. Which policies must allow the call?

choices.text: A's key policy allowing B, and B's role identity policy
An SCP in Account A that grants Account B permission to use the key
Only the key policy in Account A
Only the role's identity policy in Account B

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Cross-account access needs both sides: the resource-based policy (here, the key policy) must trust the external principal, and the principal's identity policy must allow the action on that key.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Identity policy only: the key owner must also allow it.
• Key policy only: for cross-account calls, the caller's own policy must allow it too.
• SCPs: never grant permissions.

Key takeaway: cross-account = resource policy + identity policy.

stem: A company has 200 projects and wants engineers to access only resources tagged with their own project, without writing a policy per project. Engineers sign in through an IdP that sends a project attribute. Which approach fits?

choices.text: One role per project with resource ARNs listed
One account per project
ABAC matching aws:PrincipalTag to aws:ResourceTag, with session tags
Resource policies on each resource listing every engineer's ARN

explanation:
Why this is correct:
ABAC compares principal tags (from session tags passed by the IdP) with resource tags in a small set of policies, so new projects need only tags, not new policies.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Role per project: 200 roles and policies to maintain.
• Resource policies with ARNs: unmanageable at scale.
• Account per project: heavy operational overhead.

Key takeaway: scale permissions with tags (ABAC).

stem: A multi-tenant SaaS platform runs on shared AWS infrastructure where each customer's resources are tagged with a project tag matching a project identifier. The platform wants engineers to only be able to access resources belonging to the project they are assigned to, without maintaining a separate IAM role per project as the number of projects grows into the hundreds. Which policy design best achieves this at scale?

choices.text: A unique role and managed policy per project, updated for every new project
Resource policies that list every engineer's ARN on every resource
A few ABAC policies matching principal and resource project tags
One broad policy for all engineers

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A few ABAC policies comparing principal and resource project tags scale to many tenants without per-project roles.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Role per project: explodes roles.
• ARNs in resource policies: unmanageable.
• One broad policy: no isolation.

Key takeaway: multi-tenant scale → ABAC.

stem: An ABAC policy grants access when aws:PrincipalTag/Department equals aws:ResourceTag/Department. An engineer tagged with Department=Finance reports AccessDenied when accessing a resource that appears, in the console, to be tagged Department: Finance. What is a likely cause worth investigating first?

choices.text: IAM supports ABAC only for EC2 instances, not this resource type
ABAC ignores case, so the policy syntax itself must be invalid
The resource must be recreated with the tag for ABAC to take effect
Tag keys and values are case-sensitive, so department/Department don't match

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Tag keys and values are case-sensitive in policy evaluation, so department and Department don't match.

Why the other options are wrong:
• ABAC only for EC2: false.
• ABAC ignores case: false.
• Recreate resource: not required.

Key takeaway: tag case must match exactly.

stem: A security architect is weighing attribute-based access control (ABAC) against a traditional role-based access control (RBAC) approach of creating a distinct IAM role per team/project combination. Which tradeoff accurately favors ABAC as the organization scales to hundreds of teams and projects?

choices.text: RBAC always needs fewer policies than ABAC, regardless of scale
ABAC scales by tagging; RBAC needs a new role per team/project
ABAC works only with IAM Identity Center, not with plain IAM roles
ABAC cannot be combined with explicit Deny statements, unlike RBAC

explanation:
Why this is correct:
ABAC scales by tagging principals and resources, while RBAC needs new roles or policies per team or project.

Why the other options are wrong:
• RBAC fewer policies: not at scale.
• ABAC only with Identity Center: works with IAM roles too.
• ABAC can't use Deny: it can.

Key takeaway: ABAC scales with tags.

stem: A company federates workforce users into AWS via a SAML identity provider and wants those users' IAM sessions to carry a CostCenter attribute sourced from the IdP, so that IAM ABAC policies can restrict access to only resources tagged with the matching cost center. How should this be implemented using SAML federation with IAM roles?

choices.text: Send a PrincipalTag SAML attribute that STS applies as a session tag
Session tags can't come from SAML; only AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity supports them
Use an S3 object tag on each user's home folder instead of a session tag
Tag every federated role with CostCenter manually, without IdP attributes

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Sending a PrincipalTag SAML attribute makes STS apply it as a session tag, which policies can use for ABAC.

Why the other options are wrong:
• No session tags from SAML: they're supported.
• S3 object tags: not session identity.
• Manual role tags: not per user.

Key takeaway: per-user attributes → session tags.

stem: A SaaS app needs rules like 'managers can approve expenses under $10,000 in their department', changed without redeploying code and evaluated consistently across services. Which fits?

choices.text: AWS WAF custom rules
Cognito user pool groups mapped to application roles
IAM policies for each end user
Amazon Verified Permissions with Cedar policies

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Verified Permissions externalizes application authorization into Cedar policies, evaluated via the IsAuthorized API, with attribute-based conditions (amount, department) and no code redeploys.

Why the other options are wrong:
• IAM per user: IAM governs AWS resources, not app decisions for end users.
• Groups only: too coarse for attribute conditions.
• WAF: filters requests, not business authorization.

Key takeaway: app-level fine-grained authz → Verified Permissions.

stem: A development team has built a custom multi-tenant document-sharing application where authorization logic (which user can view, edit, or share a specific document) is currently hardcoded as if/else statements scattered throughout the application code, making audits and updates difficult. Which AWS service should they adopt to externalize and centralize this application-level authorization logic?

choices.text: IAM resource-based policies attached to each document in the application database
Verified Permissions with Cedar policies, calling IsAuthorized
GuardDuty findings used to approve or deny each document request
WAF rules that inspect each request body for authorization logic

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Verified Permissions externalizes app authorization into Cedar policies evaluated by IsAuthorized.

Why the other options are wrong:
• IAM policies on documents: IAM isn't for app-level resources.
• GuardDuty: detection.
• WAF: request filtering, not authorization.

Key takeaway: app authorization → Verified Permissions.

stem: How should a security architect explain the relationship between AWS IAM and Amazon Verified Permissions when designing authorization for a cloud-native application?

choices.text: IAM governs AWS API access; Verified Permissions governs app authorization
Verified Permissions replaces IAM entirely for applications that adopt it
Verified Permissions controls only S3 access, as a bucket policy alternative
IAM and Verified Permissions are mutually exclusive in one architecture

explanation:
Why this is correct:
IAM governs access to AWS APIs. Verified Permissions governs authorization decisions inside your application. They complement each other.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Replaces IAM: no.
• S3 only: no.
• Mutually exclusive: no.

Key takeaway: AWS access vs. app access.

stem: In the Cedar policy language used by Amazon Verified Permissions, which elements does a basic permit or forbid policy statement combine to make an authorization decision?

choices.text: Principal, action, resource, and optional when/unless conditions
Only an IAM ARN and an AWS Region
A CloudFormation stack name and a deployment timestamp
An EC2 security group ID and a VPC route table entry

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A Cedar policy specifies principal, action, and resource, with optional when and unless conditions.

Why the other options are wrong:
• ARN and Region only: incomplete.
• Stack name and timestamp: unrelated.
• SG and route table: unrelated.

Key takeaway: Cedar = principal, action, resource, conditions.

stem: A team using Amazon Verified Permissions finds that an IsAuthorized API call unexpectedly returns a Deny decision for an action that the team believes should be permitted based on the policies they authored in the policy store. Which of the following is a reasonable first step to diagnose the issue?

choices.text: Check that request entity types and IDs match the schema and policies (default deny)
Assume IsAuthorized is malfunctioning and open a support case without reviewing policies
Check the account's SCPs, since Verified Permissions decisions are controlled by SCPs
Delete and recreate the policy store, since Deny decisions cannot be debugged

explanation:
Why this is correct:
An unexpected Deny often means the request's entity types or IDs don't match the schema or policy definitions. Check them first.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Service malfunction: unlikely.
• SCPs: don't affect Verified Permissions decisions.
• Recreate the store: unnecessary.

Key takeaway: debug by checking entity types and IDs.

stem: A company runs a fleet of EC2 instances behind a Network Load Balancer. Regulatory requirements mandate that TLS traffic remain encrypted from the client all the way to the application process on each instance, with no intermediate decryption at the load balancer. Which NLB configuration satisfies this requirement?

choices.text: A TLS listener with an ACM certificate that terminates and re-encrypts to targets
A TCP listener, terminating TLS on the instances
An SSL policy on the NLB that forces TLS 1.2 termination at the load balancer
An HTTPS listener with an ACM certificate and target group stickiness

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A TCP listener passes TLS through unchanged, so TLS terminates on the instances end to end.

Why the other options are wrong:
• TLS listener: terminates at the NLB.
• SSL policy forcing termination: terminates at the NLB.
• HTTPS listener: NLBs don't have HTTPS listeners.

Key takeaway: end-to-end TLS through NLB → TCP passthrough.

stem: A security engineer requested a public ACM certificate using DNS validation for a domain whose Route 53 hosted zone lives in a different AWS account than the one requesting the certificate. Three days later, the certificate status is still Pending Validation. What is the most likely cause and correct remediation?

choices.text: Certificate requests expire after 72 hours
Validation can't work across accounts, so an email-validated certificate is needed
The certificate must be requested in the hosted zone's account; no workaround exists
The CNAME record wasn't created in the other account's zone

explanation:
Why this is correct:
DNS validation needs the CNAME record in the zone that's authoritative for the domain, even if it's in another account.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Requests expire in 72 hours: they can remain pending longer.
• Cross-account impossible: just create the record there.
• Must request in the zone's account: no.

Key takeaway: create the validation CNAME wherever the zone lives.

stem: A global media company wants to minimize latency for HTTPS requests from users worldwide while serving static and dynamic content from an S3 origin and an ALB origin. Which approach both terminates TLS closest to the end user and centralizes certificate management for the custom domain?

choices.text: An NLB in front of CloudFront to terminate TLS at the edge
S3 static website hosting with HTTPS on the bucket endpoint
Regional ALBs with Route 53 latency routing and regional certificates
CloudFront in front of both origins with an ACM certificate issued in us-east-1

explanation:
Why this is correct:
CloudFront in front of both origins, with an ACM certificate in us-east-1, terminates TLS at edge locations near users.

Why the other options are wrong:
• NLB in front of CloudFront: backwards.
• S3 website endpoint: no HTTPS.
• Regional ALBs with latency routing: no edge termination.

Key takeaway: global TLS latency → CloudFront.

stem: An internal microservices platform running on ECS needs certificates for service-to-service TLS within a private VPC, but the organization does not want these certificates to be publicly trusted or discoverable via Certificate Transparency logs. Which ACM capability should be used to issue these certificates?

choices.text: ACM public certificates with DNS validation
ACM certificates with email validation instead of DNS
Self-signed OpenSSL certificates distributed via S3
AWS Private CA issuing private certificates trusted only internally

explanation:
Why this is correct:
AWS Private CA issues private certificates trusted only inside the organization, suited to service-to-service TLS.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Public ACM: for public names.
• Email validation: still public.
• Self-signed via S3: unmanaged trust.

Key takeaway: internal TLS → Private CA.

stem: A financial services company must verify the identity of every client connecting to its REST API hosted on Amazon API Gateway, rejecting any TLS connection where the client does not present a certificate signed by the company's trusted CA. Which API Gateway feature enables this?

choices.text: API Gateway resource policies restricting the source VPC endpoint
Mutual TLS on a custom domain with an S3 truststore
A Lambda authorizer that validates a bearer token
WAF rules that inspect the TLS handshake for client certificates

explanation:
Why this is correct:
API Gateway mutual TLS on a custom domain, with a truststore in S3, verifies each client's certificate.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Resource policies by VPC endpoint: not client identity.
• Bearer tokens: not certificates.
• WAF can't inspect client certs: not how it works.

Key takeaway: client certificate auth → API Gateway mTLS.

stem: Users report intermittent TLS handshake failures when connecting to an application behind a Network Load Balancer configured with a TLS listener. Investigation shows the ACM certificate attached to the listener expired two days ago and was not renewed. What is the most likely reason automatic renewal did not occur?

choices.text: NLB TLS listeners aren't eligible for ACM renewal
ACM auto-renews only certificates attached to CloudFront distributions
It was an imported certificate, which ACM doesn't renew
The account has exceeded its monthly certificate renewal quota

explanation:
Why this is correct:
ACM doesn't renew imported certificates. The imported certificate expired, causing handshake failures.

Why the other options are wrong:
• NLB not eligible: ACM-issued certificates renew on NLB.
• CloudFront only: false.
• Renewal quota: no.

Key takeaway: imported certs need manual renewal.

stem: An organization wants to enforce mutual TLS (mTLS) so that only clients presenting a certificate issued by their internal PKI can establish connections through their internet-facing Application Load Balancer, while still allowing ALB to perform Layer 7 routing. Which configuration should they implement?

choices.text: WAF rules rejecting requests without an Authorization header
An ALB listener security policy that requires TLS 1.3 only
ALB can't do mTLS, so a Classic Load Balancer must be used
ALB HTTPS listener with mutual TLS in verify mode and an S3 trust store

explanation:
Why this is correct:
ALB supports mutual TLS in verify mode with a trust store in S3 holding the CA bundle.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Authorization header rules: not mTLS.
• TLS 1.3 policy: not client auth.
• CLB required: ALB supports mTLS.

Key takeaway: mTLS at the load balancer → ALB verify mode.

stem: An ACM certificate for app.example.com was requested in eu-west-1 for a CloudFront distribution, but it doesn't appear in the distribution settings. What should be done?

choices.text: Attach it to an ALB origin in eu-west-1 instead
Request (or import) the certificate in us-east-1
Validate it again with email validation
Copy the certificate from eu-west-1 with the ACM API

explanation:
Why this is correct:
CloudFront uses ACM certificates from us-east-1 only, regardless of where the origin or viewers are.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Copying: public ACM certificates can't be copied between Regions.
• ALB origin: secures the origin connection, not the viewer-facing domain on CloudFront.
• Revalidation: validation method isn't the problem.

Key takeaway: CloudFront certificates live in us-east-1.

stem: A newly established Site-to-Site VPN connection between a customer gateway and AWS shows both IPsec tunnels in a DOWN state, and packet captures on the customer side show the local gateway is sending IKE negotiation requests. Which mismatch is the most probable root cause?

choices.text: The virtual private gateway has not been attached to an Elastic IP address
The VPC has more than one route table associated with the subnet
The VPN uses static routing instead of BGP
Mismatched pre-shared key or IKE phase 1/2 parameters

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Tunnels that won't come up usually mean a mismatched pre-shared key or IKE phase 1/phase 2 parameters.

Why the other options are wrong:
• VGW EIP: not how VGWs work.
• Multiple route tables: unrelated.
• Static routing: doesn't stop tunnels establishing.

Key takeaway: tunnels down → check PSK and IKE settings.

stem: Every new EBS volume in a Region must be encrypted with a specific customer managed key, including volumes created by services and by users who forget to choose encryption. Which setting fits?

choices.text: A tag policy requiring an Encrypted tag
An SCP denying CreateVolume unless encryption is requested
A Config rule that flags unencrypted volumes
EBS encryption by default with that CMK as the default key

explanation:
Why this is correct:
EBS encryption by default is a per-Region account setting that encrypts all new volumes and snapshot copies automatically, and you can set the default KMS key to your CMK.

Why the other options are wrong:
• SCP: blocks some calls rather than encrypting them, and can break services.
• Config rule: detective only.
• Tag policy: tags don't encrypt anything.

Key takeaway: encrypt everything automatically → encryption by default + default CMK.

stem: An administrator attempts to copy an encrypted Amazon RDS snapshot from us-east-1 to eu-west-1 and the copy operation fails with a key-related error. What is the correct fix?

choices.text: Grant the source Region's KMS key a resource policy allowing eu-west-1 to decrypt it directly
RDS snapshots cannot be copied across Regions if they are encrypted; only unencrypted snapshots support cross-Region copy
Decrypt the snapshot before copying, then re-encrypt it after it arrives in eu-west-1
Specify a KMS key that exists in the destination Region (eu-west-1) as the target encryption key for the copy operation

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Cross-Region snapshot copies must be encrypted with a KMS key in the destination Region.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Source key policy for another Region: keys are Regional.
• Can't copy encrypted snapshots: they can.
• Decrypt first: unnecessary.

Key takeaway: cross-Region encrypted copies → destination-Region key.

stem: A healthcare records company must retain compliance documents for 7 years in Amazon S3 such that no user, including the AWS account root user, can delete or overwrite the objects before the retention period expires, even if credentials are compromised. Which S3 feature and mode should be used?

choices.text: S3 Object Lock in Governance mode with a 7-year retention period
S3 Lifecycle policies that transition objects to Glacier Deep Archive after creation
S3 Object Lock in Compliance mode with a 7-year retention period
S3 Versioning combined with an MFA Delete bucket policy

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Object Lock in Compliance mode prevents deletion or retention changes by anyone, including root, for 7 years.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Governance mode: privileged users can bypass.
• Lifecycle: moves data; doesn't lock it.
• MFA Delete: the owner can disable it.

Key takeaway: no one can delete → Compliance mode.

stem: A company archives regulatory data in Amazon S3 Glacier and wants to enforce, in a way that cannot later be altered by any IAM principal including administrators, a policy that prevents deletion of archives for 10 years. Which feature should they use?

choices.text: Object Lock compliance mode on Glacier Deep Archive objects
A vault access policy with an explicit Deny for deletes
A permissions boundary denying glacier:DeleteArchive to all users
Glacier Vault Lock with a vault lock policy that becomes immutable once locked

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Glacier Vault Lock applies a vault lock policy that becomes immutable once locked, enforcing retention controls.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Object Lock on Deep Archive objects: applies to S3 buckets, not Glacier vaults.
• Vault access policy: can be changed.
• Permissions boundary: can be changed.

Key takeaway: immutable Glacier vault controls → Vault Lock.

stem: A defense contractor must store cryptographic key material in a single-tenant, FIPS 140-2 Level 3 validated hardware device under their exclusive control, because their regulatory framework prohibits AWS from having any ability to access the unencrypted key material, which AWS KMS's shared HSM fleet does not satisfy. Which service should they use?

choices.text: AWS Secrets Manager with automatic rotation enabled
AWS CloudHSM (dedicated, single-tenant cluster)
AWS KMS with an AWS managed key
AWS KMS with a customer managed key in the default key store

explanation:
Why this is correct:
CloudHSM provides a single-tenant, FIPS 140-2 Level 3 validated HSM cluster under the customer's control.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Secrets Manager: secrets storage.
• KMS AWS managed keys: shared service.
• KMS default key store: multi-tenant HSMs.

Key takeaway: single-tenant validated HSMs → CloudHSM.

stem: A security architect wants applications to keep using the familiar KMS API (Encrypt, Decrypt, GenerateDataKey) and IAM-based key policies, but requires that the underlying key material be generated, stored, and used exclusively within CloudHSM hardware that the customer controls, for regulatory reasons. What should be implemented?

choices.text: Use AWS KMS with an AWS owned key
A KMS custom key store backed by CloudHSM
Use CloudHSM's PKCS#11 library in every application instead of the KMS SDK
Envelope encryption in Secrets Manager with a CloudHSM-backed secret

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A KMS custom key store backed by CloudHSM lets apps keep using the KMS API while key material lives in the company's CloudHSM cluster.

Why the other options are wrong:
• AWS owned key: no control.
• PKCS#11 everywhere: changes applications.
• Secrets Manager: not a key store.

Key takeaway: KMS API + your HSM → custom key store.

stem: An account administrator with full IAM Administrator access attempts to use a customer managed KMS key created by another team to decrypt an S3 object, but receives an AccessDeniedException. The administrator's IAM policy grants kms:Decrypt on all resources. What is the most likely explanation?

choices.text: kms:Decrypt requires MFA to be enabled on the caller's IAM user
KMS keys ignore IAM policies entirely; only key policies matter
The key policy doesn't allow the admin (directly or via IAM delegation)
The administrator must be in the same OU as the key's creator

explanation:
Why this is correct:
IAM administrator rights don't override KMS: the key policy must allow the principal directly or delegate to IAM policies (the account root statement).

Why the other options are wrong:
• MFA requirement: not inherent.
• IAM ignored entirely: not when delegated.
• Same OU: irrelevant.

Key takeaway: key policy first for KMS.

stem: A team has an existing EBS volume attached to a running production instance that was created without encryption. They now need this volume's data encrypted at rest to meet a new compliance requirement, with minimal downtime. What is the correct sequence of steps?

choices.text: Detach the volume and run KMS EnableKeyRotation against it to encrypt existing data
Snapshot, copy with encryption, create a new volume, and swap it in
Enable EBS encryption by default; the volume is encrypted on the next reboot
Run ebs modify-volume with --encrypted to convert the volume in place

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Existing unencrypted volumes can't be encrypted in place. Snapshot, copy the snapshot with encryption, create a new volume, and swap it in.

Why the other options are wrong:
• EnableKeyRotation: unrelated.
• Encryption by default: only new volumes.
• modify-volume --encrypted: not supported.

Key takeaway: encrypt existing EBS via snapshot copy.

stem: A database team needs to enable encryption at rest on a production Amazon RDS instance that was originally launched without encryption, and cannot modify an existing instance to turn on encryption directly. What is the correct approach?

choices.text: Modify the instance and set StorageEncrypted to true in the console
Snapshot, copy with encryption and a KMS key, restore a new instance
Enable TDE in the engine, which retroactively encrypts existing storage
Ask AWS Support to perform an in-place encryption migration

explanation:
Why this is correct:
RDS encryption can't be enabled in place. Snapshot, copy with encryption and a KMS key, restore a new instance, and cut over.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Set StorageEncrypted: not allowed on existing instances.
• TDE retroactively: not the RDS mechanism.
• Support migration: not offered.

Key takeaway: encrypt existing RDS via encrypted snapshot copy.

stem: A company runs a DynamoDB global table replicated across three Regions and wants each replica's data encrypted at rest using a KMS key that shares the same key ID and key material across all Regions, simplifying key management and enabling consistent client-side encryption/decryption without Region-specific key lookups. Which KMS feature should they use?

choices.text: AWS managed keys, which have identical key material in every Region
Grants issued from one Region's key to principals in other Regions
KMS multi-Region keys (primary plus replicas)
A single-Region CMK referenced cross-Region through its key policy

explanation:
Why this is correct:
KMS multi-Region keys share key material across Regions (primary plus replicas), fitting customer managed encryption for global tables.

Why the other options are wrong:
• AWS managed keys identical across Regions: they aren't.
• Grants across Regions: keys are Regional.
• Single-Region key cross-Region: not possible.

Key takeaway: cross-Region CMKs → multi-Region keys.

stem: A team wants Amazon RDS for MySQL database credentials stored in AWS Secrets Manager to rotate automatically every 30 days without requiring any application downtime during rotation. Which rotation strategy should they configure?

choices.text: Alternating-users rotation, keeping the previous credential valid during rotation
Manual rotation via a scheduled rule that emails the DBA the new password
Disable rotation and rely only on IAM database authentication
Single-user rotation, updating the same user's password in place

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Alternating-users rotation switches between two database users, so the previous credential stays valid while the new one propagates.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Emailing passwords: insecure.
• Disable rotation: fails the requirement.
• Single-user rotation: brief window where old credentials fail.

Key takeaway: zero-downtime rotation → alternating users.

stem: A Secrets Manager rotation Lambda function configured for an RDS database consistently fails with a timeout error, and CloudWatch Logs show no connection could be established to the database host. The RDS instance resides in a private subnet with no route to the internet. What is the most likely root cause?

choices.text: The KMS key that encrypts the secret does not have rotation enabled
The rotation function isn't in a VPC that can reach RDS and Secrets Manager
The rotation role lacks the secretsmanager:GetRandomPassword permission
Rotation functions can't rotate credentials for databases in private subnets

explanation:
Why this is correct:
The rotation function must run in a VPC that can reach both the RDS instance and the Secrets Manager endpoint (via VPC endpoint or NAT). Otherwise it times out.

Why the other options are wrong:
• KMS rotation: unrelated.
• GetRandomPassword permission: would cause AccessDenied.
• Can't rotate private DBs: they can.

Key takeaway: rotation Lambdas need network paths to both.

stem: The governance team must know which of 1,200 buckets across the org contain PII, updated continuously, at controlled cost, with findings routed to Security Hub. Which approach fits?

choices.text: GuardDuty S3 Protection
Macie automated discovery via a delegated admin, integrated with Security Hub
S3 Inventory reports
Daily full Macie classification jobs over every object in every bucket

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Macie's automated sensitive data discovery samples objects across all buckets continuously for cost-effective coverage, and Macie can publish findings to Security Hub.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Daily full jobs: very costly at this scale.
• GuardDuty S3: detects access threats, not content.
• Inventory: lists objects; no classification.

Key takeaway: sensitive data in S3 → Macie; estate-wide at low cost → automated discovery.

stem: A large enterprise with 40 AWS accounts under AWS Organizations wants a single security team to run sensitive data discovery jobs against S3 buckets across all member accounts from one central location, without each account team needing to configure Macie individually. What should be implemented?

choices.text: Enable Macie in each account separately and aggregate findings in a third-party SIEM
A Macie custom data identifier shared through AWS RAM
AWS Config aggregators collecting Macie findings from each account
A Macie delegated administrator account designated through Organizations

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A Macie delegated administrator designated through Organizations manages jobs and findings for all member accounts.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Separate per account: fragmented.
• Custom identifier via RAM: not how Macie is centralized.
• Config aggregators: not Macie.

Key takeaway: org-wide Macie → delegated administrator.

stem: A security team is deciding between Amazon Macie and Amazon GuardDuty to address two separate needs: detecting compromised IAM credentials being used maliciously, and discovering S3 buckets that inadvertently contain customer PII. Which statement correctly matches each service to its purpose?

choices.text: GuardDuty for PII discovery in S3; Macie for compromised credentials
GuardDuty for threats and credentials; Macie for PII in S3
Neither service fits; AWS Config rules must be used for both needs
Both perform identical functions and are interchangeable for both needs

explanation:
Why this is correct:
GuardDuty detects threats such as compromised credentials. Macie discovers PII in S3.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Swapped: incorrect.
• Config for both: not these functions.
• Identical: different services.

Key takeaway: threats → GuardDuty; sensitive data → Macie.

stem: An application needs to encrypt a 25 MB file before storing it in S3. A developer's initial implementation calls the KMS Encrypt API directly on the full file contents and receives an error indicating the request exceeds the allowed size. What is the correct pattern to encrypt data of this size using KMS?

choices.text: Use the KMS Sign API instead of Encrypt for payloads over 4 KB
Request a quota increase to allow larger KMS Encrypt payloads
Envelope encryption: GenerateDataKey, encrypt locally, store the encrypted key
Split the file into 4 KB chunks and call KMS Encrypt on each chunk

explanation:
Why this is correct:
KMS Encrypt handles up to 4 KB. Envelope encryption generates a data key (GenerateDataKey), encrypts the file locally, and stores the encrypted data key with it.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Sign API: signing, not encryption.
• Quota increase: not possible.
• 4 KB chunks: slow and costly.

Key takeaway: large data → envelope encryption.

stem: A payments platform needs Account A to be able to use a KMS customer managed key owned by Account B to encrypt objects for exactly 24 hours during a one-time data migration, after which access must be automatically revocable without modifying the key's resource-based policy. What mechanism should Account B use?

choices.text: A permanent key policy statement for Account A, removed manually after 24 hours
A role in Account B that Account A assumes, deleted after 24 hours
Share the key through AWS RAM with a 24-hour resource share expiration
A time-bounded KMS grant, retired after the migration

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A KMS grant gives Account A temporary use of the key and can be retired after the migration, without editing the key policy.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Permanent statement removed manually: error-prone.
• Temporary role: workable but grants are purpose-built.
• RAM sharing: KMS keys aren't shared via RAM.

Key takeaway: time-bound key access → grants.

stem: A team needs to rotate an API key for a third-party SaaS service that is stored in AWS Secrets Manager. AWS Secrets Manager's built-in rotation templates only cover RDS, Redshift, and DocumentDB credential types. How should the team implement automatic rotation for this third-party API key?

choices.text: Move the key to Parameter Store, which rotates any secret type out of the box
Rotation isn't possible for non-database secrets; rotate the key manually
A custom rotation Lambda (create/set/test/finish) calling the vendor API
Enable AWS Config remediation to regenerate the key periodically

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A custom rotation Lambda implementing createSecret, setSecret, testSecret, and finishSecret can call the vendor's API to rotate the key.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Parameter Store rotation: none built in.
• Not possible: custom rotation exists.
• Config remediation: not rotation.

Key takeaway: non-database secrets → custom rotation Lambda.

stem: A security team requires that all secrets stored in AWS Secrets Manager for a regulated workload be encrypted with a customer managed KMS key that they control and can audit via CloudTrail, rather than the account's default Secrets Manager encryption key. Is this achievable, and how?

choices.text: Not achievable; secrets always use the AWS managed key aws/secretsmanager
Achievable only in the GovCloud/FedRAMP-specific partition
Achievable by specifying a customer managed KMS key on the secret
Achievable only by exporting, encrypting manually, and re-importing secrets

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Each secret can be encrypted with a customer managed KMS key you specify.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Always AWS managed: false.
• GovCloud only: false.
• Manual export and import: unnecessary.

Key takeaway: CMK for secrets → set KmsKeyId.

stem: An organization runs a Macie sensitive data discovery job configured to scan all objects in several multi-terabyte S3 buckets daily, and receives an unexpectedly large monthly Macie bill. Which change would most effectively reduce cost while still providing ongoing visibility into sensitive data risk?

choices.text: Disable Macie and rely on bucket policies to prevent sensitive uploads
Use only custom data identifiers, which are always free
