Scheduled jobs with sampling and prefix/last-modified criteria
Move data to Deep Archive, which Macie can't scan, so billing stops

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Scheduled jobs with sampling and criteria such as prefixes or last-modified dates reduce the volume scanned and cost.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Disable Macie: loses discovery.
• Custom identifiers are free: scanning still costs.
• Deep Archive to avoid scanning: evasive and impractical.

Key takeaway: control Macie cost with scoping and sampling.

stem: A backend service needs to encrypt small pieces of configuration data locally using a data key derived from a KMS customer managed key, without making a network call to KMS on every encryption operation, while still being able to decrypt via a call to KMS. Which pattern describes this correctly?

choices.text: Call KMS Encrypt for every item, since it always requires a live call anyway
Store the CMK's raw key material locally to avoid network calls
Use GenerateDataKeyWithoutPlaintext
Envelope encryption: one GenerateDataKey, local encryption

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Call GenerateDataKey once, cache the plaintext data key briefly in memory, and encrypt items locally, reducing KMS calls.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Encrypt per item: many network calls.
• Store CMK material locally: not possible and unsafe.
• WithoutPlaintext: gives no plaintext key to encrypt now.

Key takeaway: many small items → reuse a data key.

stem: A security team wants to prevent the root user in all member accounts (except the management account) from performing any actions, even if root credentials are somehow compromised, without affecting IAM users or roles. Which SCP approach achieves this per AWS best practices?

choices.text: An IAM policy denying all actions, attached to each member account's root user
A permissions boundary denying all actions, attached to each root user
An SCP denying sts:AssumeRole for OrganizationAccountAccessRole
An SCP denying all actions when aws:PrincipalArn is the root user

explanation:
Why this is correct:
An SCP denying all actions when aws:PrincipalArn is the root user blocks root usage in member accounts (SCPs don't apply to the management account).

Why the other options are wrong:
• IAM policy on accounts: can't attach to root.
• Boundary on root: not possible.
• Deny assuming OrganizationAccountAccessRole: different concern.

Key takeaway: restrict member root → SCP on root ARN.

stem: Control Tower shows a guardrail that stops users from disabling CloudTrail and another that reports buckets without encryption. What are their types and mechanisms?

choices.text: Preventive via SCPs; detective via Config rules
Both proactive via CloudFormation hooks
Preventive via Config rules; detective via SCPs
Both detective via Config rules

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Preventive controls block actions using SCPs (or RCPs). Detective controls report noncompliance using AWS Config rules. Proactive controls check resources before provisioning using CloudFormation hooks.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Both detective: the first one blocks actions.
• Reversed: SCPs block; Config detects.
• Proactive: applies to CloudFormation provisioning only.

Key takeaway: preventive = SCP, detective = Config, proactive = CFN hooks.

stem: A company adopting AWS Control Tower is designing its OU hierarchy. They need an OU where developer sandbox accounts can experiment with minimal restrictions but must never touch production networks or real customer data, and a separate OU for regulated production workloads with strict SCPs and mandatory logging. Which OU design best supports this?

choices.text: Put all accounts under the root and differentiate them with IAM policies in each account
One Workloads OU for sandbox and production, differentiated only by enforced tags
Separate Sandbox and Production OUs with different SCPs and guardrails
Nest the Sandbox OU under Production so Production SCPs also restrict sandboxes

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Separate Sandbox and Production OUs let each have its own SCPs and guardrails.

Why the other options are wrong:
• All under root with IAM: no guardrails.
• One OU with tags: weak separation.
• Sandbox under Production: inherits production restrictions.

Key takeaway: different environments → different OUs.

stem: A security team in the management account currently manages GuardDuty and Security Hub configuration for all 40 member accounts directly, requiring broad permissions in the management account, which AWS discourages. What should they do to align with best practices while keeping centralized visibility?

choices.text: Disable both services and rely on the organization trail for threat detection
Move GuardDuty and Security Hub management into each member account
Create scoped roles in the management account for the security team
Delegated administrator in a Security Tooling account

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Designating a Security Tooling account as delegated administrator moves security service management out of the management account.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Disable services: loses detection.
• Manage in each account: fragmented.
• Scoped roles in management account: still uses the management account.

Key takeaway: keep the management account minimal → delegated admin.

stem: A member account can still launch EC2 instances in ap-southeast-2 despite an SCP on its OU denying ec2:RunInstances when aws:RequestedRegion is not us-east-1. The OU also has a default FullAWSAccess SCP and a second SCP explicitly allowing ec2:RunInstances in all regions for an automation role. Why might launches still succeed, and what should the team check first?

choices.text: Trace every SCP on the account and its ancestor OUs; the deny may not be in its path
SCPs never block actions; they only generate CloudTrail warnings
The Deny is invalid because SCPs cannot use aws:RequestedRegion
SCPs use OR logic, so any Allow in the hierarchy overrides a Deny

explanation:
Why this is correct:
SCPs apply across the account and its ancestor OUs. If the deny isn't working, check each SCP in the path, including conditions and whether the deny is actually attached where expected.

Why the other options are wrong:
• SCPs only warn: they block.
• Can't use aws:RequestedRegion: they can.
• OR logic: denies win.

Key takeaway: trace the SCP inheritance path.

stem: A company wants every member account in its AWS Organization, including future accounts, to automatically send CloudTrail logs to a single centralized S3 bucket in a dedicated Log Archive account without requiring per-account configuration. Which approach satisfies this with the least ongoing operational effort?

choices.text: A trail in each member account delivering to the central bucket via a bucket policy
Control Tower guardrails alone
An organization trail delivering to the Log Archive bucket
Config aggregators in the Log Archive account collecting CloudTrail data

explanation:
Why this is correct:
An organization trail automatically logs every current and future member account to the Log Archive bucket.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Per-account trails: manual.
• Guardrails alone: don't create logging.
• Config aggregators: not CloudTrail logs.

Key takeaway: org-wide logging → organization trail.

stem: A security architect is deciding between a Service Control Policy and an IAM permissions boundary to restrict which AWS services developers can use. Which statement correctly compares the two mechanisms?

choices.text: Both can grant permissions; SCPs apply per OU while boundaries apply per role
SCPs cap every principal in an account; boundaries cap one user or role
Boundaries can apply to root users
They are functionally identical; the naming difference is purely historical

explanation:
Why this is correct:
SCPs cap permissions for every principal in the accounts they apply to. Permissions boundaries cap a single user or role.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Both grant: neither grants.
• Boundaries for root: no.
• Identical: different scope.

Key takeaway: SCP = account-wide ceiling; boundary = per principal.

stem: An administrator enables the Control Tower mandatory guardrail that disallows changes to S3 bucket encryption configuration, but a member account still shows a bucket with default encryption removed via the console, even though the console shows the OU as "Guardrail applied." What is the most likely explanation?

choices.text: Guardrails apply only to accounts created afterward
Mandatory guardrails affect only new resources, never pre-existing ones
The account has drifted from its baseline; repair the OU or account
S3 encryption changes are only detected, never prevented, by any guardrail

explanation:
Why this is correct:
If a guardrail seems not to apply, the account or OU may have drifted from the Control Tower baseline. Repair or re-register it.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Only new accounts: guardrails apply to enrolled accounts.
• Only new resources: preventive guardrails block actions.
• Never prevented: preventive guardrails exist.

Key takeaway: guardrail anomalies → check drift.

stem: A security team is choosing between maintaining a large custom library of hand-written SCPs versus adopting AWS Control Tower's preventive and detective guardrails for baseline governance across 150 accounts. What is a key tradeoff they should weigh?

choices.text: Control Tower guardrails can't coexist with any additional custom SCPs
Custom SCPs update themselves for new services; guardrails need manual updates
Custom SCPs never offer an advantage, so Control Tower should be used exclusively
Guardrails are AWS-maintained but opinionated; custom SCPs are flexible; combine both

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Control Tower guardrails are maintained by AWS but opinionated. Custom SCPs are flexible but require you to maintain them.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Can't coexist: they can.
• Custom SCPs self-update: they don't.
• Custom SCPs never useful: they are for specific needs.

Key takeaway: managed controls vs. custom flexibility.

stem: A central networking team manages a shared VPC with subnets that many application accounts need to launch EC2 instances into, without duplicating the VPC in every account or granting those accounts VPC creation permissions. Which service should they use to centrally share the subnets?

choices.text: SCPs that grant subnet access permissions to member accounts
Account Factory recreating the VPC configuration in each account
Cross-account roles letting teams modify the networking account's VPC
Share the VPC subnets with the application accounts or OUs through AWS RAM

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Sharing the VPC subnets through AWS RAM lets application accounts launch into them while networking keeps ownership.

Why the other options are wrong:
• SCPs grant access: they don't.
• Account Factory copies: separate VPCs.
• Roles modifying the networking account: over-privileged.

Key takeaway: shared subnets → RAM.

stem: A software company wants to ensure that Lambda deployment packages built by CodeBuild and delivered through CodePipeline cannot be tampered with between build and deployment, and that only artifacts produced by the trusted pipeline can be deployed to production. Which combination of controls best achieves this?

choices.text: Rely on CodePipeline's default role
Store artifacts in a public bucket and log all access with bucket policies
Sign with AWS Signer and enforce a Lambda code-signing config
Enable S3 Versioning on the artifact bucket, which guarantees integrity

explanation:
Why this is correct:
AWS Signer signs deployment packages, and a Lambda code signing configuration rejects unsigned or untrusted code.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Default pipeline role: no integrity.
• Public bucket: insecure.
• Versioning: not integrity verification.

Key takeaway: trusted Lambda code → Signer + code signing config.

stem: A platform team needs to deploy a baseline CloudFormation stack (a logging role and GuardDuty detector) automatically to every account added to an OU, including future accounts, without manually creating IAM roles in each account. Which StackSets permission model should they use, and why?

choices.text: Self-managed, because service-managed permissions cannot target OUs
Self-managed, since it extends to new OU accounts automatically
Service-managed, which auto-deploys to new OU accounts
Either model, since both detect new accounts joining an OU

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Service-managed permissions integrate with Organizations and auto-deploy stacks to new accounts in target OUs.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Self-managed can't target OUs: self-managed doesn't auto-deploy.
• Self-managed extends automatically: false.
• Either: only service-managed auto-deploys.

Key takeaway: auto-deploy to new accounts → service-managed StackSets.

stem: A platform team wants developers to self-service deploy pre-approved RDS products from Service Catalog, but developers must not be granted direct IAM permissions to call rds:CreateDBInstance, since the provisioning role should be more privileged than the developers themselves. Which Service Catalog feature enables this separation?

choices.text: Portfolio sharing, which distributes the catalog but not provisioning permissions
TagOptions, which restrict the tags developers can apply
Stack policies that block updates to specific stack resources
A launch constraint that provisions the product with an associated IAM role

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A launch constraint provisions the product with a specified IAM role, so developers don't need permissions to create RDS directly.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Portfolio sharing: distribution only.
• TagOptions: tags.
• Stack policies: updates.

Key takeaway: least privilege self-service → launch constraints.

stem: A DevSecOps team wants to prevent CloudFormation templates that create overly permissive IAM policies or unencrypted S3 buckets from ever being deployed, catching these issues automatically before the deploy stage runs in CodePipeline. Which approach best fits this requirement?

choices.text: Rely on Security Hub findings after resources reach production
An early CodeBuild stage running cfn-guard or cfn-nag
Run CloudFormation drift detection after each deployment
An SCP denying cloudformation:CreateStack to force manual review

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Running cfn-guard or cfn-nag in an early CodeBuild stage fails the pipeline on risky templates before deployment.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Security Hub after production: too late.
• Drift detection after deployment: too late.
• Deny CreateStack: blocks everything.

Key takeaway: shift-left template checks.

stem: An administrator creates a self-managed CloudFormation StackSet in the management account and targets a newly created member account, but stack instance creation fails with an error that the StackSet cannot assume a role in the target account. The AWSCloudFormationStackSetAdministrationRole exists in the management account. What is the most likely cause?

choices.text: Self-managed StackSets require the target to be the management account
The target lacks the StackSet execution role trusting the admin account
The template has a syntax error, which always appears as an assume-role failure
StackSets can deploy only to accounts in the management account's OU

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Self-managed StackSets need an execution role in each target account that trusts the administrator account's role. Without it, deployment fails.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Target must be management account: no.
• Syntax error shows as assume failure: no.
• Only management OU: no.

Key takeaway: self-managed StackSets need execution roles.

stem: A CodePipeline in Account A deploys resources into Account B via a cross-account CodeDeploy action. Deployments consistently fail at the artifact download step with an access denied error referencing the pipeline's KMS-encrypted artifact bucket, even though the cross-account IAM role in Account B already has s3:GetObject on the bucket. What additional configuration is most likely missing?

choices.text: The artifact key policy must also let the cross-account role decrypt
CodePipeline does not support cross-account deployments at all
The artifact bucket needs versioning disabled for cross-account access
The artifact bucket must be public for Account B to read the objects

explanation:
Why this is correct:
The cross-account role needs kms:Decrypt on the artifact bucket's KMS key via the key policy, plus S3 access.

Why the other options are wrong:
• No cross-account support: it's supported.
• Disable versioning: unrelated.
• Public bucket: insecure.

Key takeaway: cross-account artifacts need key access.

stem: A governance team wants every resource provisioned through Service Catalog products to automatically include a standardized CostCenter tag chosen from an approved list of values, and wants to control which portfolios of products are visible to which IAM principals. Which Service Catalog features address these two needs respectively?

choices.text: Notification constraints for tagging; template constraints for visibility
Service actions for tagging; StackSets for portfolio visibility
Launch constraints for tagging; stack policies for portfolio visibility
TagOptions for tag values; portfolio sharing for visibility

explanation:
Why this is correct:
TagOptions enforce allowed tag values on provisioned products, and portfolio sharing controls which accounts or OUs see the portfolio.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Notification/template constraints: not tagging.
• Service actions/StackSets: not the features.
• Launch constraints/stack policies: not tagging or visibility.

Key takeaway: Service Catalog tagging → TagOptions; visibility → sharing.

stem: A security review finds that the IAM service role used by a production CodeBuild project has iam:PassRole and iam:CreateRole permissions with a wildcard resource, allowing a compromised buildspec to potentially create and pass a highly privileged role to escalate access. The team wants to reduce this risk while still allowing the pipeline to deploy CloudFormation stacks that create necessary execution roles. What is the best mitigation?

choices.text: Remove all IAM permissions from the CodeBuild role, which won't affect deployments
Grant the CodeBuild role AdministratorAccess so permissions are explicit
Scope PassRole/CreateRole with a boundary; use a separate CFN service role
Disable CloudTrail logging for the role to reduce expected noise

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Scope iam:PassRole and CreateRole to specific roles with a required permissions boundary, and use a separate CloudFormation service role for deployments.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Remove all IAM permissions: may break builds.
• AdministratorAccess: worse.
• Disable CloudTrail: removes auditing.

Key takeaway: limit privilege escalation paths.

stem: A compliance auditor asks whether resources deployed by a CloudFormation StackSet across 60 accounts still match the StackSet's defined template, since some account owners have console access and could have manually modified resources. Which StackSets capability directly answers this question?

choices.text: StackSets automatic deployment
Config conformance packs, the only way to detect CloudFormation drift
Change sets, which show drift by simulating a template update
StackSets drift detection per stack instance

explanation:
Why this is correct:
StackSets drift detection checks each stack instance for drift from the template.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Automatic deployment: provisioning, not drift.
• Conformance packs only way: no.
• Change sets: preview updates, not drift.

Key takeaway: StackSet compliance → drift detection.

stem: A financial services company processing card payments needs to select AWS Security Hub standards that align with regulatory requirements while also getting broad AWS-specific best-practice coverage. Which combination of standards would most appropriately address both needs?

choices.text: Only the CIS AWS Foundations Benchmark, which covers card payment requirements
Only AWS FSBP, which maps automatically to PCI DSS controls
Standards duplicate Audit Manager
PCI DSS plus AWS FSBP (optionally CIS)

explanation:
Why this is correct:
For card payments, enable the PCI DSS standard plus AWS FSBP (and optionally CIS) in Security Hub.

Why the other options are wrong:
• CIS only: doesn't cover PCI.
• FSBP maps automatically to PCI: not fully.
• Duplicates Audit Manager: different purposes.

Key takeaway: match standards to regulations.

stem: A security team wants to deploy a standardized set of AWS Config rules mapping to an internal security baseline consistently across all 80 accounts in their AWS Organization, with new accounts automatically receiving the same rule set. What is the most operationally efficient way to achieve this?

choices.text: Create individual Config custom rules manually in each account
Trusted Advisor checks, which enforce Config rules across the organization
One rule in the management account, replicated to members by SCPs
An organization conformance pack from the delegated admin

explanation:
Why this is correct:
An organization conformance pack deployed from the delegated administrator applies the rule set to all accounts consistently.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Manual per account: toil.
• Trusted Advisor: not Config rules.
• SCP replication: not how Config works.

Key takeaway: org-wide rule sets → conformance packs.

stem: A security engineer wants to identify any S3 buckets, IAM roles, KMS keys, or Lambda functions that grant access to principals outside the organization's AWS Organizations boundary, in order to review and remove unintended external trust relationships. Which AWS feature should they use?

choices.text: Trusted Advisor security checks, which flag all externally shared resources
IAM Access Analyzer with the org or account as zone of trust
Amazon Macie, which detects external IAM trust relationships
Config aggregators, which flag cross-account policies without any rules

explanation:
Why this is correct:
IAM Access Analyzer with the organization or account as the zone of trust finds resources shared with external principals.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Trusted Advisor: limited checks.
• Macie: data classification.
• Config aggregators: no external access analysis.

Key takeaway: external access → Access Analyzer.

stem: A compliance manager needs SOC 2 evidence (Config results, CloudTrail activity, and manual attestations) continuously collected, mapped to controls, and exported as an assessment report. Which service fits?

choices.text: AWS Config alone
AWS Audit Manager with a SOC 2 framework
AWS Artifact
AWS Security Hub with the SOC 2-aligned standards enabled

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Audit Manager collects evidence from AWS sources and manual uploads, maps it to framework controls, and produces assessment reports.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Artifact: AWS's own compliance reports.
• Security Hub: findings and scores, not control-mapped evidence packages.
• Config: evaluations only.

Key takeaway: control-mapped audit evidence → Audit Manager.

stem: A security team enabled Security Hub in the delegated administrator account with us-east-1 as the aggregation Region, expecting findings from all 12 member accounts across multiple Regions to appear centrally. Findings from eu-west-1 workloads are missing even though GuardDuty and Config are active there. What is the most likely cause?

choices.text: Security Hub isn't enabled in eu-west-1 or it isn't a linked Region
Security Hub doesn't support cross-Region aggregation in any configuration
GuardDuty findings can never be forwarded to Security Hub across Regions
Delegated admin applies only to the account that created it, not members

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Findings from a Region reach the aggregation Region only if Security Hub is enabled there and the Region is linked.

Why the other options are wrong:
• No cross-Region aggregation: it exists.
• GuardDuty can't forward: it can via Security Hub.
• Delegated admin only for itself: it manages members.

Key takeaway: cross-Region aggregation needs linked Regions.

stem: An IAM administrator wants to understand the difference between IAM Access Analyzer's policy validation checks and its external access analyzer findings when reviewing a new S3 bucket policy before applying it. Which statement correctly distinguishes the two capabilities?

choices.text: External access checks syntax; policy validation finds outside principals
Validation checks a policy before use; external access findings show actual outside access
Policy validation works only on identity policies, never resource policies
They are two names for the same feature with no functional difference

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Policy validation checks a policy for errors and best practices before use. External access findings show resources currently shared outside the zone of trust.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Swapped: incorrect.
• Validation only for identity policies: it covers resource policies too.
• Same feature: different.

Key takeaway: validation = before; findings = current exposure.

stem: A security team must enforce a highly specific internal control (a custom tag-based encryption requirement unique to their organization) across 5 accounts, while also wanting to later expand a broader compliance baseline org-wide. They are deciding between a single custom AWS Config rule deployed individually versus wrapping it into a conformance pack. What is the key tradeoff?

choices.text: One rule is simpler for a narrow need; a pack is reusable for org-wide baselines
Conformance packs require Security Hub, while custom rules do not
Custom rules and packs deploy identically, so there's no tradeoff
Conformance packs can contain only AWS managed rules, not custom ones

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A single custom rule is simpler for one narrow requirement, while a conformance pack packages reusable rules for org-wide deployment.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Packs need Security Hub: no.
• Identical deployment: they differ.
• Packs only managed rules: they can include custom rules.

Key takeaway: right-size the tool.

stem: A security team wants Security Hub findings of type "high severity, S3 bucket publicly accessible" to automatically trigger a Lambda function that removes the offending public access configuration, without requiring analyst intervention for this well-understood finding type. Which architecture achieves this?

choices.text: Export findings to CSV daily and have an analyst run a remediation script
Use Config auto-remediation only
An EventBridge rule on filtered findings invoking a remediation Lambda
Use CloudTrail Insights to detect the finding and modify the bucket policy directly

explanation:
Why this is correct:
An EventBridge rule filtering high-severity public-bucket findings invokes a remediation Lambda automatically.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Daily CSV: slow and manual.
• Config remediation only: may not cover the finding source.
• CloudTrail Insights: API anomalies.

Key takeaway: auto-remediate specific findings → EventBridge filters.

stem: A compliance team already has AWS Config rules evaluating resources in real time and Security Hub aggregating findings. Leadership now asks for an auditor-ready evidence package mapped to specific SOC 2 control language, generated periodically with minimal manual effort, including evidence types Config/Security Hub don't natively produce, like manual sign-off records. What should the team do, and what is the tradeoff versus relying on Config/Security Hub alone?

choices.text: Audit Manager with a SOC 2 framework, mapping evidence to controls
Keep only Config and Security Hub, since raw exports equal SOC 2 evidence packages
Use Trusted Advisor, which produces SOC 2-mapped evidence automatically
Disable Config and Security Hub

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Audit Manager with a SOC 2 framework collects evidence from Config, Security Hub, and more, and maps it to controls for audits.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Raw exports equal evidence: auditors need mapping.
• Trusted Advisor: not SOC 2 evidence.
• Disable Config: loses evidence.

Key takeaway: audit-ready evidence → Audit Manager.

stem: A security team must detect cryptocurrency mining processes and reverse shells running inside pods on Amazon EKS worker nodes, including file access and process execution events. Which solution fits BEST?

choices.text: Enable EKS control plane audit logs delivered to CloudWatch Logs.
GuardDuty EKS Runtime Monitoring.
Enable Amazon Inspector scanning for the ECR images used by the pods.
Enable VPC Flow Logs and search manually for mining pool IP addresses.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
GuardDuty EKS Runtime Monitoring watches process and network activity inside pods to detect mining and reverse shells.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Control plane audit logs: Kubernetes API calls, not processes.
• Inspector image scans: vulnerabilities before runtime.
• Manual flow log searches: slow and incomplete.

Key takeaway: runtime threats in containers → GuardDuty Runtime Monitoring.

stem: Auditors require that API activity from every account in the organization is logged centrally, that tampering with log files can be detected, and that logs cannot be deleted for 7 years even by administrators. Which combination meets these requirements?

choices.text: CloudTrail event history with its 90-day lookback in each account.
An organization trail to a bucket with MFA Delete enabled.
Individual trails in each account delivering to local versioned buckets.
Org trail with validation to an Object Lock (compliance) bucket.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
An organization trail with log file validation, delivered to an S3 bucket with Object Lock in compliance mode, centralizes logs, proves integrity, and prevents deletion.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Event history: 90 days, per account.
• MFA Delete: owners can disable it.
• Local per-account buckets: not central.

Key takeaway: central, tamper-evident, immutable logs.

stem: A company wants to centralize CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs, Route 53 resolver logs, and third-party firewall logs into one normalized format for analysis by several SIEM tools. Which service fits BEST?

choices.text: Amazon Security Lake (OCSF, subscriber access).
AWS Security Hub custom insights across sources.
Amazon Detective behavior graphs for each source.
CloudWatch Logs Insights saved queries.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Security Lake centralizes AWS and third-party security logs in OCSF format in your own data lake, with subscriber access for analytics tools.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Security Hub insights: findings, not raw logs.
• Detective graphs: investigation, not a data lake.
• Logs Insights queries: not centralization.

Key takeaway: security data lake → Security Lake.

stem: GuardDuty reports that an EC2 instance is communicating with a known command-and-control server. The team must contain the threat while preserving evidence for forensics. Which TWO actions should it take first? (Select TWO.)

choices.text: Terminate the instance immediately to stop the communication.
Swap in an isolation security group.
Reboot the instance to clear the malicious process from memory.
Snapshot the EBS volumes (and memory).
Delete the GuardDuty finding once the instance is contained.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Swap in an isolation security group to cut C2 traffic, and snapshot the EBS volumes (and capture memory) to preserve evidence before further action.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Terminate: destroys evidence.
• Reboot: loses memory evidence.
• Delete the finding: loses the record.

Key takeaway: contain and preserve before remediating.

stem: An IAM user's access key was accidentally committed to a public repository an hour ago. What should the security engineer do FIRST?

choices.text: Rotate the IAM user's console password immediately.
Delete the public repository that contains the key.
Deactivate (then delete) the exposed key, then review CloudTrail for its activity.
Enable MFA for the IAM user to block further use of the key.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Deactivate (then delete) the exposed key immediately, then review CloudTrail for any activity with it.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Console password: not the exposed credential.
• Delete the repo: the key may already be copied.
• Enable MFA: doesn't block access keys.

Key takeaway: exposed key → deactivate first.

stem: A company wants a repeatable, automated response to high-severity GuardDuty EC2 findings: tag the instance, isolate it, snapshot volumes, and notify responders, with each step auditable. Which design fits BEST?

choices.text: A daily Lambda function that reads all findings and emails a report.
Security Hub insights reviewed manually by the on-call team.
An SNS topic that pages responders to perform the steps by hand.
EventBridge on high-severity findings starting Step Functions.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
An EventBridge rule on high-severity GuardDuty EC2 findings starts a Step Functions workflow that tags, isolates, snapshots, and notifies consistently.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Daily report: slow.
• Manual insights review: slow.
• SNS paging for manual steps: not automated.

Key takeaway: repeatable response → EventBridge + Step Functions.

stem: A company needs continuous vulnerability scanning of EC2 instances, container images in ECR, and Lambda functions, with automatic rescans when new CVEs are published. Which service fits BEST?

choices.text: Amazon GuardDuty Malware Protection.
Amazon Macie.
Amazon Inspector.
AWS Trusted Advisor.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Amazon Inspector continuously scans EC2, ECR images, and Lambda functions for vulnerabilities.

Why the other options are wrong:
• GuardDuty Malware Protection: malware.
• Macie: sensitive data.
• Trusted Advisor: best practices.

Key takeaway: vulnerability management → Inspector.

stem: Workloads in private subnets may only reach a short list of external domains (package repositories and a payment API) over HTTPS. All other outbound traffic must be blocked. Which solution fits BEST?

choices.text: Security group outbound rules that list the approved domain names.
Network ACL rules allowing port 443 to 0.0.0.0/0.
A NAT gateway with a route table limited to port 443.
Network Firewall with a stateful domain allow list (SNI).

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Network Firewall with a stateful domain allow list (using SNI for HTTPS) permits only approved domains and blocks everything else.

Why the other options are wrong:
• SGs with domain names: not supported.
• NACL to 0.0.0.0/0: allows everything.
• NAT route limited to 443: can't filter domains.

Key takeaway: egress allow lists by domain → Network Firewall.

stem: A penetration test showed that a server-side request forgery (SSRF) flaw in a web application could read IAM role credentials from the instance metadata service. Which change BEST mitigates this class of attack?

choices.text: Enable EBS encryption on all instance volumes.
Require IMDSv2 (HttpTokens=required) and keep a low hop limit.
Remove the role and store access keys in the application config.
Move the instance into a private subnet behind a NAT gateway.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Requiring IMDSv2 (HttpTokens=required) with a low hop limit blocks SSRF from reading role credentials.

Why the other options are wrong:
• EBS encryption: unrelated.
• Access keys in config: worse.
• Private subnet: SSRF still works from the app.

Key takeaway: SSRF protection → IMDSv2.

stem: A company has hundreds of projects and wants developers to access only resources tagged with their own project, without writing a new policy for every project. Users sign in through an external IdP that sends a project attribute. Which approach fits BEST?

choices.text: Resource-based policies on every resource listing user ARNs.
Separate AWS accounts for every developer.
ABAC comparing principal and resource project tags.
One IAM policy per project attached to separate roles.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
ABAC policies compare principal and resource project tags, so hundreds of projects need only a few policies.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Resource policies with ARNs: unmanageable.
• Account per developer: excessive.
• Policy per project: sprawl.

Key takeaway: project-scoped access at scale → ABAC.

stem: A role in a member account has the AdministratorAccess policy attached, yet s3:DeleteBucket calls fail with an explicit deny. The bucket policy does not mention the role. Which TWO are the MOST likely causes? (Select TWO.)

choices.text: A permissions boundary without s3:DeleteBucket.
The role's trust policy is missing the sts:AssumeRole action.
The bucket is in a different Region from the caller.
An SCP denying s3:DeleteBucket.
S3 Block Public Access is enabled at the account level.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
AdministratorAccess can still be denied by a permissions boundary that omits s3:DeleteBucket or by an SCP that denies it.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Trust policy: affects assuming, not calls afterward.
• Different Region: not an access denial cause.
• Block Public Access: unrelated to deleting buckets.

Key takeaway: effective permissions = policies ∩ boundaries ∩ SCPs.

stem: A SaaS application needs fine-grained authorization such as 'managers can approve expenses under $10,000 for their own department'. The team wants policies managed outside the application code and evaluated centrally. Which service fits BEST?

choices.text: IAM identity policies created for each end user of the application.
Amazon Verified Permissions with Cedar policies.
AWS WAF custom rules evaluating each request.
Amazon Cognito user pool groups only.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Verified Permissions with Cedar policies handles attribute-based app authorization such as amount and department limits.

Why the other options are wrong:
• IAM per end user: not for app users.
• WAF rules: not authorization logic.
• Cognito groups only: too coarse.

Key takeaway: fine-grained app authorization → Verified Permissions.

stem: A company uses an external identity provider and wants workforce users to sign in once for all AWS accounts, with users and groups created and removed in AWS automatically when HR changes them in the IdP. Which configuration fits BEST?

choices.text: Amazon Cognito user pools for workforce access.
IAM Identity Center with SAML sign-in and SCIM provisioning.
A SAML identity provider in each account with manually created roles.
IAM users in each account synchronized by a nightly script.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
IAM Identity Center with SAML sign-in from the external IdP and SCIM provisioning gives single sign-on to all accounts with automatic user sync.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Cognito for workforce: wrong tool.
• SAML per account: unmanageable.
• Synced IAM users: long-term credentials.

Key takeaway: workforce SSO + sync → Identity Center with SCIM.

stem: Encrypted data is replicated from us-east-1 to us-west-2 for disaster recovery. The team wants to decrypt the replicated data in us-west-2 without cross-Region KMS calls and without re-encrypting it. Which approach fits BEST?

choices.text: Export the key material from KMS and import it into another key.
Use a KMS multi-Region key with a replica key in us-west-2.
Create separate single-Region keys in each Region with the same alias.
Use SSE-S3 instead of KMS.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A KMS multi-Region key with a replica in us-west-2 lets data encrypted in us-east-1 be decrypted in us-west-2.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Export key material: not possible from KMS.
• Separate keys with same alias: different material.
• SSE-S3: loses customer key control.

Key takeaway: cross-Region decryption → multi-Region keys.

stem: Regulations require that financial records cannot be overwritten or deleted by anyone, including the root user, for 7 years. Which configuration meets this?

choices.text: S3 Versioning with a lifecycle rule that expires noncurrent versions after 7 years.
A bucket policy denying s3:DeleteObject.
S3 Object Lock in compliance mode with a 7-year retention period.
S3 Object Lock in governance mode with a 7-year retention period.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Object Lock in compliance mode prevents overwriting or deletion by anyone, including root, for the retention period.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Versioning with expiry: allows deletion.
• Bucket policy deny: admins can change it.
• Governance mode: privileged users can bypass.

Key takeaway: regulatory immutability → compliance mode.

stem: A regulator requires cryptographic keys to be stored in single-tenant HSMs that the company exclusively controls, while still using KMS integrations for S3 and EBS encryption. Which solution meets these requirements?

choices.text: KMS customer managed keys in the default key store.
SSE-S3 managed keys for S3 and EBS default encryption.
A CloudHSM-backed KMS custom key store.
Keys stored as secrets in AWS Secrets Manager.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A KMS custom key store backed by CloudHSM keeps keys in single-tenant HSMs the company controls, while services still use KMS.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Default key store: multi-tenant.
• SSE-S3: AWS-managed keys.
• Secrets Manager: not an HSM.

Key takeaway: single-tenant HSM keys with KMS integration → custom key store.

stem: A security standard requires that all requests to a sensitive S3 bucket use encryption in transit. Which bucket policy control enforces this?

choices.text: Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration.
Allow s3:GetObject only when s3:x-amz-server-side-encryption is aws:kms.
Enable default encryption with SSE-KMS.
Deny all S3 actions when aws:SecureTransport is false.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A bucket policy denying all actions when aws:SecureTransport is false rejects any non-HTTPS request.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Transfer Acceleration: speed.
• Server-side encryption condition: at rest.
• Default SSE-KMS: at rest.

Key takeaway: enforce TLS to S3 → SecureTransport deny.

stem: A company uses AWS Control Tower. It wants to block the creation of noncompliant resources, such as unencrypted RDS instances, at CloudFormation deployment time rather than detecting them afterward. Which type of control should it enable?

choices.text: Preventive controls implemented only as SCPs.
Security Hub standards evaluated after deployment.
Proactive controls (CloudFormation hooks).
Detective controls backed by AWS Config rules.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Control Tower proactive controls use CloudFormation hooks to block noncompliant resources before they're provisioned.

Why the other options are wrong:
• SCPs only: can't inspect resource properties at creation for every case.
• Security Hub after deployment: detective.
• Config detective controls: after the fact.

Key takeaway: block noncompliant resources before creation → proactive controls.

stem: A company must deploy the same set of 40 Config rules and remediations to every account in its organization and report compliance against that set as a unit. Which feature fits BEST?

choices.text: Organization conformance packs deployed from the delegated admin.
Individual Config rules created manually in each account.
Trusted Advisor checks enabled for the organization.
IAM Access Analyzer policy validation.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Organization conformance packs deployed from the delegated administrator push the same rules and remediations to every account.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Manual per account: toil.
• Trusted Advisor: not Config rules.
• Access Analyzer validation: policies.

Key takeaway: org-wide Config deployment → conformance packs.

stem: The company has thousands of S3 buckets across 200 accounts and wants to continuously estimate where sensitive data such as credit card numbers is stored, without paying to scan every object in full. Which feature fits BEST?

choices.text: Macie automated discovery with an org delegated admin.
Macie one-time classification jobs on every bucket every day.
GuardDuty S3 Protection enabled across all accounts.
S3 Inventory reports reviewed for sensitive file names.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Macie automated sensitive data discovery with an org delegated admin continuously samples buckets across all accounts at controlled cost.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Daily one-time jobs on every bucket: very expensive.
• GuardDuty S3 Protection: threats, not content.
• Inventory file names: unreliable.

Key takeaway: estate-wide sensitive data estimates → automated discovery.

stem: A company wants continuous threat detection across all accounts, analyzing CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs, and DNS logs without deploying agents. Which service fits?

stem: A security team wants GuardDuty to detect suspicious behavior inside EKS clusters and on EC2 hosts at the process level. Which TWO features help? (Select TWO)

choices.text: GuardDuty Runtime Monitoring with the security agent

stem: A company needs a single dashboard aggregating findings from GuardDuty, Inspector, Macie, and Config with compliance scores. Which service fits?

stem: The security team wants to be alerted within minutes when the root user signs in to any account. Which approach fits?

stem: Which TWO signals should trigger immediate security alerts? (Select TWO)

A developer creating a new Lambda layer version
A new tag added to a development S3 bucket
A scheduled EBS snapshot completing successfully
CloudTrail logging being stopped or deleted

stem: A company needs an organization-wide CloudTrail trail with logs that cannot be altered by member account administrators. Which design fits?

CloudTrail event history only, kept for the default 90 days
An organization trail delivering to an S3 bucket in a separate log archive account
Individual trails in each account, writing to local buckets that each account's admins control

explanation:

• CloudTrail event history only, kept for the…: Event history is short-term and per account.

stem: A company must record reads of objects in a sensitive S3 bucket. Which logging option captures this?

choices.text: CloudTrail data events for the bucket
AWS Config history for the bucket policy
VPC Flow Logs for the bucket's traffic
CloudTrail management events only

explanation:

Data events record object-level operations such as GetObject.

• VPC Flow Logs for the bucket's traffic: Flow Logs do not show S3 object operations.
• CloudTrail management events only: Management events exclude object reads.

stem: A company wants to centralize security logs from AWS and third-party sources in a normalized format (OCSF) for analytics. Which service fits?

stem: Security analysts need SQL queries across a year of CloudTrail events from all accounts without building ETL. Which feature fits?

choices.text: CloudTrail Lake event data stores
AWS Config aggregators by Region
S3 Inventory reports of log files
CloudWatch dashboards on API counts

explanation:

stem: Application logs contain credit card numbers that analysts must not see. Which feature masks them in CloudWatch Logs?

choices.text: CloudWatch Logs data protection policies
CloudWatch Logs retention settings
CloudWatch Logs metric filter patterns
CloudWatch Logs subscription filters

explanation:

Data protection policies detect and mask sensitive data in log events.

stem: Which TWO measures protect the integrity of CloudTrail logs? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Grant all developers write access to the log bucket
Disable encryption on the bucket to allow validation
Enable log file integrity validation
Store logs in the same account that generates them only
Apply S3 Object Lock on the log bucket

explanation:

Integrity validation detects changes, and Object Lock prevents deletion or modification.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Grant all developers write access to the log…: Broad write access allows tampering.
• Disable encryption on the bucket to allow…: Encryption does not prevent validation.
• Store logs in the same account that…: Same-account storage lets admins alter logs.

stem: A new CloudTrail trail delivers no logs to its S3 bucket. What is the most likely cause?

choices.text: The bucket has versioning enabled, which blocks CloudTrail writes
The bucket policy does not allow CloudTrail to write objects
The trail was created in a Region with no EC2 instances running
The bucket name contains lowercase letters and hyphens only

• The trail was created in a Region with no…: EC2 presence is irrelevant.
• The bucket name contains lowercase letters…: Lowercase names with hyphens are valid.

stem: GuardDuty findings are not appearing in Security Hub for some member accounts. Which TWO checks are most relevant? (Select TWO)

The GuardDuty integration is enabled in Security Hub

stem: The CloudWatch agent on EC2 instances sends no logs. Which TWO causes are likely? (Select TWO)

stem: A company wants to detect unusual API activity volumes, such as a spike in IAM actions, without writing rules. Which feature fits?

stem: A company wants to detect when S3 buckets become publicly accessible or shared externally. Which TWO services help? (Select TWO)

stem: DNS queries from VPC workloads must be logged for threat hunting. Which feature fits?

stem: A company enabled GuardDuty but sees no findings from a new Region where workloads run. What is the likely reason?

stem: Which service continuously scans EC2 instances, ECR images, and Lambda functions for software vulnerabilities?

stem: A company wants documented, tested incident response procedures for compromised EC2 instances. Which practice fits?

stem: A company wants a forensics account prepared in advance so responders can analyze compromised resources safely. Which TWO elements should it include? (Select TWO)

stem: GuardDuty reports an EC2 instance communicating with a command-and-control server. Which FIRST steps preserve evidence while containing the threat? (Select TWO)

• Rotate the role's long-term access keys in…: Roles do not have long-term access keys.

stem: A company wants automated containment when GuardDuty reports high-severity findings. Which design fits?

stem: A company wants to test its incident response by simulating compromised credentials in a controlled environment. Which approach fits?

Run planned simulations in a non-production account with defined scope and runbooks
Test only in production during peak hours without informing anyone

Why this is correct:

Why the other options are wrong:
• Leak real production credentials publicly to…: Leaking real credentials is dangerous.

• Mount the volume on the compromised instance…: The compromised instance is untrusted.
• Attach the original volume to a busy…: Production servers risk contamination.
• Download the snapshot to a personal laptop…: Personal laptops are insecure.

stem: After containment, how should a compromised EC2 instance be replaced?

Clone the compromised instance to create additional capacity
Launch a new instance from a known-good, patched AMI with rotated credentials

stem: Which AWS responsibility applies during a security incident affecting a customer's EC2 instance?

stem: A company must be able to recover quickly from ransomware that encrypts data in accounts. Which TWO controls help? (Select TWO)

• Backups stored in the same account with full…: Same-account backups can be deleted by attackers.
• No backups, relying on attackers to provide keys: Paying attackers is unreliable.

stem: A public web application needs protection against SQL injection and bot traffic. Which service fits?

AWS WAF with managed rule groups and Bot Control

• Network ACLs that deny traffic from all…: NACLs cannot inspect requests.
• VPC Flow Logs analyzed daily for suspicious…: Daily analysis does not block.

stem: A company needs enhanced DDoS protection, cost protection for scaling during attacks, and 24/7 expert support. Which service fits?

stem: An application behind CloudFront must ensure the ALB origin accepts traffic only from CloudFront. Which TWO controls help? (Select TWO)
