Key takeaway: Domain egress filtering → Network Firewall.

stem: Private instances must access S3 without internet, and only the company's buckets may be reached through the path. Which TWO controls fit? (Select TWO)

choices.text: A NAT gateway with a route for all S3 traffic
A second internet gateway attached to the VPC
Public IPs on instances for direct S3 access
An endpoint policy allowing only company buckets
An S3 gateway endpoint in the VPC

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Gateway endpoints keep traffic private, and endpoint policies restrict which buckets are reachable.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A NAT gateway with a route for all S3 traffic: NAT routes over the internet.
• A second internet gateway attached to the VPC: A VPC has one internet gateway.
• Public IPs on instances for direct S3 access: Public IPs expose instances.

Key takeaway: Private S3 access with endpoint policies prevents exfiltration.

stem: Which network control can explicitly deny traffic from a specific IP range at the subnet level?

choices.text: Endpoint policies
Network ACL deny rules
Route table entries
Security group rules

explanation:
Why this is correct:
NACLs support explicit deny rules at the subnet boundary.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Endpoint policies: Endpoint policies control endpoint access.
• Route table entries: Route tables route, not filter.
• Security group rules: Security groups only allow.

Key takeaway: Explicit IP denies → NACLs.

stem: A company must find unintended internet-reachable paths to sensitive subnets across all VPCs. Which service fits?

choices.text: Network Access Analyzer
AWS Budgets alerts
Amazon Macie scans
CloudWatch Synthetics

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Network Access Analyzer identifies network paths that violate defined requirements.

Why the other options are wrong:
• AWS Budgets alerts: Budgets track spending.
• Amazon Macie scans: Macie finds sensitive data.
• CloudWatch Synthetics: Synthetics tests endpoints.

Key takeaway: Find unintended network access with Network Access Analyzer.

stem: An API Gateway REST API must be protected from request floods by individual clients. Which TWO controls help? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Removing authentication to reduce processing time
Increasing the Lambda function's memory setting
Disabling CloudWatch logging for the API stage
AWS WAF rate-based rules on the API stage
Usage plans with throttling limits per API key

explanation:
Why this is correct:
WAF rate-based rules and usage plan throttling limit request floods.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Removing authentication to reduce processing…: Removing auth increases risk.
• Increasing the Lambda function's memory setting: Memory does not stop floods.
• Disabling CloudWatch logging for the API stage: Disabling logs removes visibility.

Key takeaway: Throttle abusive clients with WAF and usage plans.

stem: A company wants to restrict access to a CloudFront distribution to paying subscribers. Which feature fits?

choices.text: CloudFront real-time logs to Kinesis
CloudFront signed URLs or signed cookies
CloudFront compression for text files
CloudFront Origin Shield in one Region

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Signed URLs or cookies control who can access content.

Why the other options are wrong:
• CloudFront real-time logs to Kinesis: Real-time logs record requests.
• CloudFront compression for text files: Compression reduces size.
• CloudFront Origin Shield in one Region: Origin Shield reduces origin load.

Key takeaway: Restrict premium content with signed URLs or cookies.

stem: A company wants to verify that only approved, signed container images run on EKS. Which approach fits?

choices.text: Allow any image with a 'latest' tag from any registry to run in the cluster
Disable image pulls entirely and copy files manually into running pods
Sign images with AWS Signer and verify signatures with an admission controller
Rely on developers to confirm image origins in pull request comments

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Signing with verification at admission ensures only trusted images run.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Allow any image with a 'latest' tag from any…: Arbitrary images are untrusted.
• Disable image pulls entirely and copy files…: Manual copying is impractical and insecure.
• Rely on developers to confirm image origins…: Comments are not enforcement.

Key takeaway: Enforce trusted images with signing and admission control.

stem: Lambda functions must only run code signed by the security team. Which feature fits?

choices.text: Lambda code signing configuration with AWS Signer profiles
Lambda environment variables encrypted with KMS
Lambda reserved concurrency set to zero on all functions
Lambda layers shared across all functions

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Code signing configurations reject deployments that are not signed by trusted profiles.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Lambda environment variables encrypted with KMS: Encrypting variables does not verify code.
• Lambda reserved concurrency set to zero on…: Zero concurrency stops execution.
• Lambda layers shared across all functions: Layers share code.

Key takeaway: Enforce trusted Lambda code with code signing.

stem: EC2 instances should be built from hardened images consistently. Which service automates this?

choices.text: EC2 Image Builder with hardening components
Amazon Macie scans of AMI metadata
Amazon Lightsail snapshots of running instances
AWS Backup plans for EC2 volumes

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Image Builder builds, tests, and distributes hardened images automatically.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Amazon Macie scans of AMI metadata: Macie scans S3 data.
• Amazon Lightsail snapshots of running instances: Lightsail snapshots are for Lightsail.
• AWS Backup plans for EC2 volumes: Backup protects data.

Key takeaway: Automate hardened images with Image Builder.

stem: Which TWO measures isolate a sensitive database tier in a VPC? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Share the database subnet with every account in the organization
Allow 0.0.0.0/0 on the database port for flexibility
Allow inbound traffic only from the application tier's security group
Assign public IPs so administrators can connect from anywhere
Place the database in private subnets without internet routes

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Private placement and tightly scoped security groups isolate the database tier.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Share the database subnet with every account…: Broad sharing increases exposure.
• Allow 0.0.0.0/0 on the database port for…: Open ports expose the database.
• Assign public IPs so administrators can…: Public IPs expose the database.

Key takeaway: Isolate databases with private subnets and scoped security groups.

stem: East-west traffic between VPCs must be inspected by IPS with centralized rules. Which design fits?

choices.text: VPC peering mesh with NACLs allowing all traffic between VPCs
A single EC2 firewall instance in one AZ handling every flow
Security groups with broad allow rules on every instance in each of the connected VPCs
Network Firewall in an inspection VPC behind a transit gateway with appliance mode

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Centralized Network Firewall inspection through a transit gateway covers east-west traffic.

Why the other options are wrong:
• VPC peering mesh with NACLs allowing all…: Peering bypasses central inspection.
• A single EC2 firewall instance in one AZ…: A single instance is a bottleneck.
• Security groups with broad allow rules on…: Security groups do not provide IPS.

Key takeaway: Inspect east-west traffic centrally.

stem: DNS queries from VPC workloads to known malicious domains must be blocked. Which feature fits?

choices.text: Route 53 latency routing
Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall
Route 53 public DNSSEC keys
Route 53 health checks

explanation:
Why this is correct:
DNS Firewall blocks queries to domains on block lists.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Route 53 latency routing: Latency routing chooses Regions.
• Route 53 public DNSSEC keys: DNSSEC signs zones.
• Route 53 health checks: Health checks monitor endpoints.

Key takeaway: Block malicious domains with DNS Firewall.

stem: Employees must access internal web apps without a VPN, with identity and device checks on every request. Which service fits?

choices.text: Amazon CloudFront
Amazon Route 53
AWS Verified Access
AWS Direct Connect

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Verified Access evaluates identity and device posture for each request to private apps.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Amazon CloudFront: CloudFront is a CDN.
• Amazon Route 53: Route 53 is DNS.
• AWS Direct Connect: Direct Connect is private connectivity.

Key takeaway: Zero-trust app access → Verified Access.

stem: Workforce users must sign in once with corporate credentials and MFA to access many AWS accounts. Which service fits?

choices.text: IAM users created in every account with the same password
AWS IAM Identity Center with an external identity provider
A shared root user login for each account's administrators
Amazon Cognito user pools for employee console access

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Identity Center federates with corporate IdPs for SSO and MFA across accounts.

Why the other options are wrong:
• IAM users created in every account with the…: Duplicate IAM users are hard to manage.
• A shared root user login for each account's…: Shared root logins are insecure.
• Amazon Cognito user pools for employee…: Cognito targets application users.

Key takeaway: Workforce SSO → IAM Identity Center.

stem: A mobile app must let users sign in with social providers and receive temporary AWS credentials scoped to their own data. Which combination fits?

choices.text: A single shared IAM role whose keys are embedded in the app
IAM users for each app user with long-term access keys
API keys generated per user and stored in DynamoDB tables
Cognito user pools with identity pools and IAM policy variables

explanation:
Why this is correct:
User pools authenticate users, and identity pools issue scoped temporary credentials.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A single shared IAM role whose keys are…: Embedded keys leak.
• IAM users for each app user with long-term…: IAM users do not scale to app users.
• API keys generated per user and stored in…: API keys are not AWS credentials.

Key takeaway: App users to AWS credentials → Cognito pools.

stem: A CI system outside AWS must deploy resources without long-term AWS access keys. Which approach fits?

choices.text: OIDC federation to an IAM role with a trust policy scoped to the repository
The root user's access keys stored as encrypted CI variables
A shared deployment IAM user used by all repositories
An IAM user's access keys stored in the CI system's own encrypted secret store

explanation:
Why this is correct:
OIDC federation provides short-lived credentials without stored keys.

Why the other options are wrong:
• The root user's access keys stored as…: Root keys must never be used.
• A shared deployment IAM user used by all…: Shared users violate least privilege.
• An IAM user's access keys stored in the CI…: Stored keys are long-term.

Key takeaway: Keyless CI with OIDC federation.

stem: On-premises servers need AWS API access without long-term keys. Which feature fits?

choices.text: Cognito user pools configured for server workloads
The EC2 instance metadata service reached over the internet
IAM Roles Anywhere with X.509 certificates from a trusted CA
IAM users with access keys rotated every year manually

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Roles Anywhere lets workloads outside AWS obtain temporary credentials using certificates.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Cognito user pools configured for server…: Cognito is for app users.
• The EC2 instance metadata service reached…: IMDS is not reachable from on-premises.
• IAM users with access keys rotated every…: Access keys are long-term.

Key takeaway: Temporary credentials for on-premises workloads → Roles Anywhere.

stem: Which TWO practices protect the root user of each account? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Share the root password with all administrators
Enable MFA and avoid daily use of the root user
Disable CloudTrail to hide root activity logs
Create access keys for automation using root
Delete root access keys and monitor root sign-ins

explanation:
Why this is correct:
MFA, no access keys, minimal use, and monitoring protect the root user.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Share the root password with all administrators: Sharing root credentials is dangerous.
• Disable CloudTrail to hide root activity logs: Disabling logs removes visibility.
• Create access keys for automation using root: Root keys must not be used for automation.

Key takeaway: Lock down and monitor the root user.

stem: Developers must create IAM roles for their apps but not grant more than a defined set of permissions. Which feature fits?

choices.text: A monthly review of roles by the security team
The AdministratorAccess policy attached to developers
Inline policies written by developers without any limits
Permissions boundaries required on developer-created roles

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Permissions boundaries cap the maximum permissions of roles developers create.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A monthly review of roles by the security team: Reviews detect late.
• The AdministratorAccess policy attached to…: Admin access defeats the goal.
• Inline policies written by developers…: Unlimited policies allow escalation.

Key takeaway: Cap delegated permissions with boundaries.

stem: An IAM identity policy allows s3:PutObject, but an SCP denies it for the account. What is the result?

choices.text: The request is denied because explicit denies override allows
The request is retried until one of the policies changes
The request is allowed only for the account's administrators
The request is allowed because identity policies take priority

explanation:
Why this is correct:
An explicit deny in any applicable policy overrides allows.

Why the other options are wrong:
• The request is retried until one of the…: Evaluation is deterministic.
• The request is allowed only for the…: Administrators are also bound by SCPs.
• The request is allowed because identity…: Identity policies do not override SCP denies.

Key takeaway: Explicit deny always wins.

stem: Access to resources must depend on matching project tags on both the user and the resource. Which approach fits?

choices.text: Attribute-based access control using aws:PrincipalTag and aws:ResourceTag conditions
Security groups that filter traffic based on project tags
A separate IAM policy for each user that lists every allowed resource ARN explicitly by hand
A public bucket per project with obscure bucket names

explanation:
Why this is correct:
ABAC grants access when principal and resource tags match, scaling without per-resource policies.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Security groups that filter traffic based on…: Security groups filter network traffic.
• A separate IAM policy for each user that…: Listing ARNs does not scale.
• A public bucket per project with obscure…: Public buckets are insecure.

Key takeaway: Scale permissions with ABAC tags.

stem: An application needs fine-grained authorization, such as 'managers can approve expenses in their department,' managed outside code. Which service fits?

choices.text: CloudFront geo restrictions per department
Network ACLs that filter requests by department
Amazon Verified Permissions with Cedar policies
IAM policies attached to each application end user

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Verified Permissions evaluates Cedar policies for application authorization.

Why the other options are wrong:
• CloudFront geo restrictions per department: Geo restrictions filter countries.
• Network ACLs that filter requests by department: NACLs filter network traffic.
• IAM policies attached to each application…: IAM is not designed for app end-user authorization.

Key takeaway: Externalize app authorization with Verified Permissions.

stem: A company wants to identify IAM roles and S3 buckets shared with principals outside its organization. Which service fits?

choices.text: AWS Trusted Advisor cost optimization checks for each account
Amazon Inspector vulnerability findings
AWS Budgets alerts per account
IAM Access Analyzer with the organization as the zone of trust

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Access Analyzer reports resources shared outside the zone of trust.

Why the other options are wrong:
• AWS Trusted Advisor cost optimization checks…: Cost checks do not analyze access.
• Amazon Inspector vulnerability findings: Inspector scans vulnerabilities.
• AWS Budgets alerts per account: Budgets track spend.

Key takeaway: Find external access with Access Analyzer.

stem: Which TWO features help move toward least privilege for existing roles? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Sharing one role among all applications in the account
IAM last accessed information for services and actions
Using wildcard actions for flexibility in policies
Attaching AdministratorAccess temporarily to all roles
Access Analyzer policy generation from CloudTrail activity

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Generated policies and last-accessed data show which permissions are actually needed.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Sharing one role among all applications in…: Shared roles grant excess.
• Using wildcard actions for flexibility in…: Wildcards grant excess.
• Attaching AdministratorAccess temporarily to…: Admin access is the opposite of least privilege.

Key takeaway: Refine permissions with usage data.

stem: A role in Account A must be assumed only by a specific role in Account B and only when an external ID is provided. Where is this enforced?

choices.text: In the permissions policy of an unrelated IAM user
In an S3 bucket policy attached to a bucket that lives in Account A
In the role's trust policy with the principal and sts:ExternalId condition
In a security group attached to the role's instances

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Trust policies control who can assume a role, including external ID conditions.

Why the other options are wrong:
• In the permissions policy of an unrelated…: Unrelated user policies do not affect trust.
• In an S3 bucket policy attached to a bucket…: Bucket policies control S3 access.
• In a security group attached to the role's…: Security groups do not control role assumption.

Key takeaway: Control role assumption with trust policies.

stem: An S3 bucket policy grants access to a role in another account, but requests are still denied. What else is required?

choices.text: The bucket must be made public so cross-account access works
The requester must use the root user of the other account
The bucket must use S3 Standard-IA storage before any cross-account access works
The other account's role must also have an identity policy allowing the action

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Cross-account access requires both the resource policy and the caller's identity policy to allow the action.

Why the other options are wrong:
• The bucket must be made public so…: Public access is not required.
• The requester must use the root user of the…: Root use is not required.
• The bucket must use S3 Standard-IA storage…: Storage class is unrelated.

Key takeaway: Cross-account access needs both sides to allow.

stem: Which TWO mechanisms provide temporary credentials to AWS workloads? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Root user access keys
Lambda execution roles
Hard-coded API keys
IAM user access keys
IAM roles for EC2 instance profiles

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Instance profiles and execution roles deliver temporary credentials automatically.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Root user access keys: Root keys are long-term and dangerous.
• Hard-coded API keys: Hard-coded keys are long-term.
• IAM user access keys: Access keys are long-term.

Key takeaway: Workloads should use roles for temporary credentials.

stem: Access to a sensitive S3 bucket must require that requests come from the company's organization only. Which condition key helps?

choices.text: aws:PrincipalOrgID in the bucket policy
aws:SourceIp listing all home IPs
s3:x-amz-acl set to public-read
aws:RequestedRegion for us-east-1

explanation:
Why this is correct:
aws:PrincipalOrgID restricts access to principals in the specified organization.

Why the other options are wrong:
• aws:SourceIp listing all home IPs: IP lists are brittle and not identity-based.
• s3:x-amz-acl set to public-read: Public-read grants access to everyone.
• aws:RequestedRegion for us-east-1: Region conditions do not restrict identities.

Key takeaway: Restrict to your organization with PrincipalOrgID.

stem: Temporary elevated access to production must be requested, approved, and expire automatically. Which approach fits?

choices.text: A shared break-glass password posted in the team chat channel
Permanent administrator access granted to every engineer in all of the production accounts
Just-in-time elevated access through IAM Identity Center with approvals and time limits
New IAM users created for each change and deleted when remembered

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Time-bound, approved elevation grants access only when needed.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A shared break-glass password posted in the…: Shared passwords are insecure.
• Permanent administrator access granted to…: Permanent admin violates least privilege.
• New IAM users created for each change and…: Manual user lifecycle is error-prone.

Key takeaway: Use just-in-time, expiring access.

stem: All client connections to an S3 bucket must use TLS. Which control enforces this?

choices.text: S3 Transfer Acceleration enabled for the bucket
S3 default encryption with SSE-S3 enabled on the bucket for all objects
S3 Versioning enabled with MFA Delete on the bucket
A bucket policy denying requests when aws:SecureTransport is false

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A SecureTransport condition rejects non-TLS requests.

Why the other options are wrong:
• S3 Transfer Acceleration enabled for the bucket: Acceleration speeds uploads.
• S3 default encryption with SSE-S3 enabled on…: Default encryption is at rest.
• S3 Versioning enabled with MFA Delete on the…: Versioning protects versions.

Key takeaway: Enforce TLS to S3 with SecureTransport conditions.

stem: Internal microservices need TLS certificates from a private hierarchy with automated renewal. Which TWO services help? (Select TWO)

choices.text: AWS Certificate Manager for issuing and renewing
Self-signed certificates copied manually
KMS keys used directly as certificates
Route 53 DNSSEC key signing keys
AWS Private Certificate Authority

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Private CA issues private certificates, and ACM manages issuance and renewal for integrated services.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Self-signed certificates copied manually: Manual self-signed certificates are hard to manage.
• KMS keys used directly as certificates: KMS keys are not certificates.
• Route 53 DNSSEC key signing keys: DNSSEC keys sign DNS.

Key takeaway: Private PKI → Private CA with ACM.

stem: Traffic from an ALB to backend targets must remain encrypted. Which configuration fits?

choices.text: An HTTP target group with a larger timeout
An HTTPS target group with TLS on the targets
A NAT gateway between the ALB and targets
A TCP listener on the ALB with no TLS

explanation:
Why this is correct:
HTTPS target groups re-encrypt traffic to targets.

Why the other options are wrong:
• An HTTP target group with a larger timeout: HTTP is unencrypted.
• A NAT gateway between the ALB and targets: NAT does not encrypt.
• A TCP listener on the ALB with no TLS: ALBs do not offer TCP listeners.

Key takeaway: Re-encrypt to backends for end-to-end TLS.

stem: Hybrid traffic over Direct Connect must be encrypted. Which TWO options fit? (Select TWO)

choices.text: A public VIF without any VPN
Jumbo frames on the private VIF
Site-to-Site VPN over Direct Connect
BGP communities on routes
MACsec on supported dedicated connections

explanation:
Why this is correct:
MACsec and VPN over DX provide encryption for hybrid traffic.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A public VIF without any VPN: A public VIF alone is not encrypted.
• Jumbo frames on the private VIF: MTU settings do not encrypt.
• BGP communities on routes: Communities influence routing.

Key takeaway: Encrypt DX with MACsec or VPN.

stem: Data at rest in S3 must be encrypted with keys the company controls and whose use is logged. Which option fits?

choices.text: SSE-KMS with a customer managed key
SSE-S3 with Amazon S3 managed keys
Client-side base64 encoding of objects
S3 Object Lock in governance mode

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Customer managed KMS keys provide control and CloudTrail logging of key use.

Why the other options are wrong:
• SSE-S3 with Amazon S3 managed keys: SSE-S3 keys are managed by S3.
• Client-side base64 encoding of objects: Base64 is not encryption.
• S3 Object Lock in governance mode: Object Lock prevents deletion.

Key takeaway: Controlled at-rest encryption → SSE-KMS with CMKs.

stem: An existing unencrypted RDS database must be encrypted. What is the correct approach?

choices.text: Increase the storage size to trigger automatic encryption
Snapshot, copy the snapshot with encryption enabled, and restore a new instance
Enable Multi-AZ, which encrypts the storage automatically
Enable encryption in place from the instance's modify settings in the console

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Encryption cannot be enabled in place; restoring from an encrypted snapshot copy creates an encrypted instance.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Increase the storage size to trigger…: Storage size does not encrypt.
• Enable Multi-AZ, which encrypts the storage…: Multi-AZ does not encrypt.
• Enable encryption in place from the…: In-place encryption is not supported.

Key takeaway: Encrypt existing RDS via encrypted snapshot copies.

stem: Backups must be protected from deletion, even by administrators, for a retention period. Which feature fits?

choices.text: S3 Intelligent-Tiering on backup data
EBS snapshots with a descriptive name
AWS Backup plans with short retention
AWS Backup Vault Lock in compliance mode

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Vault Lock in compliance mode prevents deletion or changes to retention.

Why the other options are wrong:
• S3 Intelligent-Tiering on backup data: Tiering changes cost.
• EBS snapshots with a descriptive name: Names do not protect.
• AWS Backup plans with short retention: Short retention does not prevent deletion.

Key takeaway: Immutable backups → Backup Vault Lock.

stem: Which TWO actions ensure all new EBS volumes and snapshots are encrypted? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Attach volumes only to large instance types
Rename volumes to include the word 'encrypted'
Disable snapshots for all volumes in the account
Enable EBS encryption by default in each Region
Use an SCP denying creation of unencrypted volumes

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Default encryption encrypts new volumes, and an SCP prevents exceptions.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Attach volumes only to large instance types: Instance size does not encrypt.
• Rename volumes to include the word 'encrypted': Names do not encrypt.
• Disable snapshots for all volumes in the account: Disabling snapshots harms recovery.

Key takeaway: Enforce EBS encryption by default and with SCPs.

stem: DynamoDB table data must be encrypted with a key the company manages and can audit. Which option fits?

choices.text: Customer managed KMS key for DynamoDB encryption at rest
DynamoDB TTL on every item in the table
DynamoDB Streams enabled on the table
Client-side base64 encoding of attribute values

explanation:
Why this is correct:
DynamoDB supports customer managed keys for encryption at rest with auditing.

Why the other options are wrong:
• DynamoDB TTL on every item in the table: TTL expires items.
• DynamoDB Streams enabled on the table: Streams capture changes.
• Client-side base64 encoding of attribute values: Base64 is not encryption.

Key takeaway: Customer-controlled DynamoDB encryption → CMK.

stem: Database credentials must be rotated automatically without application downtime. Which approach fits?

choices.text: Storing the password in environment variables
Secrets Manager rotation using the alternating users strategy
Manual password changes followed by application restarts
Hard-coding the password in the application

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Alternating users rotation keeps a valid credential available during rotation.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Storing the password in environment variables: Environment variables do not rotate.
• Manual password changes followed by…: Manual changes cause downtime.
• Hard-coding the password in the application: Hard-coding prevents rotation.

Key takeaway: Zero-downtime credential rotation with Secrets Manager.

stem: A KMS key must be usable by a role in another account for decryption only. Which TWO changes are required? (Select TWO)

choices.text: The external account receives the key's material
The key is converted into an AWS managed key
The external role's IAM policy allows kms:Decrypt on the key
The key is made public so any account can use it
The key policy grants kms:Decrypt to the external role

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Cross-account KMS use requires the key policy and the caller's IAM policy to allow the action.

Why the other options are wrong:
• The external account receives the key's material: Key material never leaves KMS.
• The key is converted into an AWS managed key: AWS managed keys cannot be shared cross-account.
• The key is made public so any account can use it: KMS keys cannot be made public this way and should not be.

Key takeaway: Cross-account KMS needs key policy and IAM policy.

stem: Regulations require encryption keys stored in single-tenant HSMs under exclusive customer control. Which option fits?

choices.text: SSE-S3 managed keys for all data
AWS managed KMS keys created by each service
Secrets Manager secrets for keys
AWS CloudHSM, or a KMS custom key store backed by CloudHSM

explanation:
Why this is correct:
CloudHSM provides dedicated HSMs under customer control.

Why the other options are wrong:
• SSE-S3 managed keys for all data: SSE-S3 keys are managed by AWS.
• AWS managed KMS keys created by each service: AWS managed keys are not exclusive.
• Secrets Manager secrets for keys: Secrets Manager stores secrets, not HSM keys.

Key takeaway: Dedicated HSM control → CloudHSM.

stem: A company wants to discover PII across S3 buckets in all accounts and route findings to Security Hub. Which setup fits?

choices.text: AWS Config rules checking bucket encryption settings only
Amazon Macie with a delegated administrator and Security Hub integration
Amazon Inspector with EC2 scanning enabled in every account
GuardDuty malware protection for EC2 volumes in all accounts

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Macie discovers sensitive data and publishes findings to Security Hub.

Why the other options are wrong:
• AWS Config rules checking bucket encryption…: Encryption checks do not find PII.
• Amazon Inspector with EC2 scanning enabled…: Inspector scans vulnerabilities.
• GuardDuty malware protection for EC2 volumes…: Malware protection scans volumes for malware.

Key takeaway: Organization-wide PII discovery → Macie.

stem: A Lambda function needs an API key at runtime, and the key must be rotated without redeploying. Which approach fits?

choices.text: Store the key in the function's description field
Email the key to the developers after rotation
Fetch the key from Secrets Manager at runtime with caching
Hard-code the key and redeploy after each rotation

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Runtime retrieval picks up rotated values without redeployment.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Store the key in the function's description…: Descriptions are not secret storage.
• Email the key to the developers after rotation: Emailing keys is insecure.
• Hard-code the key and redeploy after each…: Hard-coding requires redeploys.

Key takeaway: Fetch secrets at runtime.

stem: Data encrypted by an application must be decryptable only when the same tenant context is supplied. Which KMS feature fits?

choices.text: Encryption context
Grants only
Key rotation
Key aliases

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Encryption context binds additional authenticated data; decryption requires the same context.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Grants only: Grants delegate permissions but do not bind context to ciphertext.
• Key rotation: Rotation changes key material.
• Key aliases: Aliases are names.

Key takeaway: Bind ciphertext to context with encryption context.

stem: Which TWO practices reduce the risk of secrets leaking from source code? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Share secrets in team chat channels
Store secrets in Secrets Manager or Parameter Store
Commit .env files with credentials to the repository
Print secrets in build logs for debugging
Scan repositories and pipelines for secrets

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Secret scanning catches leaks, and managed secret stores keep secrets out of code.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Share secrets in team chat channels: Chat channels expose secrets.
• Commit .env files with credentials to the…: Committed credentials leak.
• Print secrets in build logs for debugging: Logs expose secrets.

Key takeaway: Scan for secrets and use secret stores.

stem: API traffic to a public API must use modern TLS versions only. Which setting helps?

choices.text: A usage plan with throttling settings
A request validator for the API body
A security policy on the custom domain enforcing TLS 1.2 or higher
A larger integration timeout configured on the API stage

explanation:
Why this is correct:
API Gateway custom domain security policies set minimum TLS versions.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A usage plan with throttling settings: Usage plans throttle.
• A request validator for the API body: Validators check requests.
• A larger integration timeout configured on…: Timeouts do not affect TLS.

Key takeaway: Enforce minimum TLS with security policies.

stem: A company wants a governed multi-account environment with guardrails and centralized logging from the start. Which service fits?

choices.text: AWS Control Tower
AWS Resource Groups
AWS Service Catalog
AWS Budgets

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Control Tower sets up a landing zone with guardrails and centralized logging.

Why the other options are wrong:
• AWS Resource Groups: Resource Groups organize resources.
• AWS Service Catalog: Service Catalog provides approved products.
• AWS Budgets: Budgets track spend.

Key takeaway: Governed landing zone → Control Tower.

stem: A company wants to prevent member accounts from disabling GuardDuty, Security Hub, or CloudTrail. Which control fits?

choices.text: CloudWatch dashboards of service status
A monthly audit report sent to account owners
IAM users with read-only access in each account
SCPs denying disable and delete actions for these services

explanation:
Why this is correct:
SCPs prevent member accounts from disabling security services.

Why the other options are wrong:
• CloudWatch dashboards of service status: Dashboards do not prevent.
• A monthly audit report sent to account owners: Reports detect after the fact.
• IAM users with read-only access in each account: Read-only users do not restrict admins.

Key takeaway: Protect security services with SCPs.

stem: Security services should be managed from a dedicated security account rather than the management account. Which feature fits?

choices.text: Delegated administrator for each security service
Root user sharing with the security team
Cross-account email notifications only
IAM users created in every member account

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Delegated administrators let a security account manage services organization-wide.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Root user sharing with the security team: Root sharing is insecure.
• Cross-account email notifications only: Emails do not delegate management.
• IAM users created in every member account: Per-account users are hard to manage.

Key takeaway: Delegate security administration to a dedicated account.

stem: A company must restrict all accounts to approved Regions, with an exception for global services. Which approach fits?

choices.text: A wiki page listing approved Regions for all engineers to follow
CloudTrail alerts sent whenever an unapproved Region is used
IAM policies in every account that are written independently and maintained by each account's own team
An SCP denying actions outside approved Regions using aws:RequestedRegion with exemptions for global services

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A Region-restriction SCP with exemptions for global services enforces approved Regions.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A wiki page listing approved Regions for all…: Documentation does not enforce.
• CloudTrail alerts sent whenever an…: Alerts detect but do not prevent.
• IAM policies in every account that are…: Independent policies drift.

Key takeaway: Restrict Regions with SCPs.

stem: Infrastructure templates must be checked for security misconfigurations before deployment. Which approach fits?

choices.text: Remove security requirements so that templates always pass
Run CloudFormation Guard or cfn-nag checks in the pipeline and fail on violations
Deploy first and let AWS Config detect any problems in production at a later time
Review templates manually only when an incident happens

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Policy-as-code checks prevent insecure infrastructure from deploying.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Remove security requirements so that…: Removing requirements weakens security.
• Deploy first and let AWS Config detect any…: Detecting after deployment allows exposure.
• Review templates manually only when an…: Reactive reviews are too late.

Key takeaway: Shift security left with policy-as-code.

stem: A pipeline must ensure only approved, tested artifacts reach production and record who approved them. Which TWO elements fit? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Deploying directly from laptops when the pipeline is slow
Disabling CloudTrail for the pipeline account to reduce cost
Pipeline execution history and CloudTrail records of approvals
Developers approving their own changes to save time
A manual approval action restricted to a security approver group

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Restricted approvals and recorded history provide separation of duties and evidence.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Deploying directly from laptops when the…: Laptop deploys bypass controls.
• Disabling CloudTrail for the pipeline…: Disabling CloudTrail removes evidence.
• Developers approving their own changes to…: Self-approval defeats separation of duties.

Key takeaway: Enforce and record deployment approvals.

stem: A company must continuously evaluate resources against rules such as 'EBS volumes must be encrypted' across all accounts. Which service fits?

choices.text: Amazon SQS dead-letter queues
AWS Trusted Advisor cost optimization checks
Amazon CloudFront access logs
AWS Config with organization rules or conformance packs

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Config evaluates resource configurations continuously against rules.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Amazon SQS dead-letter queues: DLQs hold failed messages.
• AWS Trusted Advisor cost optimization checks: Cost checks do not evaluate encryption rules.
• Amazon CloudFront access logs: CloudFront logs record requests.

Key takeaway: Continuous compliance evaluation → AWS Config.

stem: Auditors need AWS compliance reports such as SOC and ISO attestations. Where can the company download them?

choices.text: AWS Artifact
AWS Config
Amazon Inspector
AWS Audit Manager

explanation:
Why this is correct:
AWS Artifact provides AWS compliance reports and agreements.

Why the other options are wrong:
• AWS Config: Config evaluates resources.
• Amazon Inspector: Inspector scans vulnerabilities.
• AWS Audit Manager: Audit Manager collects the customer's own evidence.

Key takeaway: AWS compliance reports → AWS Artifact.

stem: A company wants to collect evidence continuously for its own compliance audits mapped to frameworks. Which service fits?

choices.text: Amazon Detective
AWS Audit Manager
AWS Artifact
AWS Shield

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Audit Manager automates evidence collection mapped to control frameworks.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Amazon Detective: Detective investigates.
• AWS Artifact: Artifact provides AWS's reports, not customer evidence.
• AWS Shield: Shield mitigates DDoS.

Key takeaway: Continuous audit evidence → Audit Manager.

stem: Which TWO actions help keep resources compliant after deployment? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Disabling Config to reduce recording costs
Granting everyone permission to change policies
Config rules with automatic remediation
Manual reviews once every two years
Security Hub standards with alerts on failed controls

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Automated remediation and continuous control checks keep resources compliant.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Disabling Config to reduce recording costs: Disabling Config removes visibility.
• Granting everyone permission to change policies: Broad permissions increase drift.
• Manual reviews once every two years: Rare reviews miss drift.

Key takeaway: Continuously detect and remediate drift.

stem: A company must ensure EC2 instances launch only from approved hardened AMIs. Which TWO controls help? (Select TWO)

choices.text: An email reminder to use approved AMIs each month
Disabling CloudTrail so AMI usage is not tracked
Tags added to instances after launch describing the AMI
IAM or SCP conditions restricting RunInstances to approved AMI IDs or owners
AWS Config rules detecting instances from unapproved AMIs

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Preventive conditions block unapproved launches, and Config detects exceptions.

Why the other options are wrong:
• An email reminder to use approved AMIs each…: Reminders do not enforce.
• Disabling CloudTrail so AMI usage is not tracked: Disabling CloudTrail removes auditing.
• Tags added to instances after launch…: Tags do not enforce.

Key takeaway: Enforce approved AMIs preventively and detectively.

stem: New accounts must receive baseline security configuration automatically. Which approach fits?

choices.text: A checklist followed manually by a security engineer
Control Tower Account Factory with customizations or StackSets auto-deployment
An email asking each owner to configure security
A single stack deployed only in the organization's management account

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Automated baselines apply security configuration to every new account.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A checklist followed manually by a security…: Manual checklists are inconsistent.
• An email asking each owner to configure security: Emails do not enforce.
• A single stack deployed only in the…: Management-only stacks do not reach members.

Key takeaway: Automate account security baselines.

stem: A company requires MFA for all IAM users before they can perform any action except managing their own MFA device. Which approach fits?

choices.text: A bucket policy on every S3 bucket requiring MFA for all object reads
An email sent to all users every month reminding them to enable MFA on their IAM user accounts
An IAM policy that denies actions when aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent is false, with MFA-management exceptions
A CloudWatch dashboard showing which IAM users have MFA devices assigned

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A conditional deny enforces MFA while allowing users to set up their MFA devices.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A bucket policy on every S3 bucket requiring…: Bucket policies cover only S3.
• An email sent to all users every month…: Reminders do not enforce.
• A CloudWatch dashboard showing which IAM…: Dashboards do not enforce.

Key takeaway: Enforce MFA with conditional deny policies.

stem: Users authenticated through SAML federation must have their corporate department passed to AWS for ABAC decisions. Which feature fits?

choices.text: Session tags passed in the SAML assertion
Resource tags on the SAML provider itself
Security group tags on the user's instance
IAM user tags set manually per account

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Session tags from the identity provider carry attributes into AWS sessions for ABAC.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Resource tags on the SAML provider itself: Provider tags do not describe users.
• Security group tags on the user's instance: Security group tags do not describe identities.
• IAM user tags set manually per account: Federated users are not IAM users.

Key takeaway: Pass identity attributes with session tags.

stem: A third-party SaaS vendor needs to assume a role in the company's account. How should the confused deputy problem be prevented?

choices.text: Grant the vendor's account full administrator access
Require a unique external ID in the role's trust policy
Share an IAM user's access keys with the vendor instead
Make the vendor's role assumable by any AWS principal

explanation:
Why this is correct:
An external ID condition ensures the vendor assumes the role only on behalf of this customer.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Grant the vendor's account full…: Admin access is excessive.
• Share an IAM user's access keys with the…: Shared keys are long-term credentials.
• Make the vendor's role assumable by any AWS…: Allowing any principal is dangerous.

Key takeaway: Prevent confused deputy with external IDs.

stem: A service principal such as SNS must publish to an SQS queue only on behalf of a specific topic. Which condition prevents cross-service confused deputy issues?

choices.text: aws:SecureTransport set to false in the queue policy
aws:RequestedRegion listing every Region in the policy
aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent for the service principal
aws:SourceArn (or aws:SourceAccount) in the queue policy

explanation:
Why this is correct:
SourceArn and SourceAccount conditions restrict service principals to acting for specific resources.

Why the other options are wrong:
• aws:SecureTransport set to false in the…: Allowing insecure transport is unrelated and weakens security.
• aws:RequestedRegion listing every Region in…: Region conditions do not bind resources.
• aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent for the service…: Service principals do not use MFA.

Key takeaway: Bind service principals with SourceArn conditions.

stem: Which TWO policy types can restrict the maximum permissions of a principal without granting permissions themselves? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Access control lists
Resource-based policies
Service control policies
Identity-based policies
Permissions boundaries

explanation:
Why this is correct:
SCPs and permissions boundaries set maximum permissions but do not grant access.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Access control lists: ACLs grant access to resources.
• Resource-based policies: Resource policies grant permissions.
• Identity-based policies: Identity policies grant permissions.

Key takeaway: SCPs and boundaries limit; other policies grant.

stem: EKS pods need AWS permissions scoped per Kubernetes service account. Which feature fits?

choices.text: EKS Pod Identity or IAM roles for service accounts
A single node instance role shared by every pod
The cluster creator's credentials inside each pod
IAM user access keys stored in Kubernetes secrets

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Pod Identity and IRSA map service accounts to IAM roles with scoped permissions.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A single node instance role shared by every pod: Node roles give all pods the same access.
• The cluster creator's credentials inside…: Creator credentials are overly privileged.
• IAM user access keys stored in Kubernetes…: Stored keys are long-term.

Key takeaway: Per-pod IAM on EKS → Pod Identity or IRSA.

stem: An organization wants to block all principals from outside the organization from accessing its resources, even if a resource policy is misconfigured. Which feature fits?

choices.text: Tag policies applied to every account in the organization
Resource control policies (RCPs) in AWS Organizations
Backup policies defining retention for every resource
AI services opt-out policies for the organization

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Resource control policies set organization-wide maximum permissions on resources, such as blocking external access.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Tag policies applied to every account in the…: Tag policies standardize tags.
• Backup policies defining retention for every…: Backup policies manage backups.
• AI services opt-out policies for the…: Opt-out policies control AI data use.

Key takeaway: Organization-wide resource guardrails → RCPs.

stem: A company must prevent deletion of compliance records in S3 by anyone, including the root user, for seven years. Which feature fits?

choices.text: S3 Lifecycle expiration rules
S3 Versioning without MFA Delete
S3 Object Lock in governance mode
S3 Object Lock in compliance mode

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Compliance mode prevents deletion by any user during the retention period.

Why the other options are wrong:
• S3 Lifecycle expiration rules: Expiration deletes objects.
• S3 Versioning without MFA Delete: Versions can still be deleted.
• S3 Object Lock in governance mode: Governance mode can be bypassed with permissions.

Key takeaway: Immutable records → Object Lock compliance mode.

stem: High-volume S3 uploads with SSE-KMS incur large KMS request costs. Which feature reduces them?

choices.text: S3 Bucket Keys
S3 Object Lambda
S3 Access Points
S3 Select queries

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Bucket Keys reduce KMS calls by using a bucket-level key.

Why the other options are wrong:
• S3 Object Lambda: Object Lambda transforms reads.
• S3 Access Points: Access Points manage access paths.
• S3 Select queries: S3 Select filters objects.

Key takeaway: Reduce KMS costs with S3 Bucket Keys.

stem: A company wants KMS key material generated outside AWS and imported, with the ability to delete it immediately if needed. Which option fits?

choices.text: AWS owned keys used by default
SSE-S3 managed keys for S3 only
Customer managed keys with imported key material
AWS managed keys created by each service

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Imported key material gives control over key origin and allows immediate deletion.

Why the other options are wrong:
• AWS owned keys used by default: AWS owned keys are not controlled by customers.
• SSE-S3 managed keys for S3 only: SSE-S3 keys are managed by S3.
• AWS managed keys created by each service: AWS managed keys are generated by AWS.

Key takeaway: Control key origin with imported key material.

stem: Which TWO actions reduce the risk of a KMS key being scheduled for deletion accidentally? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Store key IDs only in developers' notes
Use a waiting period of the minimum days only
Alarm on ScheduleKeyDeletion events from CloudTrail
Grant all developers kms:* on every key
Restrict kms:ScheduleKeyDeletion in key policies and SCPs

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Restricting deletion permissions and alerting on deletion requests prevent and detect accidents during the waiting period.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Store key IDs only in developers' notes: Notes do not protect keys.
• Use a waiting period of the minimum days only: Short waiting periods reduce reaction time.
• Grant all developers kms:* on every key: Broad permissions increase risk.

Key takeaway: Restrict and monitor key deletion.

stem: A company must encrypt data in transit between EC2 instances without changing applications, on supported instance types. Which fact applies?

choices.text: Encryption is enabled only when traffic goes through NAT
VPC traffic between instances is never encrypted, and no options exist for it
Encryption requires public IP addresses on both instances
Supported Nitro-based instances automatically encrypt traffic between them

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Certain Nitro-based instance types encrypt in-transit traffic between supported instances automatically.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Encryption is enabled only when traffic goes…: NAT does not encrypt.
• VPC traffic between instances is never…: Options exist.
• Encryption requires public IP addresses on…: Public IPs do not encrypt.

Key takeaway: Nitro instances can encrypt in transit automatically.

stem: Developers must deploy only approved, preconfigured infrastructure products that include security baselines. Which service fits?

choices.text: AWS Service Catalog with launch constraints
AWS Resource Groups with tags only
Amazon Route 53 with private zones
AWS Trusted Advisor with cost optimization checks

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Service Catalog provides approved products and launch constraints for governed self-service.

Why the other options are wrong:
• AWS Resource Groups with tags only: Resource Groups organize resources.
• Amazon Route 53 with private zones: Route 53 is DNS.
• AWS Trusted Advisor with cost optimization…: Trusted Advisor gives recommendations.

Key takeaway: Governed self-service → Service Catalog.

stem: A company must prove that controls in its AWS environment are operating over time for an auditor, using automated evidence. Which TWO services help? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Amazon Lightsail snapshots
AWS Config conformance packs
Amazon Polly speech output
AWS Artifact reports only
AWS Audit Manager assessments

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Audit Manager collects evidence mapped to frameworks, and Config conformance packs continuously evaluate controls.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Amazon Lightsail snapshots: Snapshots are backups.
• Amazon Polly speech output: Polly is speech synthesis.
• AWS Artifact reports only: Artifact provides AWS's own reports, not the customer's control evidence.

Key takeaway: Automate customer compliance evidence.
